prompt: Which tool turns a .java source file into a .class file?
optionA: javac
optionB: java
optionC: jar
optionD: jshell
correctAnswerText: javac
explanation: javac is the compiler; it writes bytecode into .class files. The java launcher then starts a JVM that runs them.

prompt: What does the JVM actually execute when you run a Java program?
optionA: The .java source, line by line
optionB: Native machine code from javac
optionC: An .exe built by the JDK linker
optionD: Bytecode from the .class files
correctAnswerText: Bytecode from the .class files
explanation: javac produces platform-neutral bytecode, and the JVM interprets or JIT-compiles that bytecode on whatever machine it runs on.

prompt: What does a JDK contain that a plain runtime (JRE) does not?
optionA: The garbage collector that frees the memory
optionB: Development tools such as the javac compiler
optionC: The JVM that executes the compiled bytecode
optionD: The core class library such as java.lang
correctAnswerText: Development tools such as the javac compiler
explanation: The JDK is the runtime plus development tools (javac, jar, javadoc, jdb). The JVM, class library and GC are already in the runtime.

prompt: How many bits does a Java int occupy, on every platform?
optionC: It depends on the OS
explanation: Java fixes primitive sizes in the language spec: int is always 32-bit signed, unlike C where it varies by platform.

prompt: What is the type of the literal 3.14 written with no suffix?
optionA: long
optionB: double
optionC: float
optionD: BigDecimal
correctAnswerText: double
explanation: A decimal literal with no suffix is a double. You need an f suffix (3.14f) to get a float.

prompt: Which suffix makes an integer literal a long, as in 5000000000?
optionA: I
optionB: F
optionC: L
optionD: D
correctAnswerText: L
explanation: An L suffix (uppercase is preferred, since lowercase l looks like 1) makes it a long literal; without it the literal is an int.

prompt: What does a Java char hold?
optionA: A 16-bit unsigned UTF-16 code unit
optionB: A one-letter String object reference
optionC: A 32-bit signed Unicode code point
optionD: An 8-bit signed ASCII byte value
correctAnswerText: A 16-bit unsigned UTF-16 code unit
explanation: char is a 16-bit unsigned integer type holding a UTF-16 code unit, which is why char arithmetic like c + 1 works.

prompt: Which class is commonly wrapped around System.in to read typed numbers and words?
optionA: java.util.Scanner
optionB: java.lang.System
optionC: java.io.PrintStream
optionD: java.util.Formatter
correctAnswerText: java.util.Scanner
explanation: new Scanner(System.in) tokenises standard input and offers nextInt, nextDouble, next and nextLine.

prompt: Where may the var keyword (Java 10 and later) be used to declare a variable?
optionA: Local variables that have an initialiser
optionB: Anywhere a primitive type is declared
optionC: Fields, parameters and local variables
optionD: Method return types and class fields
correctAnswerText: Local variables that have an initialiser
explanation: var is local variable type inference. It needs an initialiser to infer from and cannot be used for fields or method parameters.

prompt: Why can you use String without writing any import statement?
optionA: Every class in the JDK is visible by default
optionB: It is in java.lang, imported automatically
optionC: It is a primitive type built into the JVM
optionD: The compiler imports all of java.util
correctAnswerText: It is in java.lang, imported automatically
explanation: java.lang (String, Math, System, Integer…) is imported implicitly. String is a class, not a primitive.

prompt: A .class file compiled on Windows runs unchanged on Linux. What makes that possible?
optionA: Both systems share the same CPU instruction set
optionB: javac embeds machine code for every platform
optionC: Bytecode is neutral; each OS has its own JVM
optionD: Linux recompiles the .java file when it loads
correctAnswerText: Bytecode is neutral; each OS has its own JVM
explanation: The platform-specific part is the JVM, not the program. The same bytecode runs on any OS that has a JVM.

prompt: Why does int x = 3.5; fail to compile while double d = 3; compiles?
optionA: double to int may lose data, so it needs a cast
optionB: int cannot hold any value that has a decimal
optionC: double to int is a runtime error, not compile
optionD: Literals must always match the variable type
correctAnswerText: double to int may lose data, so it needs a cast
explanation: Widening (int to double) is automatic because nothing is lost; narrowing (double to int) may lose data, so Java demands an explicit cast.

prompt: Why is == the wrong way to check whether two Strings hold the same text?
optionA: It compares the lengths of the two strings
optionB: It always throws for objects created by new
optionC: It compares references, not the characters
optionD: It compares only the first character of each
correctAnswerText: It compares references, not the characters
explanation: == on objects asks "same object?". Two equal strings can be different objects, so use equals() to compare content.

prompt: Why does double avg = 7 / 2; store 3.0 rather than 3.5?
optionA: The / operator truncates for every number type
optionB: 7 / 2 is int division, done before the widening
optionC: double cannot represent the value 3.5 exactly
optionD: Assignment to double always rounds down values
correctAnswerText: 7 / 2 is int division, done before the widening
explanation: Both operands are int, so the division is int division (3); only then is 3 widened to 3.0. Write 7 / 2.0 or cast an operand.

prompt: byte b = 10; b = b + 1; does not compile. Why?
optionA: byte values cannot be used with the + operator
optionB: A byte variable cannot be reassigned once set
optionC: The literal 1 is a long, so the sum is a long
optionD: b + 1 is promoted to int, which needs a cast back
correctAnswerText: b + 1 is promoted to int, which needs a cast back
explanation: Arithmetic on byte, short and char is done in int. Assigning that int back to a byte is narrowing, so it needs (byte).

prompt: byte b = 10; b += 1; compiles even though b = b + 1; does not. Why?
optionA: The += operator works only on the byte type
optionB: Compound assignment includes an implicit cast
optionC: The compiler treats b += 1 as b = 11 directly
optionD: b += 1 is checked only when the program runs
correctAnswerText: Compound assignment includes an implicit cast
explanation: b += 1 means b = (byte)(b + 1). The hidden cast is convenient, and also why b += 1 on 127 silently wraps to -128.

prompt: Calling name.toUpperCase(); on its own line leaves name unchanged. Why?
optionA: It modifies a copy stored in the string pool
optionB: toUpperCase only works on string literals
optionC: The change is applied lazily on the next read
optionD: Strings are immutable; it returns a new String
correctAnswerText: Strings are immutable; it returns a new String
explanation: No String method changes the original. The upper-case version is returned and must be assigned: name = name.toUpperCase();

prompt: Why does nextLine() often return an empty string right after nextInt()?
optionA: nextLine skips the first line of every input
optionB: nextInt closes the Scanner once it is done
optionC: Scanner needs a reset() between the two calls
optionD: nextInt leaves the newline unread in the input
correctAnswerText: nextInt leaves the newline unread in the input
explanation: nextInt consumes the digits but not the Enter that followed. nextLine then reads up to that newline and returns "". Call nextLine() once to discard it.

prompt: Why is var x; followed later by x = 5; rejected by the compiler?
optionA: var declarations must be marked as final
optionB: var variables can never be assigned again
optionC: The type is inferred from the initialiser only
optionD: var may hold only objects, never an int value
correctAnswerText: The type is inferred from the initialiser only
explanation: var fixes the type at the declaration, from the expression on its right. With no initialiser there is nothing to infer from.

prompt: Why does float rate = 1.5; fail to compile?
optionA: 1.5 is too large for the float range
optionB: 1.5 is a double, and double to float narrows
optionC: float variables must be declared as final
optionD: float cannot store any fractional values
correctAnswerText: 1.5 is a double, and double to float narrows
explanation: Unsuffixed decimal literals are double. Narrowing to float needs 1.5f or an explicit (float) cast.

prompt:
What does this print?
System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5);
explanation: + is evaluated left to right: 1 + 2 = 3 (int), then 3 + "3" = "33", and from there each + is concatenation: "334", "3345".
a++ yields 5 then a becomes 6; ++a makes a 7 and yields 7. So b = 5 + 7 = 12 and a ends at 7.
Casting a double to int truncates toward zero; it does not round. Use Math.round if rounding is what you want.

prompt:
What does this print?
System.out.println(10 / 4 * 2.0);
explanation: / and * are left-associative: 10 / 4 is int division (2), then 2 * 2.0 is 4.0. The double arrives too late to save the division.

optionB: B
optionD: C
correctAnswerText: C
explanation: c += 2 adds 2 to the code of A (65) and casts back to char, giving 67, which prints as the character C.

prompt:
What does this print?
System.out.println('A' + 1);
optionB: A1
optionD: B
explanation: char + int is promoted to int, so the result is 65 + 1 = 66 and println(int) prints the number. Contrast with c += 1, which casts back.

prompt:
What does this print?
System.out.println(17 % 5 + " " + (-17 % 5));
explanation: Java's % takes the sign of the left operand: -17 = -3 * 5 + (-2). That is why n % 2 == 1 misses negative odd numbers.
concat returns a new String that is thrown away; s still refers to "Java", whose length is 4.
x *= expr means x = x * (expr). The whole right side 2 + 3 is evaluated first, so x = 7 * 5 = 35.

prompt:
What does this print?
System.out.println(3 + 4 * 2 - 6 / 4);
explanation: * and / bind first: 4 * 2 = 8 and 6 / 4 = 1 (int division). Then 3 + 8 - 1 = 10.

prompt: long big = 3000000000; fails to compile with "integer number too large". What is wrong?
optionA: A long must be assigned with new Long(...)
optionB: The literal is an int and exceeds the int range
optionC: long cannot hold a value as large as three billion
optionD: Large literals must be written with underscores
correctAnswerText: The literal is an int and exceeds the int range
explanation: The literal is typed before assignment, and an unsuffixed integer literal is an int (max about 2.1 billion). Write 3000000000L.

optionA: long is too small to hold eighty-six billion
optionB: println truncates long values to nine digits
optionC: Multiplying five literals loses the high bits
optionD: The product overflows int before it is widened
correctAnswerText: The product overflows int before it is widened
explanation: Every operand is an int, so the multiplication is done in int and wraps around; only the wrapped result is widened to long. Make one operand 24L.

optionA: false then false
optionB: true then false
optionC: false then true
optionD: true then true
correctAnswerText: false then true
explanation: new String creates a distinct object, so == (identity) is false; equals compares the characters, so it is true.

optionA: Create a second Scanner for the name
optionB: Call sc.close() before reading the name
optionC: Call sc.nextLine() once after nextInt()
optionD: Use sc.next() instead of sc.nextInt()
correctAnswerText: Call sc.nextLine() once after nextInt()
explanation: The Enter after 21 is still in the buffer; nextLine consumes just that. Discard it with an extra nextLine() (or read every line with nextLine and parse).

optionA: Binary doubles cannot hold 0.1 exactly
optionB: The sum is computed as float, then widened
optionC: Literal 0.3 is rounded to 0 by the compiler
optionD: The == operator is not defined for double
correctAnswerText: Binary doubles cannot hold 0.1 exactly
explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form; their sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare doubles with a tolerance, or use BigDecimal.

optionA: Line 1: an int literal cannot be put in a char
optionB: Line 2: c + 1 is a non-constant int expression
optionC: Neither line fails; both values are in range
optionD: Both lines: char only accepts quoted literals
correctAnswerText: Line 2: c + 1 is a non-constant int expression
explanation: A constant int that fits (97) may be assigned to a char. c + 1 is an int computed from a variable, so narrowing it to char needs a cast.

optionA: short variables cannot hold negative values
optionB: Unary minus promotes s to int before negating
optionC: Negation of a short is only legal on a literal
optionD: A variable may not appear on both sides of =
correctAnswerText: Unary minus promotes s to int before negating
explanation: Unary numeric promotion turns short into int, so -s is an int; assigning it back to short needs (short).

optionA: 127, because the cast clamps to the maximum
optionB: 200, because the cast leaves the value as is
optionC: -56, because only the low 8 bits are kept
optionD: Nothing; it throws an overflow exception
correctAnswerText: -56, because only the low 8 bits are kept
explanation: A narrowing cast keeps the low 8 bits. 200 is 11001000 in binary, which as a signed byte is 200 - 256 = -56. Java never clamps or throws here.

optionA: int cannot be converted to boolean
optionB: x is reassigned, so a warning is shown
optionC: Missing return statement in method main
optionD: It compiles and prints five as expected
correctAnswerText: int cannot be converted to boolean
explanation: x = 5 is an assignment whose value is the int 5. Java (unlike C) requires a boolean condition, so the typo is caught at compile time.

optionA: var variables are final once they are set
optionB: var can only be assigned values of type String
optionC: count was inferred as int; 2.5 would be lossy
optionD: A var must be reassigned with the var keyword
correctAnswerText: count was inferred as int; 2.5 would be lossy
explanation: var is static typing with inference: count is an int forever. Assigning a double would narrow, which is a compile error.

prompt: A team debates var. Which use of it is the best judgement?
optionA: var map = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();
optionB: var x = 0; used as a long counter of bytes read
optionC: var result = service.process(input, flags);
optionD: var everywhere, so that types never need writing
correctAnswerText: var map = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();
explanation: var helps when the type is obvious from the right-hand side. It hurts when it hides an unknown return type, or infers int where long was needed.

prompt: A fee-payment module stores amounts in rupees and paise. Which representation is the sound choice?
optionA: double, rounded when the value is printed
optionB: float, since it uses less memory than double
optionC: int rupees, dropping paise to keep it simple
optionD: BigDecimal, or a long count of paise
correctAnswerText: BigDecimal, or a long count of paise
explanation: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions, and errors accumulate across sums. Money needs exact decimal arithmetic.

prompt: A field holds System.currentTimeMillis() values. A reviewer suggests int to save memory. Best response?
optionA: Use double, so the field can never overflow at all
optionB: Use int: four bytes saved per field is worth it
optionC: Use short, and store the time in minutes instead
optionD: Keep long: millisecond times exceed the int range
correctAnswerText: Keep long: millisecond times exceed the int range
explanation: Epoch milliseconds are around 1.7 trillion; int tops out near 2.1 billion. The four bytes are not worth silent overflow.

prompt: A loop appends 10,000 roll numbers into one report string with s = s + roll;. What is the better approach?
optionA: Keep s = s + roll; the JIT removes all copying
optionB: Use s.concat(roll) since it edits s in place
optionC: Store the text in a char variable to save space
optionD: Append to one StringBuilder, then call toString
correctAnswerText: Append to one StringBuilder, then call toString
explanation: Each s + roll builds a new String and copies everything so far, which is quadratic. A StringBuilder grows one buffer.

prompt: A contest problem reads a million integers and Scanner times out. Which change is best?
optionA: Read all input with System.in.read() per byte
optionB: Read lines with BufferedReader and parse them
optionC: Increase the JVM heap so Scanner runs faster
optionD: Call nextInt in a tighter loop with fewer vars
correctAnswerText: Read lines with BufferedReader and parse them
explanation: Scanner is convenient but slow (regex-based tokenising). BufferedReader with Integer.parseInt or a StringTokenizer is the usual fast path.

prompt: An average of 79.6 must be shown as a whole-number score. Which conversion is the right choice?
optionA: (int) (avg + 1), which gives 80
optionB: Math.round(avg), which gives 80
optionC: (byte) avg, which gives 79
optionD: (int) avg, which gives 79
correctAnswerText: Math.round(avg), which gives 80
explanation: A cast truncates, so (int) 79.6 is 79; adding 1 breaks exact whole numbers. Math.round rounds to nearest, which is what a score needs.

prompt: A student record has a marks field that may be "not yet entered". int or Integer?
optionA: int, using -1 and a comment to explain it
optionB: double, so NaN can mean not entered
optionC: Integer, so null can mean not entered
optionD: int, since 0 can mean not entered
correctAnswerText: Integer, so null can mean not entered
explanation: A real score can be 0, so 0 is ambiguous; magic -1 is easy to forget. Integer makes absence explicit (and code must handle null).

prompt: The number 18 (minimum age) appears in six places in a codebase. What is the best change?
optionA: static final int MIN_AGE = 18; used everywhere
optionB: A comment beside each 18 saying it is the age
optionC: Leave it; literals are faster than any field
optionD: A static int field that any class may update
correctAnswerText: static final int MIN_AGE = 18; used everywhere
explanation: A named static final constant documents intent and changes in one place. A mutable static invites accidental edits, and the compiler inlines constants anyway.

prompt: A reviewer wants float instead of double for a dozen local variables in a GPA calculation "to save memory". Is it worth it?
optionA: Yes: float is always faster on modern CPUs
optionB: Yes: float is exact where double is not
optionC: No: float cannot store any values below 1
optionD: No: the saving is trivial and precision drops
correctAnswerText: No: the saving is trivial and precision drops
explanation: float keeps about 7 significant digits versus about 15 for double. For a few locals the memory saving is negligible, so double is the sensible default.

prompt: Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b is true, but with 128 it is false. What rule should a team adopt?
optionA: Compare wrapper objects with equals(), never ==
optionB: Raise the Integer cache size in JVM options
optionC: Use == only for values below 128 to be safe
optionD: Always compare wrappers using their hashCode
correctAnswerText: Compare wrapper objects with equals(), never ==
explanation: Integer.valueOf caches -128..127, so == accidentally works for small values. Code that relies on that breaks on real data; equals (or unboxing) is always correct.

prompt: Which statement leaves the innermost enclosing loop immediately?
optionA: continue
optionB: yield
optionC: break
optionD: return 0
correctAnswerText: break
explanation: break ends the innermost loop (or switch) and execution continues after it. continue only ends the current iteration.

prompt: What does continue do inside a loop body?
optionA: Skips the rest of this iteration only
optionB: Ends the loop and runs the next statement
optionC: Pauses the loop until input is received
optionD: Restarts the loop from its first iteration
correctAnswerText: Skips the rest of this iteration only
explanation: continue jumps to the next iteration (in a for loop, via the update expression); the loop itself carries on.

prompt: Which Java loop always runs its body at least once?
optionA: do-while
optionB: enhanced for
optionC: while
optionD: for
correctAnswerText: do-while
explanation: do-while tests its condition after the body, so the body runs once even if the condition is false from the start.

prompt: From which Java version are switch expressions with case X -> labels a standard feature?
optionA: Java 21
optionB: Java 11
optionC: Java 8
optionD: Java 14
correctAnswerText: Java 14
explanation: Switch expressions and arrow labels were previewed in 12 and 13 and became standard in Java 14, so Java 17 has them.

prompt: Inside a block { … } in a switch expression, which keyword hands back the value?
optionA: yield
optionB: break
optionC: return
optionD: emit
correctAnswerText: yield
explanation: yield gives the switch expression its value from a block. return would try to leave the enclosing method.

prompt: The enhanced for loop for (T x : source) accepts which kinds of source?
optionA: Any object that has a size() method
optionB: Only java.util collections, not arrays
optionC: Only arrays of primitive element types
optionD: Arrays and any Iterable such as a List
correctAnswerText: Arrays and any Iterable such as a List
explanation: for-each works on arrays and on anything implementing Iterable (List, Set and so on).

prompt: With outer: written before an outer loop, what does break outer; do inside an inner loop?
optionA: Exits the loop labelled outer entirely
optionB: Skips one iteration of the outer loop
optionC: Jumps back to the line labelled outer
optionD: Exits only the inner loop it appears in
correctAnswerText: Exits the loop labelled outer entirely
explanation: A labelled break ends the loop carrying that label, however deeply nested the break is. It is not a goto.

prompt: In Java 17, which of these selector types can a switch NOT be used on?
optionA: an enum
optionB: long
optionC: String
optionD: char
correctAnswerText: long
explanation: Java 17 switches on int-compatible types (byte, short, char, int), their wrappers, String and enums. long, float, double and boolean are not allowed.

prompt: Which is the correct form of Java's conditional (ternary) operator?
optionA: if condition then valueA else valueB
optionB: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
optionC: condition ?? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
optionD: condition : valueIfTrue ? valueIfFalse
correctAnswerText: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
explanation: cond ? a : b evaluates to a when cond is true and b otherwise. It is an expression, so it can sit on the right of =.

prompt: When does the default branch of a switch run?
optionA: When no case label matches the selector
optionB: Always, after the matching case finishes
optionC: Before any case label is checked at all
optionD: Only when the selector value is null
correctAnswerText: When no case label matches the selector
explanation: default is the catch-all for unmatched values. (A null selector throws NullPointerException in Java 17; default does not catch it.)

prompt: In a classic case X: switch, what happens when a matching case has no break?
optionA: The default branch is run straight after it
optionB: The switch exits silently after that case
optionC: Execution runs on into the next case body
optionD: The compiler rejects the switch statement
correctAnswerText: Execution runs on into the next case body
explanation: Colon-style cases fall through: once a label matches, statements run until a break or the end of the switch, ignoring later labels.

prompt: Why does an arrow-style case X -> switch not need break statements?
optionA: Only the matched arrow's body runs; no fall-through
optionB: Arrow cases can only contain a single expression
optionC: The compiler inserts a break before every case
optionD: It still falls through, but only into the default
correctAnswerText: Only the matched arrow's body runs; no fall-through
explanation: Arrow labels run exactly the code to the right of the matching arrow. Several values share a branch with case 1, 2 -> instead of fall-through.

prompt: Why must a switch expression on a String always have a default branch?
optionA: It must yield a value for every possible input
optionB: Switch expressions need at least three cases
optionC: Strings cannot be compared without a default
optionD: default is needed to catch a null selector
correctAnswerText: It must yield a value for every possible input
explanation: An expression must produce a value. Cases can never list every String, so default is required. An enum switch can be exhaustive by covering all constants.

prompt: What is the real difference between while (c) { … } and do { … } while (c);?
optionA: while allows break, but do-while does not allow it
optionB: do-while repeats until the condition becomes true
optionC: Where the test happens: before or after the body
optionD: do-while can only be used with a counter variable
correctAnswerText: Where the test happens: before or after the body
explanation: while tests first and may run zero times; do-while tests after and runs at least once. Both repeat while the condition is true.

prompt: Why is for (;;) { … } an infinite loop?
optionA: Its counter starts at an undefined value
optionB: A missing condition is treated as true
optionC: It runs until the stack runs out of space
optionD: The empty header is a compiler shortcut
correctAnswerText: A missing condition is treated as true
explanation: All three parts of a for header are optional; an omitted condition counts as true. Only break, return or an exception ends it.

prompt: Why is if (s != null && s.length() > 0) safe when s is null?
optionA: && checks both sides and catches the exception
optionB: length() returns 0 when called on a null value
optionC: The compiler removes the call when s is null
optionD: && skips the right side once the left is false
correctAnswerText: && skips the right side once the left is false
explanation: && short-circuits: if s != null is false, s.length() is never evaluated. With & both sides run and it would throw.

prompt: Why can continue safely be used in a for loop but easily hang a while loop?
optionA: In a for loop it still runs the update i++
optionB: while loops restart their counter on continue
optionC: A for loop ignores continue for its last pass
optionD: continue is not permitted inside while loops
correctAnswerText: In a for loop it still runs the update i++
explanation: In a for loop, continue jumps to the update expression. In a while loop the increment is in the body, so continue can skip it forever.

prompt:
if (a) if (b) x(); else y();
With no braces, which if does the else belong to?
optionA: The nearest one, if (b)
optionB: Neither; it will not compile
optionC: The outer one, if (a)
optionD: Both of them at the same time
correctAnswerText: The nearest one, if (b)
explanation: An else binds to the nearest unmatched if, whatever the indentation suggests. Braces remove the ambiguity.

prompt: A variable i declared in for (int i = 0; …) is used after the loop ends. What happens?
optionA: It throws an exception when it is read
optionB: It holds 0, its value before the loop
optionC: Compile error: i is out of scope there
optionD: It holds the value that ended the loop
correctAnswerText: Compile error: i is out of scope there
explanation: A variable declared in the for header exists only in the loop. Declare it before the loop if its final value is needed.

prompt: Why does the block after if (marks > 90); { … } run no matter what marks is?
optionA: Blocks after an if always run at least once
optionB: The ; is the if's empty body; the block is separate
optionC: A semicolon turns the condition into true
optionD: Java evaluates the block before testing the if
correctAnswerText: The ; is the if's empty body; the block is separate
explanation: The semicolon is an empty statement that the if controls. The braces that follow are just an ordinary block that always runs.

prompt: Which loop header prints exactly 5 4 3 2 1 when the body is print(i + " ")?
optionA: for (int i = 4; i >= 0; i--)
optionB: for (int i = 5; i > 0; i--)
optionC: for (int i = 5; i > 1; i--)

optionB: i % 2 == 0 is never true for the value 0
optionC: while loops cannot contain a continue
optionD: At i = 0, continue skips i++ every time
correctAnswerText: At i = 0, continue skips i++ every time
explanation: i starts even, so continue jumps straight back to the test and i++ is never reached; i stays 0 forever.

optionA: b++ is not allowed on a byte, so b never changes
optionB: A byte counter cannot be compared against an int
optionC: byte wraps from 127 to -128, so b < 200 stays true
optionD: The literal 200 is narrowed to a byte, giving -56
correctAnswerText: byte wraps from 127 to -128, so b < 200 stays true
explanation: b is promoted to int for the comparison, but b itself can never exceed 127; b++ wraps it to -128 and the condition is always true.

optionA: No break, so later cases overwrite msg
optionB: The case labels need double quotes, not single
optionC: Assignments inside a case are discarded
optionD: char selectors always reach the default
correctAnswerText: No break, so later cases overwrite msg
explanation: Case A matches and then falls through B and default, each assignment replacing the last. Add break, or rewrite with arrow labels.

optionA: big, because the block is not part of the if
optionB: Nothing, because 2 is not greater than 5
optionC: big twice, once for the if and once for the block
optionD: Nothing; the code fails with a compile error
correctAnswerText: big, because the block is not part of the if
explanation: The ; after the condition is the if's whole body. The following block is unconditional, so "big" prints once.

prompt:
for (double d = 0; d != 1.0; d += 0.1) { … }
This runs forever. What is the fix?
optionA: Use d += 0.10 so the step is exact

correctAnswerText: Use an int counter, or test d < 1.0

correctAnswerText: The switch expression does not cover all inputs
explanation: A switch expression must be exhaustive. With String cases you need a default branch; the compiler refuses otherwise.

prompt: A String read from a form is null, and a classic switch on it has a default branch. What happens in Java 17?

correctAnswerText: It throws NullPointerException at the switch
explanation: Before pattern-matching switch (Java 21), switching on null throws NPE before any label is tested. Check for null first.

optionB: i < n stops before adding n; use i <= n

correctAnswerText: i < n stops before adding n; use i <= n

optionC: A while loop must have more than one statement

prompt: An enum OrderStatus is mapped to display text. New statuses get added every few months. Which form is best?
optionA: An if-else chain comparing each constant with ==
optionB: A switch expression covering every constant, no default
optionC: A classic switch with breaks and a default branch
optionD: A switch expression with a default returning ""
correctAnswerText: A switch expression covering every constant, no default
explanation: An exhaustive switch expression over an enum makes the compiler flag every place a new constant is unhandled. A default silently swallows it.

prompt: A search over a 2D grid uses break outer; once a seat is found. A reviewer wants it changed. Best alternative?
optionA: Use a boolean flag tested in both loop conditions
optionB: Move the loops into a method that returns on a hit
optionC: Throw an exception when found and catch it outside
optionD: Keep scanning the whole grid and ignore later hits
correctAnswerText: Move the loops into a method that returns on a hit
explanation: A small method like findSeat that returns the result states the exit plainly and is testable. Flags add noise; exceptions for control flow are slow and misleading.

prompt: You must double every value in an int[] in place. Which loop is the right choice?
optionA: A while loop over a copy of the array
optionB: An index loop, assigning a[i] = a[i] * 2
optionC: A do-while loop, so the first runs once
optionD: A for-each loop, assigning x = x * 2
correctAnswerText: An index loop, assigning a[i] = a[i] * 2
explanation: The for-each variable is a copy of each element, so assigning to it changes nothing. Writing back needs the index.

prompt: A program reads marks until the user types -1. When is while (true) with one break a reasonable shape?
optionA: When the exit test falls mid-body after the read
optionB: Never; while (true) is always a design mistake
optionC: Only when it is guaranteed to run fewer than 10 times
optionD: Only when the loop also has several continues
correctAnswerText: When the exit test falls mid-body after the read
explanation: Read, test for the sentinel, then process: the natural exit is in the middle, and a single clearly placed break expresses it honestly.

prompt: A method nests four ifs deep to validate input before doing its work. What is the cleaner structure?
optionA: A switch statement on the number of checks passed
optionB: Guard clauses that return early on each failure
optionC: One giant condition joined with && and ||
optionD: A labelled block exited by break on any failure
correctAnswerText: Guard clauses that return early on each failure
explanation: Early returns for invalid cases flatten the method so the main work sits at the top level, and each rule reads on its own line.

prompt: A switch on a semester number 1–8 has a default for "impossible" values. What should that default do?
optionA: Throw an IllegalArgumentException naming the value
optionB: Return 0 so the caller can carry on as normal
optionC: Do nothing, since the case cannot happen
optionD: Print a warning and return the first semester
correctAnswerText: Throw an IllegalArgumentException naming the value
explanation: An "impossible" value means a bug upstream. Failing loudly with the bad value exposes it; a quiet fallback hides wrong data.

prompt: A console menu must show, read a choice, and repeat until the user picks Exit. Which loop fits best?
optionA: A recursive call to the menu method each time
optionB: while (false), with the body copied above it
optionC: do-while, since the menu must show at least once
optionD: for, with a fixed count of how many choices exist
correctAnswerText: do-while, since the menu must show at least once
explanation: The body must run before the condition means anything, which is exactly do-while. Recursion grows the stack with every choice.

optionA: No: logged-in non-admins would get the login page
optionB: Yes, as long as braces are added around each call
optionC: No: logged-in admins would now get the user page
optionD: Yes: the two versions behave in exactly the same way
correctAnswerText: No: logged-in non-admins would get the login page
explanation: Nesting was justified because the inner else (showUser) had its own meaning. Merging sends every case where either test fails to showLogin.

prompt: A loop must visit the rates 0.0, 0.1, 0.2 … 2.0, twenty-one values in all. Which design is most reliable?
optionA: Loop an int k from 0 to 20 and use rate = k / 10.0
optionB: Loop a float from 0.0f while rate <= 2.0f, adding 0.1f
optionC: Loop a double from 0.0 while rate != 2.0, adding 0.1
optionD: Loop a double adding 0.1, rounding it after each pass
correctAnswerText: Loop an int k from 0 to 20 and use rate = k / 10.0
explanation: An integer counter gives an exact number of iterations; the rate is derived each pass. Adding 0.1 drifts: the double never equals 2.0 exactly and the float version stops at 1.9000003, one value short.

prompt: Days 6 and 7 should both map to "weekend". Which is the best way to express that in Java 17?
optionA: Two separate cases, each returning "weekend"
optionB: case 6: with no break, falling into case 7:
optionC: An if before the switch that handles 6 and 7
optionD: case 6, 7 -> "weekend" in an arrow switch
correctAnswerText: case 6, 7 -> "weekend" in an arrow switch
explanation: Grouped labels state the intent directly. Deliberate fall-through works but reads exactly like a forgotten break.

prompt: What does each element of new int[5] hold before anything is assigned?
optionA: Garbage left in memory
optionB: null
explanation: Array elements are always initialised to their type's default: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for references.

prompt: What does each element of new String[3] hold right after creation?
optionA: null
optionD: "null"
correctAnswerText: null
explanation: An array of references starts filled with null. No String objects are created until you assign them.

prompt: How do you get the number of elements in an array named marks?
optionA: marks.length
optionB: marks.length()
optionC: marks.size()
optionD: marks.count
correctAnswerText: marks.length
explanation: length is a final field on arrays, written without parentheses. String uses length(), and collections use size().

prompt: For an array a with 10 elements, what are the first and last valid indexes?
optionA: 0 and 10
optionB: 0 and 9
optionC: 1 and 9
optionD: 1 and 10
correctAnswerText: 0 and 9
explanation: Indexes run from 0 to length - 1. Index 10 would be one past the end.

prompt: Which exception is thrown when code reads a[a.length]?
optionA: IllegalArgumentException
optionB: NullPointerException
optionC: NegativeArraySizeException
optionD: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
correctAnswerText: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
explanation: Every array access is bounds-checked at run time; an index below 0 or at/after length throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

prompt: Which call turns int[] a = {1, 2} into the text "[1, 2]"?
optionA: String.valueOf(a)
optionB: Arrays.asString(a)
optionC: a.toString()
optionD: Arrays.toString(a)
correctAnswerText: Arrays.toString(a)
explanation: java.util.Arrays.toString formats the elements. An array's own toString gives a type-and-hash string such as [I@1b6d3586.

prompt: What does Arrays.sort(nums) do to an int[] named nums?
optionA: Sorts nums itself into descending order
optionB: Returns true if nums was already sorted
optionC: Sorts nums itself into ascending order
optionD: Returns a sorted copy, nums is unchanged
correctAnswerText: Sorts nums itself into ascending order
explanation: Arrays.sort is void and sorts in place, ascending. Copy first if the original order still matters.

prompt: Once new int[5] has been created, can that array object grow to six elements?
optionA: Yes; assigning a[5] extends it by one
optionB: Yes; calling a.resize(6) changes its size
optionC: No; its length is fixed for its lifetime
optionD: Only if the array was declared as final
correctAnswerText: No; its length is fixed for its lifetime
explanation: Array length is set at creation. "Growing" means creating a bigger array and copying, which is what Arrays.copyOf and ArrayList do.

prompt: For int[][] grid = new int[3][4];, what are grid.length and grid[0].length?
optionA: 12 and 4
optionB: 3 and 12
optionC: 4 and 3
optionD: 3 and 4
correctAnswerText: 3 and 4
explanation: A 2D array is an array of rows: grid.length is the row count (3) and grid[0].length is the length of the first row (4).

prompt: What does Arrays.copyOf(a, n) return when n is larger than a.length?
optionA: A new array of length n, padded with defaults
optionB: Nothing; it throws an out-of-bounds error
optionC: The same array a, extended to length n
optionD: A new array of a.length, ignoring n
correctAnswerText: A new array of length n, padded with defaults
explanation: copyOf always returns a new array of exactly n elements, copying what fits and filling the rest with 0, false or null.

prompt: Why does System.out.println(marks) print something like [I@1b6d3586 for an int[]?
optionA: int arrays must be cast to String[] to be printed
optionB: println prints the raw bytes of the first element
optionC: Arrays inherit Object.toString: type code plus hash
optionD: The array is empty, so a memory address is shown
correctAnswerText: Arrays inherit Object.toString: type code plus hash
explanation: Arrays do not override toString, so you get "[I" (int array) plus a hash code. Use Arrays.toString to see contents.

prompt: int[] a = {1, 2}; int[] b = a; b[0] = 9; — why does a[0] become 9 as well?
optionA: b[0] = 9 writes to every array of that size
optionB: Assigning b = a copies every element across
optionC: Changes to b are synced back into a later
optionD: a and b refer to the very same array object
correctAnswerText: a and b refer to the very same array object
explanation: b = a copies the reference, not the array. Both names now point at one object, so a write through either is seen by both.

prompt: Two separately created int[] arrays both hold {1, 2, 3}. Why is x == y false?
optionA: Arrays can only be compared inside a loop
optionB: == compares references; use Arrays.equals
optionC: == on arrays compares their lengths only
optionD: == compares only the first elements of each
correctAnswerText: == compares references; use Arrays.equals
explanation: == asks whether they are the same object. Arrays.equals(x, y) compares lengths and elements.

prompt: Why can the rows of a Java 2D array have different lengths?
optionA: Java pads short rows with zeros to match
optionB: Only String[][] arrays may be jagged
optionC: It is an array of separate row arrays
optionD: The rows share one block, split unevenly
correctAnswerText: It is an array of separate row arrays
explanation: int[][] is an array whose elements are int[] references; each row is its own array with its own length.

prompt: Why can a method change the elements of an array argument but not make the caller's variable point elsewhere?
optionA: Arrays are passed by reference, variables by value
optionB: It gets a copy of the reference to the same array
optionC: The JVM copies the array back when it returns
optionD: Array parameters are implicitly declared final
correctAnswerText: It gets a copy of the reference to the same array
explanation: Java passes everything by value; for an array the value is a reference. The method can reach the same elements, but reassigning its copy does not touch the caller's variable.

prompt: Why would you call Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE) before a shortest-path loop?
optionA: To make the array read-only during the loop
optionB: To set every slot to "unknown" in one call
optionC: To allocate the array with a larger capacity
optionD: To sort dist so the smallest value is first
correctAnswerText: To set every slot to "unknown" in one call
explanation: fill assigns one value to every element, replacing the default 0 with a meaningful starting value such as "infinitely far".

prompt: int[] x = {1, 2}; compiles but a later x = {4, 5}; does not. Why?
optionA: The bare {…} form is allowed only in a declaration
optionB: x = {4, 5} needs a length to be written first
optionC: An array variable can be assigned only once
optionD: Braces create a List, which is not an int[]
correctAnswerText: The bare {…} form is allowed only in a declaration
explanation: The shorthand initialiser works only where the type is declared. Elsewhere write x = new int[]{4, 5};.

prompt: A boolean[] visited array is created to track seats. Why is no initialising loop needed?
optionA: The JVM fills it lazily on first read
optionB: Every element already starts as true
optionC: Every element already starts as false
optionD: Every element starts as null until set
correctAnswerText: Every element already starts as false
explanation: Java guarantees default values for array elements: false for boolean (and '\u0000' for char), so "nothing visited yet" is free.

prompt: Why can for (int x : a) not be used to set every element of a to zero?
optionA: for-each visits the elements in random order
optionB: Assigning to x inside for-each throws
optionC: for-each loops can only read String arrays
optionD: x is a copy of each element, not the slot
correctAnswerText: x is a copy of each element, not the slot
explanation: The loop variable receives each value; assigning to it changes only the local copy. Use an index loop or Arrays.fill.

prompt: Why must an array be sorted before Arrays.binarySearch is used on it?
optionA: It halves the range assuming order to decide
optionB: It compares hash codes stored in sorted order
optionC: It only accepts arrays marked as sorted
optionD: It sorts the array first, which takes time
correctAnswerText: It halves the range assuming order to decide
explanation: Each step compares with the middle and discards half. That is only valid if the order tells you which half can hold the key.

explanation: length is the capacity (3), not how many slots are filled; unfilled slots are null, and string concatenation prints "null".

explanation: new int[2][3] is 2 rows of 3 zeros. deepToString recurses into each row; plain toString would print two [I@… hashes.

optionD: It skips a[0], so the sum is short by one item

grow reassigns its own copy of the reference to a new array; the caller's g still points to {7}. Return the new array instead.

optionA: Compile error: the second size is required
optionB: It works; rows are created when first written
optionC: ArrayIndexOutOfBounds: rows have length zero
optionD: NullPointerException: no row has been created
correctAnswerText: NullPointerException: no row has been created

optionA: Only the last element becomes 75

optionC: Compile error: m cannot be assigned to
optionD: marks becomes {45, 60, 75} as intended
correctAnswerText: marks is unchanged; only the copy m changes
explanation: m holds a copy of each value; the array slots are never written. Use for (int i = 0; i < marks.length; i++) marks[i] += 5;.

prompt: Arrays.binarySearch(new int[]{5, 1, 4, 2}, 5) returns a negative number although 5 is in the array. Why?
optionA: binarySearch cannot find the very first element
optionB: The array is unsorted, so the result is undefined
optionC: binarySearch needs Integer[], not int[], to work
optionD: A negative return value means it was found first
correctAnswerText: The array is unsorted, so the result is undefined
explanation: Binary search compares with the middle and discards a half; on unsorted data it discards the half holding 5 and reports "not found" (here -5).

optionA: Sort with Arrays.sort(ranked.clone()) instead
optionB: Declare scores as final so it cannot change
optionC: int[] ranked = scores.clone(); before sorting
optionD: Assign ranked = scores after the sort is done
correctAnswerText: int[] ranked = scores.clone(); before sorting
explanation: ranked = scores shares one array. Clone (or Arrays.copyOf) to get an independent copy, then sort that. Sorting a throwaway clone sorts nothing you keep.

optionA: Compile error: s[0] was never assigned
optionB: It prints 0, the length of an empty string
optionC: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at s[0]
optionD: NullPointerException, since s[0] is null
correctAnswerText: NullPointerException, since s[0] is null
explanation: The array exists but its elements are null; calling a method on null throws NPE. The compiler does not track array element assignment.

prompt: A test compares expected and actual int[] with expected.equals(actual) and it fails, though the contents match. Why?
optionA: Arrays use Object.equals, which checks identity
optionB: equals on arrays always returns false by design
optionC: equals on int[] compares only the array lengths
optionD: equals must be called on actual, not on expected
correctAnswerText: Arrays use Object.equals, which checks identity
explanation: Arrays do not override equals, so it is the same as ==. Use Arrays.equals (or assertArrayEquals in a test).

optionA: 99: clone returns the very same 2D array
optionB: 99: clone copied the row references only
optionC: 1: clone made a fully independent copy
optionD: 1: b[0][0] = 99 writes to a temporary row
correctAnswerText: 99: clone copied the row references only
explanation: clone on a 2D array copies the outer array of row references; both outer arrays share the same rows. Clone each row for a deep copy.

optionA: Change the comparison from > to >=
optionB: Loop by index instead of for-each
optionC: Start max at temps[0] rather than at 0
optionD: Declare max as long to widen the range
correctAnswerText: Start max at temps[0] rather than at 0
explanation: 0 is larger than every element, so it is never replaced. Seed with the first element (or Integer.MIN_VALUE).

prompt: A program collects registrations until the form closes; the count is unknown. Best container?
optionA: A String[1000], assuming that will be enough
optionB: A String[] sized to Integer.MAX_VALUE up front
optionC: An ArrayList, which grows as entries arrive
optionD: A new array, one slot larger, per registration
correctAnswerText: An ArrayList, which grows as entries arrive
explanation: Arrays are fixed-size. A guessed size overflows or wastes memory, and growing by one each time is quadratic copying. ArrayList handles growth properly.

prompt: A simulation keeps one million sensor readings that never change in number. int[] or Integer[]?
optionA: Integer[]: objects are faster to access
optionB: int[]: values stored directly, no boxing
optionC: Integer[]: it supports Arrays.sort, int[] not
optionD: Either; both use the same amount of memory
correctAnswerText: int[]: values stored directly, no boxing
explanation: Integer[] holds a million references to separate objects (several times the memory, plus boxing cost). int[] stores the values contiguously.

prompt: findBacklogs(rollNo) returns a String[] of subjects. When a student has none, what should it return?
optionA: A String[1] holding the text "none"
optionB: An empty array, new String[0]
optionC: null, to signal there were none
optionD: An array holding one empty String
correctAnswerText: An empty array, new String[0]
explanation: An empty array lets callers loop without a null check and cannot be mistaken for real data. null forces every caller to remember a special case.

prompt: A Timetable class returns its private int[] slots from getSlots(). Callers have been editing it. Best fix?
optionA: Make the slots field final in the class
optionB: Add a comment asking callers not to edit
optionC: Mark getSlots() as a static method instead
optionD: Return slots.clone() so callers get a copy
correctAnswerText: Return slots.clone() so callers get a copy
explanation: final stops reassigning the field, not changing its elements. Returning a copy keeps the class in control of its own state.

prompt: Code keeps names[], rolls[] and marks[] in step by index, and sorting by marks scrambles them. Best redesign?
optionA: Store everything as text in one String[] array
optionB: Sort all three arrays with the same algorithm
optionC: One Student[] array whose objects hold all three
optionD: Use a 2D Object[][] with a column per field
correctAnswerText: One Student[] array whose objects hold all three
explanation: Parallel arrays rely on every operation moving all of them together. Grouping the fields in one object makes that impossible to get wrong.

prompt: You need to check once whether a roll number is in an unsorted int[] of 500. Sort then binarySearch, or scan?
optionA: Scan: one O(n) pass beats O(n log n) sorting
optionB: Sort then binarySearch, since log n is faster
optionC: Sort, since the scan cannot find duplicates
optionD: Convert to a String and use contains() on it
correctAnswerText: Scan: one O(n) pass beats O(n log n) sorting
explanation: Sorting costs more than the single scan it replaces. Sorting pays off only when many lookups share one sort.

prompt: To count each lowercase letter in a long string, a HashMap<Character, Integer> or an int[26]?
optionA: HashMap, because it uses less memory than int[26]
optionB: HashMap, since arrays cannot be indexed by chars
optionC: A String[26], adding one letter per occurrence
optionD: int[26] indexed by c - 'a': small fixed key range
correctAnswerText: int[26] indexed by c - 'a': small fixed key range
explanation: When keys are a small dense range, an array is simpler and faster: no boxing, no hashing. A map earns its place when keys are sparse or unknown.

prompt: You are writing your own growable array. When it is full, how should the new capacity be chosen?
optionA: Grow by a factor such as double the size
optionB: Grow by exactly one slot each time
optionC: Allocate the largest possible array once
optionD: Grow by a fixed ten slots each time
correctAnswerText: Grow by a factor such as double the size
explanation: Multiplying capacity makes copying cost amortised O(1) per add. Fixed increments make n adds cost O(n²) in total.

prompt: A teammate copies arrays with a hand-written for loop each time. What is the strongest argument for Arrays.copyOf?
optionA: It makes a deep copy of nested arrays too
optionB: It states the intent and gets bounds right
optionC: It also sorts the copy as it is created
optionD: It shares storage, so no memory is used
correctAnswerText: It states the intent and gets bounds right
explanation: copyOf (and copyOfRange) name what is happening and handle sizing and padding, removing a common off-by-one source. It is still a shallow copy.

prompt: Marks for 60 students in 5 subjects are mostly processed one student at a time. Which layout fits best?
optionA: int[60][5], so each row is one student
optionB: Sixty separate int[5] local variables
optionC: int[5][60], so each row is one subject
optionD: int[300] with i * 60 + j used everywhere
correctAnswerText: int[60][5], so each row is one student
explanation: Match the outer index to how the data is used: marks[s] then gives one student's row directly. The flat form hides intent and invites index bugs.

prompt: What return type is declared for a method that returns no value?
optionA: Object
optionB: void
optionC: empty
optionD: null
correctAnswerText: void
explanation: void means the method returns nothing; it may still use a bare return; to exit early.

prompt: In Java, what makes up a method's signature for overloading purposes?
optionA: Its name and its parameter types
optionB: Its access modifier and its name
optionC: Its name and its return type
optionD: Its return type and parameter names
correctAnswerText: Its name and its parameter types
explanation: The signature is the name plus the ordered parameter types. Return type and parameter names are not part of it.

prompt: Which keyword makes a method belong to the class rather than to each object?
optionA: public
optionB: void
optionC: final
optionD: static
correctAnswerText: static
explanation: A static method is called on the class (Math.max) and needs no object; instance methods need an object to run on.

prompt: Which parameter declaration lets a method accept any number of int arguments?
optionA: int nums...
optionB: int* nums
optionC: int[*] nums
optionD: int... nums
correctAnswerText: int... nums
explanation: Varargs are written Type... name. Inside the method, nums is an int[].

prompt: How does Java pass arguments to methods?
optionA: Always by reference, for every type
optionB: Always by value, including references
optionC: Primitives by value, objects by reference

prompt: In a recursive method, what is the base case?

prompt: Where in a parameter list may a varargs parameter appear?

prompt: Where can a local variable declared inside a method be used?
optionA: In any method that the method itself calls

prompt: What does static main need in order to call an instance method of its own class?

prompt: Why can two methods not be overloaded by return type alone?

prompt: A method does marks = marks + 5; on its int parameter. Why is the caller's variable unchanged?

prompt: Why can a static method not use this or read an instance field directly?

prompt: A field int count; defaults to 0, but a local int count; cannot be read before assignment. Why the difference?

prompt: register(name, email, phone, city, branch, year, section) takes seven parameters and callers swap them by mistake. Best change?

prompt: A method sums the numbers 1 to n, where n may be a million. Recursion or a loop?

optionD: Recursion: it is always faster than a loop in Java
correctAnswerText: A loop: a million frames would overflow the stack
explanation: Java does not eliminate tail calls, so depth n means n frames. For linear work over large n, iteration (or n * (n + 1) / 2) is the sound choice.

prompt: topThree(int[] marks) sorts the caller's array and returns its last three. A reviewer objects. Why?

correctAnswerText: It silently reorders data the caller still owns
explanation: A method named topThree is not expected to change its input. Work on a copy unless mutating the argument is the method's stated purpose.

prompt: Calls read printReport(r, true, false), and nobody remembers what the flags mean. Which redesign is best?
optionA: Add a third boolean for the next new option
optionB: Keep it and add a comment at every call site

optionD: Named methods such as printSummary(r) instead
correctAnswerText: Named methods such as printSummary(r) instead
explanation: Bare flags hide intent and invite swapped arguments; int codes are no better. Named methods (or an options object) make each call read clearly.

prompt: Most callers of average(...) already hold a List<Integer> of marks from the database. Which parameter type fits best?
optionA: A List<Integer>, matching what callers hold
optionB: Integer... marks, to keep the boxing step

optionD: int... marks, so they unpack the list first
correctAnswerText: A List<Integer>, matching what callers hold
explanation: Varargs suit a few literal values typed at the call site. When callers already have a collection, accepting it avoids conversion at every call.

prompt: findStudent(roll) may find nobody. Which return design makes the "not found" case hardest to ignore?
optionA: A Student whose fields are all blank
optionB: A Student with roll number set to -1
optionC: Optional<Student>, empty when absent
optionD: null, documented in the method comment
correctAnswerText: Optional<Student>, empty when absent
explanation: Optional puts absence in the type, so the caller must deal with it. null and dummy objects compile happily and fail later.

prompt: Naive recursive fib(45) takes seconds. What is the best improvement that keeps a recursive solution?
optionA: Switch the return type from int to long
optionB: Increase the thread stack size with -Xss
optionC: Make the method static so calls are cheaper
optionD: Cache each fib(n) result in an array or map
correctAnswerText: Cache each fib(n) result in an array or map
explanation: The time goes on recomputing the same subproblems exponentially many times. Memoisation computes each once, giving linear time.

prompt: A 120-line method reads input, validates it, computes fees and prints a receipt. What is the strongest reason to split it?
optionA: Splitting removes the need for any parameters
optionB: Shorter methods always run faster on the JVM
optionC: Java limits methods to fifty lines of code
optionD: Each part can be named, tested and reused alone
correctAnswerText: Each part can be named, tested and reused alone
explanation: Separate methods for separate jobs let the fee logic be tested without console input and read as a sequence of named steps.

prompt: Helper methods share a static int total that each one adds to. Tests pass alone but fail together. Best remedy?
optionA: Make total volatile so updates are visible
optionB: Reset total to 0 at the start of every test
optionC: Rename total so the tests stop clashing

correctAnswerText: Pass values in and return results instead
explanation: Static mutable state leaks between calls and tests. Resetting hides it; methods that take inputs and return outputs remove it.

optionA: super(...)

optionD: base(...)
correctAnswerText: super(...)
explanation: super(...) invokes a constructor of the direct superclass; this(...) calls another constructor of the same class. Java has no parent or base keyword.

prompt: In Java, what does encapsulation usually look like in a class?
optionA: Public fields that every class can read directly
optionB: Final fields copied in from an outer parent class
optionC: Private fields reached only through its methods

correctAnswerText: Private fields reached only through its methods
explanation: Encapsulation hides state behind the class boundary: fields are private and other code goes through methods that can validate and protect the object.

prompt: How many classes can a single Java class directly extend?
optionA: Two at most, provided both of them are abstract

correctAnswerText: Exactly one, though it may implement many interfaces
explanation: Java allows single class inheritance (every class extends exactly one class, Object by default) and multiple inheritance of interface types.

prompt: What is method overloading?
optionA: Same method name with different parameter lists

optionD: A subclass replacing a method it has inherited
correctAnswerText: Same method name with different parameter lists
explanation: Overloading is several methods sharing a name but differing in parameters, chosen at compile time. Replacing an inherited method is overriding.

prompt: Which modifier stops a subclass from overriding a method?
optionA: final
optionB: sealed
optionC: const

correctAnswerText: final
explanation: A final method cannot be overridden. sealed (Java 17) limits which classes may extend a type, not which methods may be overridden; const is reserved but unused.

prompt: What can you NOT do with an abstract class?
optionA: Declare concrete methods with a body inside it

correctAnswerText: Create an object of it directly with new
explanation: An abstract class cannot be instantiated. It can still have constructors (run by subclasses), concrete methods, fields, and be used as a reference type.

prompt: How many copies of a static field exist when a class has five objects?
optionA: One, shared by the class and all five objects

correctAnswerText: One, shared by the class and all five objects
explanation: A static field belongs to the class, so there is exactly one copy no matter how many instances exist (per class loader).

prompt: What does Object.toString() print for a class that does not override it?

prompt: Since Java 8, what is a default method in an interface?

correctAnswerText: A method with a body that implementers inherit
explanation: Default methods (Java 8+) carry an implementation inside the interface; implementing classes get it for free and may override it.

prompt: Which relationship does composition describe between two classes?

explanation: Composition is has-a: a Car holds an Engine field and delegates to it. Inheritance is is-a.

prompt: Why must a class that overrides equals also override hashCode?
optionA: hashCode is what equals calls to compare the fields

correctAnswerText: Equal objects must give equal hash codes for hashing
explanation: HashMap and HashSet find the bucket by hashCode before calling equals. If two equal objects hash differently, the collection never compares them and treats them as different.

prompt: Why must this(...) or super(...) be the first statement in a constructor?
optionA: It makes the constructor run faster during class loading

correctAnswerText: The object must be fully set up before its own code runs
explanation: Java guarantees the superclass part of an object is initialised before subclass code touches it, so the chained call has to happen before anything else (Java 17 rule).

prompt: With Shape s = new Circle(); s.draw(); what decides which draw() body runs?

prompt: A subclass declares a field with the same name as a parent field. What happens?

correctAnswerText: It hides the parent field; access follows declared type

prompt: Why is a static method with the same signature in a subclass not an override?

correctAnswerText: Static calls bind to a class at compile time, not to objects

prompt: What can an abstract class offer that an interface cannot, even in Java 17?

correctAnswerText: Instance fields and constructors that subclasses share

prompt: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance for reusing code?
