optionD: Identity hash codes differ, so equals is never consulted
correctAnswerText: Identity hash codes differ, so equals is never consulted
explanation: Each object keeps Object.hashCode, so the two land in different buckets and the set never asks equals. Equal objects must produce equal hash codes.

prompt: Point declares public boolean equals(Point p) and a correct hashCode. a.equals(b) is true for two equal points, yet list.contains(new Point(1, 2)) is false. Why?
optionA: The list keeps copies, so the stored point has changed
optionB: contains compares hash codes only and never equals
optionC: ArrayList needs Comparable before contains can work
optionD: equals(Point) overloads; contains calls equals(Object)
correctAnswerText: equals(Point) overloads; contains calls equals(Object)
explanation: Collections call equals(Object). A method taking Point is a new overload, so the inherited identity equals still runs. @Override would have caught this at compile time.

optionA: Base.describe() runs, and it has no label to print
optionB: Base runs Item.describe() before Item's fields are set
optionC: String fields are always null inside any constructor
optionD: Private fields are invisible to an overriding method
correctAnswerText: Base runs Item.describe() before Item's fields are set
explanation: The Base constructor runs first and dispatches to the overridden describe(); Item's field initialisers only run after super() returns. Never call overridable methods from a constructor.

prompt: Key hashes on its id field. After set.add(k); k.id = 2; the set reports contains(k) false but size() 1. What went wrong?
optionA: The key changed its hash after being stored in a bucket
optionB: contains uses == and the id field change broke identity
optionC: HashSet copies keys, so k no longer refers to the entry
optionD: Changing a field invalidates the set and empties it
correctAnswerText: The key changed its hash after being stored in a bucket
explanation: The entry sits in the bucket for hash 1; the lookup now searches the bucket for hash 2. Fields used by hashCode must not change while the object is a key.

optionA: The implicit super() has no no-arg Account to call
optionB: this.rate is illegal in a constructor of a subclass
optionC: A subclass may not declare any extra fields at all
optionD: Savings must declare an owner field of its own
correctAnswerText: The implicit super() has no no-arg Account to call
explanation: With no explicit call, the compiler inserts super(), but Account only has Account(String). Savings must call super(owner) itself.

optionA: Shape must be abstract before area is overridden
optionB: An override may not narrow access from public
optionC: protected methods cannot return a double value
optionD: An override must also change its return type
correctAnswerText: An override may not narrow access from public
explanation: Code holding a Shape may call area() publicly; a Circle must keep that promise. Overrides can widen access but never weaken it.

prompt: Course keeps a private List<String> students and getStudents() returns that field. Callers now add students and skip the seat limit check in enroll(). What is the flaw?
optionA: Private fields cannot hold collections safely
optionB: The enroll method should be marked final instead
optionC: The list field should have been declared static
optionD: The getter hands out the internal list for editing
correctAnswerText: The getter hands out the internal list for editing
explanation: Private only protects the reference, not the object it points to. Return List.copyOf(students) or an unmodifiable view so all changes go through enroll().

optionA: Title[body]
optionB: Title[body]Sign
optionC: TitleSign[body]
optionD: [body]Sign
correctAnswerText: Title[body]Sign
explanation: Signed.render runs (dynamic dispatch), calls Titled.render through super, which calls Report.render. Each layer wraps the one beneath it.

optionA: Private methods are not overridden, so tag() binds to Parent
optionB: show() is declared in Parent, so it uses Parent methods only
optionC: Child.tag() has package access, which hides it from Parent
optionD: The JVM picks the first method that it loaded with that name
correctAnswerText: Private methods are not overridden, so tag() binds to Parent
explanation: A private method is invisible to subclasses, so Child.tag() is an unrelated new method. Inside Parent, tag() is bound to Parent's private version.

prompt: Square extends Rect and its setters keep width and height equal. A test does Rect r = new Square(); r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); and expects area 20 but gets 16. What is the real problem?
optionA: area() must be overridden in Square to compute it correctly
optionB: The test should have declared the variable as a Square
optionC: Square breaks what Rect promises, so it is no true subtype
optionD: The setters should be static so that both share one value
correctAnswerText: Square breaks what Rect promises, so it is no true subtype
explanation: Code written for Rect assumes width and height change independently. A subclass that breaks its parent's contract violates substitutability (Liskov), whatever the maths says.

prompt: A teammate writes class UndoStack extends ArrayList<Action> to get storage for free. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Hold a list privately; extending exposes add(i, x) and more
optionB: Extend LinkedList instead, since it is faster at the ends
optionC: Fine as is; extending the list is the quickest reuse there is
optionD: Make UndoStack an interface so ArrayList can implement it
correctAnswerText: Hold a list privately; extending exposes add(i, x) and more
explanation: Extending inherits every list method, so callers can insert into the middle and break stack order. Composition exposes only push, pop and peek.

prompt: UPI, card and wallet payments all need a transactionId, an amount and the same audit steps, but differ in how they charge. Which design fits best?
optionA: An interface for callers plus an abstract base for shared state
optionB: One interface with default methods holding the shared fields
optionC: A single concrete class with a switch on the payment type
optionD: Three unrelated classes, each copying the audit code it needs
correctAnswerText: An interface for callers plus an abstract base for shared state
explanation: Interfaces cannot hold instance fields, so shared state and template steps belong in an abstract class; callers still depend on the interface so new types stay pluggable.

prompt: A Notifier interface has forty implementations across teams. You need a new method on it. What is the soundest way to add it?
optionA: A static method, since those can be overridden per class
optionB: A default method, so existing implementations keep compiling
optionC: An abstract method, forcing all forty classes to update now
optionD: A new abstract class that all forty must switch to extend
correctAnswerText: A default method, so existing implementations keep compiling
explanation: Default methods exist precisely to evolve interfaces without breaking implementers. The cost is a sensible default; implementations that need more can override it.

prompt: Money is used as a HashMap key and passed between threads. Why make it a final class with final fields and no setters?
optionA: Final classes run faster because the JVM can skip GC on them
optionB: It is the only way to let Money override equals and hashCode
optionC: Its hash never changes and it is safe to share without locks
optionD: It lets subclasses add a currency field without any changes
correctAnswerText: Its hash never changes and it is safe to share without locks
explanation: An immutable value cannot drift after it is used as a key, and needs no synchronisation. final on the class stops a subclass from adding mutable state.

prompt: A college system has Employee > Teacher > HOD > Principal as a class chain, and a teacher can become HOD mid-year. How do you judge it?
optionA: Make every class abstract so the chain cannot break
optionB: Add one more subclass level for each new designation
optionC: Roles change, so give Employee a role object instead
optionD: Sound, since each level is a kind of the one above
correctAnswerText: Roles change, so give Employee a role object instead
explanation: An object cannot change its class. When a "type" can change at run time it is state, so model it as a field (a Role) rather than a subclass.

prompt: Point.equals uses instanceof Point; ColorPoint extends Point and adds colour to its own equals. What is the trade-off to judge?
optionA: instanceof is slower, so getClass is always better
optionB: ColorPoint cannot override equals once Point does
optionC: Point equals ColorPoint but not back: symmetry breaks
optionD: No issue: instanceof keeps equals symmetric for all
correctAnswerText: Point equals ColorPoint but not back: symmetry breaks
explanation: p.equals(cp) is true while cp.equals(p) is false. Either compare getClass() (no subclass equality) or make the class final; there is no way to add a field and keep the contract.

prompt: An Order class has a public setter for every field, including status and total. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Mark every setter final so subclasses cannot misuse it
optionB: Fine: private fields with setters is full encapsulation
optionC: Make the fields public, since setters add nothing here
optionD: Prefer methods like cancel() that keep the rules inside
correctAnswerText: Prefer methods like cancel() that keep the rules inside
explanation: Setters on everything let any caller put an order into an impossible state. Behaviour methods (cancel, addItem) enforce the transitions and recompute the total.

prompt: An SmsSender is written as a class of static methods that call the gateway directly. Tests now send real SMS. What is the better design?
optionA: An instance behind an interface, injected where used
optionB: Copy the static methods into each calling class
optionC: Keep it static but wrap every call in a try block
optionD: Make the class final so tests cannot subclass it
correctAnswerText: An instance behind an interface, injected where used
explanation: Static calls cannot be swapped. An interface plus an injected instance lets tests pass a fake sender; static suits pure helpers like Math.max, not things with side effects.

prompt: Every service class extends BaseLogger just to call log(). Later one service also needs to extend a framework class. How do you judge the original choice?
optionA: Sound: logging is shared, so inheriting it is ideal
optionB: Poor: log() should have been made private instead
optionC: Sound: Java lets the service extend both classes
optionD: Poor: it spent the one superclass slot on a helper
correctAnswerText: Poor: it spent the one superclass slot on a helper
explanation: Java allows one superclass, and a service is not "a kind of logger". A logger field (composition) gives the same reuse and leaves the extends slot free.

prompt: An abstract ReportJob has process() that calls load(), transform() and save() in order, and subclasses fill those in. Should process() be final?
optionA: Yes: final makes the three steps run in parallel
optionB: Yes: subclasses fill the steps but keep the order fixed
optionC: No: making it final would stop the class compiling
optionD: No: final methods cannot call abstract methods at all
correctAnswerText: Yes: subclasses fill the steps but keep the order fixed
explanation: This is the template method pattern. A final process() guarantees the sequence while the abstract steps remain the extension points.

prompt: Which class is the common parent of every exception and error in Java?
optionA: Throwable
optionB: RuntimeException
optionC: Exception
optionD: Error
correctAnswerText: Throwable
explanation: Throwable sits at the top with two branches: Exception (including RuntimeException) and Error. Only Throwable and its subclasses can be thrown.

prompt: Which of these is a checked exception?
optionA: IOException
optionB: IllegalArgumentException
optionC: NullPointerException
optionD: ArithmeticException
correctAnswerText: IOException
explanation: IOException extends Exception but not RuntimeException, so the compiler forces it to be caught or declared. The other three are RuntimeExceptions.

prompt: Which exceptions does the compiler NOT force you to catch or declare?
optionA: Only those thrown from inside a static method
optionB: RuntimeException, Error and their subclasses
optionC: Any exception whose class name ends in Error
optionD: Every subclass of Exception without exception
correctAnswerText: RuntimeException, Error and their subclasses
explanation: Unchecked throwables are RuntimeException and Error with their subclasses. Everything else under Throwable is checked.

prompt: Which keyword in a method signature declares that the method may throw a checked exception?
optionA: throws
optionB: throw
optionC: raises
optionD: catch
correctAnswerText: throws
explanation: throws appears in the signature (void load() throws IOException); throw is the statement that actually raises an exception object.

prompt: What must a type implement to be used in a try-with-resources header?
optionA: Serializable
optionB: Iterable
optionC: Runnable
optionD: AutoCloseable
correctAnswerText: AutoCloseable
explanation: try-with-resources (Java 7+) calls close() automatically, so the resource must implement AutoCloseable (Closeable extends it).

prompt: When does a finally block run?
optionA: Only when no catch block matched the exception
optionB: Only when the try block completes with no error
optionC: Only when the try block throws some exception
optionD: After the try, whether or not an exception occurred
correctAnswerText: After the try, whether or not an exception occurred
explanation: finally runs on normal completion, on a caught or uncaught exception, and even after return. Only things like System.exit or a JVM crash skip it.

prompt: Which exception does the integer expression 10 / 0 throw in Java?
optionA: NumberFormatException
optionB: IllegalStateException
optionC: ArithmeticException
optionD: It returns Infinity
correctAnswerText: ArithmeticException
explanation: Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException ("/ by zero"). Floating-point division (10.0 / 0) gives Infinity instead.

prompt: What kind of problem does a subclass of Error, such as OutOfMemoryError, signal?
optionA: A checked condition the caller is expected to retry
optionB: A bad user input that the app should validate again
optionC: A serious JVM-level failure an app should not handle
optionD: A missing file that the program must create first
correctAnswerText: A serious JVM-level failure an app should not handle
explanation: Errors mark conditions the application usually cannot recover from (out of memory, stack overflow). They are unchecked and normally left uncaught.

prompt: What is the Java 7+ syntax for one catch block that handles two exception types?
optionA: catch (IOException | SQLException e)
optionB: catch (IOException, SQLException e)
optionC: catch (IOException e, SQLException f)
optionD: catch (IOException & SQLException e)
correctAnswerText: catch (IOException | SQLException e)
explanation: Multi-catch joins types with a vertical bar; the variable is implicitly final. The types must not be subclasses of one another.

prompt: Which Throwable method returns the exception that was wrapped inside another?
optionA: getSuppressed()
optionB: getStackTrace()
optionC: getMessage()
optionD: getCause()
correctAnswerText: getCause()
explanation: The cause is set through a constructor like new ServiceException("msg", e) or initCause, and read back with getCause(). Stack traces print it as "Caused by:".

prompt: What is the idea behind making the compiler enforce checked exceptions?
optionA: Unchecked exceptions cannot carry any message or cause
optionB: It stops programs from ever crashing on bad input data
optionC: Callers must plan for failures they can reasonably expect
optionD: Checked exceptions are faster to throw than other kinds
correctAnswerText: Callers must plan for failures they can reasonably expect
explanation: A missing file or a dropped connection is a normal possibility, so the signature advertises it and the caller must decide what to do. Programming bugs are left unchecked.

prompt: Why must a catch for a subclass exception come before a catch for its superclass?
optionA: The JVM sorts catches by name and needs subclasses listed first
optionB: A superclass catch rethrows anything it does not recognise
optionC: Catches are tried in order, so the subclass one would be unreachable
optionD: Superclass catches only work when placed last for performance
correctAnswerText: Catches are tried in order, so the subclass one would be unreachable
explanation: The first matching catch wins. If catch (Exception) came first, a later catch (IOException) could never run, and javac rejects it as already caught.

prompt: Why is try-with-resources preferred over closing a resource by hand in finally?
optionA: It turns every checked exception into an unchecked one
optionB: It always closes and keeps a close failure as suppressed
optionC: It lets the resource be shared safely between threads
optionD: It keeps the resource open longer so it can be reused
correctAnswerText: It always closes and keeps a close failure as suppressed
explanation: A hand-written finally needs null checks and can let a close() exception hide the real one. try-with-resources closes reliably and records the close failure as suppressed.

prompt: In try-with-resources, what is a suppressed exception?
optionA: An exception caught by an empty catch block somewhere
optionB: An exception the JVM decided was too minor to report
optionC: A close() failure attached to the exception from the body
optionD: A warning hidden by the @SuppressWarnings annotation
correctAnswerText: A close() failure attached to the exception from the body
explanation: If the body throws and close() also throws, the body exception propagates and the close exception is added to it, readable via getSuppressed().

prompt: Why is catch (Exception e) { } with an empty body considered harmful?
optionA: It makes the JVM retry the try block in an endless loop
optionB: The failure vanishes and the program goes on in a bad state
optionC: Empty blocks make the class fail to compile in Java 17
optionD: The exception is rethrown twice and logged twice over
correctAnswerText: The failure vanishes and the program goes on in a bad state
explanation: Swallowing removes the evidence: no log, no stack trace, and later code works on half-finished data. A crash would at least have pointed at the problem.

prompt: Why would a repository wrap a SQLException in its own DataAccessFailure with the original as cause?
optionA: It hides the SQL failure so nobody needs to look at it
optionB: Only wrapped exceptions are allowed to have messages
optionC: Wrapping makes the database retry the failed query
optionD: Callers see one error type and the root cause is kept
correctAnswerText: Callers see one error type and the root cause is kept
explanation: Wrapping gives the layer above an abstraction it understands while getCause() still carries the JDBC detail for debugging.

prompt: When should a custom exception extend RuntimeException rather than Exception?
optionA: When it will be thrown from inside a constructor body
optionB: When callers usually cannot do anything useful to recover
optionC: When the class is declared in a different package
optionD: When the exception needs to carry a message or a cause
correctAnswerText: When callers usually cannot do anything useful to recover
explanation: Checked is for failures the immediate caller is expected to handle. For bugs or failures handled centrally, unchecked avoids throws clauses on every layer.

prompt: Why may an overriding method not declare a broader checked exception than the method it overrides?
optionA: Overriding methods may not declare any exceptions at all
optionB: Broader exceptions are always unchecked in subclasses
optionC: Code written against the parent type has not planned for it
optionD: The JVM cannot store two throws clauses for one method name
correctAnswerText: Code written against the parent type has not planned for it
explanation: A caller holding the parent type only catches what the parent declared. The override may throw fewer or narrower checked exceptions, never new broader ones.

prompt: Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException, which is unchecked. What does that design choice imply?
optionA: The method can never fail, so the exception is cosmetic
optionB: The exception is caught inside parseInt and converted
optionC: Callers are expected to pass valid text or check it first
optionD: It must be declared with throws by every single caller
correctAnswerText: Callers are expected to pass valid text or check it first
explanation: Being unchecked treats bad input as a caller mistake. When the text comes from a user, you still validate or catch it, but the compiler will not remind you.

prompt: In a stack trace, what does the topmost "at ..." line usually tell you?
optionA: The line where the exception was finally caught
optionB: The last line of the program that ran successfully
optionC: The method and line where the exception was thrown
optionD: The first method main called when the program began
correctAnswerText: The method and line where the exception was thrown
explanation: Frames are listed from the throw point downward to main; the top frame is where it originated, and "Caused by:" sections show wrapped causes.

optionA: TXCFE
optionB: TCE
optionC: TCFE
optionD: TFCE
correctAnswerText: TCFE
explanation: The throw skips the rest of the try (no X), the matching catch runs, then finally, then normal flow continues after the statement.

optionA: It throws an exception
optionD: It does not compile
explanation: finally runs after the try has prepared its return value; a return inside finally replaces it. It compiles (javac only warns), which is why the pattern is dangerous.

optionC: It does not compile
explanation: The value of x (1) is captured when return executes. finally then changes the local variable, but the already-captured int is what the method returns.

optionA: open1 body close1 open2 close2
optionB: open1 open2 body close2 close1
optionC: open1 open2 body close1 close2
optionD: open2 open1 body close1 close2
correctAnswerText: open1 open2 body close2 close1
explanation: Resources open in declaration order and close in reverse, so r2 (which may depend on r1) closes before r1.

optionA: close failed | 1
optionB: close failed | 0
optionC: query failed | 0
optionD: query failed | 1
correctAnswerText: query failed | 1
explanation: The body exception is the primary one; the close failure is attached to it as one suppressed exception rather than replacing it.

optionA: bad 0
optionB: bad 12
optionC: bad -1
optionD: parsed 12
correctAnswerText: bad -1
explanation: parseInt throws before the assignment completes, so qty keeps -1 and "parsed" is never printed.

optionA: RTE then EX
optionB: EX
optionC: IAE
optionD: RTE
correctAnswerText: RTE
explanation: A NullPointerException is a RuntimeException. The first catch that matches handles it, and only one catch block ever runs.

prompt: You want a checked InsufficientBalanceException that carries a message. Which declaration does that?
optionA: class InsufficientBalanceException implements Throwable { InsufficientBalanceException(String m) { super(m); } }
optionB: class InsufficientBalanceException extends Exception { InsufficientBalanceException(String m) { super(m); } }
optionC: class InsufficientBalanceException extends Error { InsufficientBalanceException(String m) { super(m); } }
optionD: class InsufficientBalanceException extends RuntimeException { InsufficientBalanceException(String m) { super(m); } }
correctAnswerText: class InsufficientBalanceException extends Exception { InsufficientBalanceException(String m) { super(m); } }
explanation: Extending Exception (not RuntimeException) makes it checked, and passing the message to super stores it for getMessage(). Throwable is a class, not an interface.

prompt: main contains only String s = Files.readString(Path.of("notes.txt")); (Java 11+). What happens when you compile it?
optionA: Error: unreported IOException must be caught or declared
optionB: It compiles; a missing file just returns an empty string
optionC: It compiles; a missing file just returns null at runtime
optionD: Error: Files.readString cannot be called from main
correctAnswerText: Error: unreported IOException must be caught or declared
explanation: Files.readString declares IOException, a checked exception. Wrap it in try/catch or add throws IOException to main; a missing file raises NoSuchFileException at run time.

optionA: config.txt <- config.txt
optionB: load failed <- config.txt
optionC: load failed <- null
optionD: config.txt <- load failed
correctAnswerText: load failed <- config.txt
explanation: The outer exception carries its own message, and getCause() returns the FileNotFoundException passed to its constructor.

optionA: Two catch blocks may not both print to standard output
optionB: IOException is already caught by the Exception block
optionC: FileReader cannot be closed inside the try block itself
optionD: Exception must be declared with throws on the method
correctAnswerText: IOException is already caught by the Exception block
explanation: javac reports "exception IOException has already been caught". Specific types must be caught before their supertypes.

optionA: The exception is logged but the method still continues
optionB: finally runs before try, so the throw is never reached
optionC: RuntimeExceptions are ignored unless they are declared
optionD: The return in finally discards the in-flight exception
correctAnswerText: The return in finally discards the in-flight exception
explanation: A return (or throw) in finally completes the method abruptly and the pending exception is silently lost. The caller receives "saved".

prompt: try throws IllegalStateException("payment failed"); finally then throws NullPointerException("cleanup failed"). The caller logs e.getMessage() and e.getSuppressed().length. What does it see?
optionA: cleanup failed 0
optionB: payment failed 0
optionC: payment failed 1
optionD: cleanup failed 1
correctAnswerText: cleanup failed 0
explanation: An exception from a plain finally replaces the original outright; unlike try-with-resources nothing is recorded as suppressed. The real cause is lost.

prompt: catch (SQLException e) { throw new ServiceException("order failed"); } The production log shows only "order failed" and a trace ending in the service. What is wrong?
optionA: ServiceException must extend SQLException to work
optionB: The SQLException was not passed on as the cause
optionC: The log level hides causes of checked exceptions
optionD: Stack traces never include the repository layer
correctAnswerText: The SQLException was not passed on as the cause
explanation: Without new ServiceException("order failed", e) the original exception and its trace are discarded. Always chain the cause when wrapping.

prompt: An import job sets int age = 0; try { age = Integer.parseInt(cell); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { } and later reports dozens of students aged 0. What is the defect?
optionA: parseInt returns 0 whenever its text has any spaces
optionB: The catch block runs even when parsing has succeeded
optionC: NumberFormatException resets every int field to 0
optionD: Bad rows are swallowed and saved with a fake default
correctAnswerText: Bad rows are swallowed and saved with a fake default
explanation: The empty catch turns invalid input into plausible-looking data. Reject or report the row instead of silently keeping the default.

prompt: A report method does BufferedReader r = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(f)); reads lines, then calls r.close() at the end. After many malformed files the server hits "Too many open files". Why?
optionA: A read error skips close(), so the file handle leaks
optionB: close() only works when it is called from finally
optionC: BufferedReader never closes the FileReader beneath it
optionD: The OS limits how often one file may be opened
correctAnswerText: A read error skips close(), so the file handle leaks
explanation: When parsing throws, execution jumps past r.close(). try-with-resources guarantees the close on every path.

prompt: A developer wraps getAddress().getCity() in catch (NullPointerException e) { return "Unknown"; } to stop crashes. What is the real problem with this fix?
optionA: It hides any null bug in the call, not just a missing address
optionB: The return inside catch skips the method's finally block
optionC: It turns the NullPointerException into a checked exception
optionD: NullPointerException cannot be caught by application code
correctAnswerText: It hides any null bug in the call, not just a missing address
explanation: Any NPE anywhere in that expression, including real bugs, now becomes "Unknown". Check for the expected null (or use Optional) and let unexpected ones fail loudly.

prompt: main declares throws IOException, yet names.forEach(n -> Files.readString(Path.of(n))); fails with "unreported exception IOException". Why?
optionA: Files.readString cannot be used inside a lambda
optionB: main must catch IOException instead of declaring it
optionC: forEach only accepts lambdas that return a value
optionD: Consumer.accept declares no checked exceptions
correctAnswerText: Consumer.accept declares no checked exceptions
explanation: The lambda body is the accept method of Consumer, which throws nothing checked, so main's throws clause does not help. Catch inside the lambda or use a plain loop.

prompt: One failed request writes the same stack trace five times in the log. Each layer does catch (Exception e) { log.error("failed", e); throw e; }. What is the diagnosis?
optionA: Every layer logs and rethrows; log once where it is handled
optionB: The logger is configured with five separate appenders
optionC: The JVM retries the request once for each catch block
optionD: throw e creates a fresh exception at every single layer
correctAnswerText: Every layer logs and rethrows; log once where it is handled
explanation: Log-and-rethrow duplicates noise and makes counting failures impossible. Either handle and log, or rethrow (wrapped) without logging.

prompt: A worker loop does try { Thread.sleep(1000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } and the app cannot shut it down cleanly. Why?
optionA: Thread.sleep ignores interrupts while it is sleeping
optionB: The empty catch restarts the thread from the top
optionC: The interrupt signal is swallowed and the flag cleared
optionD: InterruptedException can only be caught on main
correctAnswerText: The interrupt signal is swallowed and the flag cleared
explanation: Throwing InterruptedException clears the interrupted flag. Restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() or exit the loop so the shutdown request is honoured.

prompt: A team debates whether every method in a Spring service should declare throws Exception "to be safe". Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Yes: Spring requires throws Exception on service methods
optionB: Yes: declaring everything is the safest Java practice
optionC: No: methods in Spring may not declare any exception
optionD: No: it hides what can fail and forces callers to catch all
correctAnswerText: No: it hides what can fail and forces callers to catch all
explanation: throws Exception carries no information and pushes blanket catches upward. Declare the specific checked exceptions a caller can act on, or use unchecked ones.

prompt: A REST API has thirty controllers, each with its own try/catch turning exceptions into JSON errors in slightly different shapes. What is the better approach?
optionA: One @RestControllerAdvice mapping exceptions to responses
optionB: Keep the per-controller catches but copy them more carefully
optionC: Return HTTP 200 with an error flag for every failure
optionD: Catch Throwable in main so no controller ever needs to
correctAnswerText: One @RestControllerAdvice mapping exceptions to responses
explanation: Central handling gives one consistent error format and keeps controllers focused on the happy path; services throw meaningful exceptions and the advice maps them to status codes.

prompt: findByEmail(email) is used by a signup page that checks whether an email is free. Should it throw UserNotFoundException when nobody matches?
optionA: No: absence is expected here, so return Optional<User>
optionB: No: it should return null and document it nowhere
optionC: Yes: every missing record must always be an exception
optionD: Yes: exceptions are cheaper than an Optional wrapper
correctAnswerText: No: absence is expected here, so return Optional<User>
explanation: Exceptions are for exceptional outcomes. When "not found" is a normal answer, Optional makes it explicit without using exceptions for control flow; a getById that must succeed may still throw.

prompt: One proposal uses a single AppException with an int code for every failure; another uses a small hierarchy like NotFound, Conflict and ValidationFailed. Which is better and why?
optionA: The single class: int codes are faster to compare than types
optionB: The hierarchy: callers catch by type, not by magic numbers
optionC: The single class: fewer classes always means simpler code
optionD: The hierarchy, but only if each type is a checked exception
correctAnswerText: The hierarchy: callers catch by type, not by magic numbers
explanation: Types let catch blocks and a global handler dispatch cleanly and let the compiler help. A code field forces switch statements on numbers everywhere.

prompt: A background job runner wraps each job in catch (Throwable t) { log(t); } and moves on to the next job. When is that defensible?
optionA: Everywhere: catching Throwable is always the safest
optionB: Never: catching Throwable fails to compile in Java
optionC: At the top level only, logging fully, never mid-logic
optionD: Only when the job code throws checked exceptions
correctAnswerText: At the top level only, logging fully, never mid-logic
explanation: A top-level boundary may log and keep the worker alive, but catching Throwable deep in logic would swallow Errors like OutOfMemoryError and hide bugs.

prompt: An API returns e.printStackTrace() text in the JSON body "to help frontend developers debug". How do you judge it?
optionA: Good practice: more detail always helps API consumers
optionB: Fine as long as the frontend hides it from the users
optionC: Log the trace server-side; send a safe message and an id
optionD: Acceptable because stack traces never contain secrets
correctAnswerText: Log the trace server-side; send a safe message and an id
explanation: Traces reveal class names, library versions and sometimes SQL or data, which helps attackers. Return a clean error with a correlation id and keep detail in server logs.

prompt: A payment client retries three times on any Exception. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Sound: any exception may succeed on another try
optionB: Sound, but it should retry ten times instead
optionC: Retry only on NullPointerException and errors
optionD: Retry only transient failures such as timeouts
correctAnswerText: Retry only transient failures such as timeouts
explanation: Validation errors or "card declined" will fail every time, and blind retries of a payment can charge twice. Retry what is transient, and make retried calls idempotent.

prompt: Where should a low-level SQLException be translated into a domain exception such as OrderStoreFailure?
optionA: At the repository boundary, chaining the original cause
optionB: Nowhere: let SQLException flow up to the browser as is
optionC: In the controller, so the web layer knows the SQL detail
optionD: In the database driver, by editing its source code
correctAnswerText: At the repository boundary, chaining the original cause
explanation: Translating where the technology lives keeps JDBC types out of service code and lets the storage change without rewriting callers; the cause keeps the detail.

prompt: Should a BankAccount constructor throw IllegalArgumentException for a negative opening balance, or accept it and let later methods check?
optionA: Throw a checked Exception so callers must retry it
optionB: Throw at construction so no invalid object can exist
optionC: Accept it; validation belongs only in the database
optionD: Accept it and print a warning to the console instead
correctAnswerText: Throw at construction so no invalid object can exist
explanation: Failing fast puts the error next to its cause. An object that can exist in an invalid state forces every method to re-check, and one will forget.

prompt: You write a SerialPortSession class that must release a hardware port. What is the best way to make sure callers release it?
optionA: Implement AutoCloseable so callers use try-with-resources
optionB: Ask callers to remember to call release() at the end
optionC: Release the port in an overridden finalize() method
optionD: Release the port in a static block of the class
correctAnswerText: Implement AutoCloseable so callers use try-with-resources
explanation: AutoCloseable lets the language guarantee release on every path. finalize() is deprecated and runs unpredictably, if at all.

prompt: Which collection interface does not allow duplicate elements?
optionA: Queue
optionB: Deque
optionC: List
optionD: Set
correctAnswerText: Set
explanation: A Set holds each element at most once, as decided by equals (or by compare for sorted sets). Lists and queues keep duplicates.

prompt: Which Map implementation keeps its keys in sorted order?
optionA: TreeMap
optionB: HashMap
optionC: IdentityHashMap
optionD: LinkedHashMap
correctAnswerText: TreeMap
explanation: TreeMap is a red-black tree ordered by natural order or a Comparator. HashMap has no order; LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order.

prompt: Which Map iterates its entries in the order they were first inserted?
optionA: EnumMap
optionB: LinkedHashMap
optionC: TreeMap
optionD: HashMap
correctAnswerText: LinkedHashMap
explanation: LinkedHashMap threads a linked list through its entries, so iteration follows insertion order (or access order if configured).

prompt: On a Queue, which method removes and returns the head, or returns null if it is empty?
optionA: element()
optionB: poll()
optionC: peek()
optionD: remove()
correctAnswerText: poll()
explanation: poll removes the head or returns null; remove does the same but throws when empty; peek and element only look without removing.

prompt: Which method does a class implement to give its objects a natural ordering?
optionA: equals(Object o)
optionB: compare(T a, T b)
optionC: sortKey()
optionD: compareTo(T other)
correctAnswerText: compareTo(T other)
explanation: Comparable<T> declares compareTo, implemented by the class itself. compare(a, b) belongs to Comparator, an external ordering.

prompt: What should compare(a, b) return when a should come before b?
optionA: Exactly zero
optionB: A negative number
optionC: A positive number
optionD: The boolean true
correctAnswerText: A negative number
explanation: Negative means a sorts first, zero means equal for ordering purposes, positive means a sorts after b. Only the sign matters.

prompt: What kind of list does List.of("a", "b") (Java 9+) return?
optionA: A fixed-size list whose items can be replaced
optionB: A thread-safe list that locks on every change
optionC: A normal ArrayList that can grow and shrink
optionD: An unmodifiable list that rejects any change
correctAnswerText: An unmodifiable list that rejects any change
explanation: List.of returns an unmodifiable list: add, remove and set all throw UnsupportedOperationException, and null elements are rejected.

prompt: Which exception do ArrayList iterators typically throw when the list is structurally changed mid-loop?
optionA: IllegalStateException
optionB: UnsupportedOperationException
optionC: ConcurrentModificationException
optionD: IndexOutOfBoundsException
correctAnswerText: ConcurrentModificationException
explanation: ArrayList iterators are fail-fast: they track a modification count and throw ConcurrentModificationException when it changes behind their back, even in a single thread.

prompt: How many null keys can a HashMap hold?
optionA: Unlimited
optionB: One
optionC: None
optionD: One per bucket
correctAnswerText: One
explanation: HashMap allows a single null key (keys are unique) and any number of null values. TreeMap with natural ordering and Map.of reject null keys.

prompt: What does the type List<? extends Number> describe?
optionA: A list of Number or any supertype such as Object
optionB: A list that can only ever hold Integer elements
optionC: A list that may mix Number and every other type
optionD: A list of some one type that is Number or a subtype
correctAnswerText: A list of some one type that is Number or a subtype
explanation: An upper-bounded wildcard: it could be a List<Integer>, List<Double> or List<Number>. You can read Numbers from it but not safely add to it.

prompt: Why is list.get(5000) fast on an ArrayList but slow on a LinkedList?
optionA: LinkedList sorts itself before it answers any get call
optionB: LinkedList copies its whole content on every single read
optionC: ArrayList caches every value that has been read before
optionD: ArrayList indexes an array; LinkedList walks node by node
correctAnswerText: ArrayList indexes an array; LinkedList walks node by node
explanation: ArrayList is backed by an array, so get(i) is O(1). LinkedList must follow links from the nearer end, which is O(n).

prompt: How does a HashMap find the entry for a key on get(key)?
optionA: equals is called on every key until one of them matches
optionB: The key's toString is used as an index into an array
optionC: Keys are kept sorted and found with a binary search
optionD: hashCode picks a bucket; equals finds the key within it
correctAnswerText: hashCode picks a bucket; equals finds the key within it
explanation: The hash narrows the search to one bucket, then equals confirms the exact key. That is why both methods must agree for keys.

prompt: Why are String and Integer such safe choices for HashMap keys?
optionA: They are final, so HashMap can skip calling equals
optionB: They have no hashCode, so collisions cannot happen
optionC: They are stored outside the map and never compared
optionD: They are immutable, so their hash can never change
correctAnswerText: They are immutable, so their hash can never change
explanation: An immutable key keeps the same hashCode for its whole life, so it stays findable in the bucket it was stored in.

prompt: What is the main difference between Comparable and Comparator?
optionA: Comparable is checked at run time; Comparator at compile time
optionB: Comparable is one built-in order; Comparator is any outside one
optionC: Comparable is for lists; Comparator is only for maps and sets
optionD: Comparable sorts in ascending order; Comparator only descending
correctAnswerText: Comparable is one built-in order; Comparator is any outside one
explanation: A class implements Comparable once to define its natural order. Comparators are separate objects, so you can have many orders (by name, by marks) without touching the class.

prompt: Why is Iterator.remove() safe during a loop while list.remove(x) is not?
optionA: list.remove is slower and the loop times out because of it
optionB: Iterator.remove works on a copy and leaves the list alone
optionC: Iterator.remove only marks items and deletes them later
optionD: The iterator updates its own expected count as it removes
correctAnswerText: The iterator updates its own expected count as it removes
explanation: The iterator knows about its own changes and keeps its bookkeeping in step. A change made through the list directly is detected as foreign and fails fast.

prompt: A method copies items from src into dest. Why is its signature copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dest)?
optionA: super makes dest immutable while it is being copied
optionB: src only produces Ts; dest only needs to accept Ts
optionC: extends is for reading lists and super is for sorting
optionD: Wildcards make the copy run in parallel across threads
correctAnswerText: src only produces Ts; dest only needs to accept Ts
explanation: Producer extends, consumer super (PECS): reading from src needs it to yield Ts, writing to dest needs it to accept Ts, and both bounds widen what callers can pass.

prompt: Integer is a subtype of Number, so why can a List<Integer> not be passed where List<Number> is required?
optionA: Integer is final and so cannot be stored as a Number
optionB: List<Number> may only hold primitive number values
optionC: Otherwise a Double could be added to a list of Integers
optionD: Generic types are erased, so they cannot be compared
correctAnswerText: Otherwise a Double could be added to a list of Integers
explanation: Generics are invariant: a List<Number> accepts add(3.5), which would corrupt a List<Integer>. Use List<? extends Number> when you only read.

prompt: How does Collections.unmodifiableList(list) differ from List.copyOf(list)?
optionA: The first is sorted; the second keeps insertion order
optionB: The first allows add calls; the second rejects them all
optionC: The first is a live read-only view; the second a snapshot
optionD: The first makes a deep copy; the second a shallow one
correctAnswerText: The first is a live read-only view; the second a snapshot
explanation: unmodifiableList wraps the original, so later changes to it show through. List.copyOf (Java 10+) copies the elements into a new unmodifiable list.

prompt: Why should code never rely on the iteration order of a HashSet or HashMap?
optionA: They sort elements by hashCode, which callers cannot see
optionB: They iterate in random order that changes on every loop
optionC: They always iterate in reverse insertion order instead
optionD: Order follows bucket layout, which can change on resize
correctAnswerText: Order follows bucket layout, which can change on resize
explanation: Order depends on hash values and table capacity, so it can shift when the map grows or the JDK changes. Use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap when order matters.

prompt: Why does the Java documentation recommend ArrayDeque over the old Stack class?
optionA: Stack cannot store objects, only primitive int values
optionB: ArrayDeque is the only one that supports push and pop
optionC: Stack was removed from the JDK in Java 9 and later
optionD: Stack extends Vector, so it is synchronised and leaky
correctAnswerText: Stack extends Vector, so it is synchronised and leaky
explanation: Stack inherits Vector's locking and its index methods, which let callers break LIFO order. Deque gives push/pop/peek without either cost.

optionA: [banana, cherry, mango, Apple]
optionB: [Apple, banana, cherry, mango]
optionC: [Apple, mango, banana, cherry]
optionD: [mango, Apple, banana, cherry]
correctAnswerText: [Apple, banana, cherry, mango]
explanation: TreeSet uses String's natural order, which compares character codes; uppercase letters sort before lowercase, so "Apple" comes first.

optionA: {ravi=1, anu=2, kiran=3}
optionB: {anu=2, kiran=3, ravi=9}
optionC: {anu=2, kiran=3, ravi=1}
optionD: {ravi=9, anu=2, kiran=3}
correctAnswerText: {ravi=9, anu=2, kiran=3}
explanation: Re-inserting an existing key replaces its value but keeps its original position in insertion order.

optionA: 2 Pune Hyderabad
optionB: 1 null Hyderabad
optionC: 1 Hyderabad Pune
optionD: 1 Pune Hyderabad
correctAnswerText: 1 Pune Hyderabad
explanation: Keys are unique, so the second put replaces the value and returns the previous one ("Pune"). The map still has one entry.
remove(int index) is chosen over remove(Object) for an int literal, so the element at index 1 (20) goes. Use remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) to remove the value 1.

optionA: [a, b, c] UOE
optionB: [z, b, c, d]
optionC: [z, b, c] UOE
optionD: UOE before any list is printed
correctAnswerText: [z, b, c] UOE
explanation: Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view over an array: set works because it replaces in place, but add would need to grow the array and throws.

optionA: [fig, pear, kiwi, date, apple]
optionB: [fig, date, kiwi, pear, apple]
optionC: [apple, pear, kiwi, date, fig]
optionD: [fig, pear, kiwi, apple, date]
correctAnswerText: [fig, pear, kiwi, date, apple]
explanation: Shortest first; the three four-letter words tie on length and are then ordered in reverse alphabetical order: pear, kiwi, date.

optionA: {be=2, or=1, not=1, to=2}
optionB: {be=2, not=1, or=1, to=2}
optionC: {be=1, not=1, or=1, to=1}
optionD: {to=2, be=2, or=1, not=1}
correctAnswerText: {be=2, not=1, or=1, to=2}
explanation: merge inserts 1 for a new key or sums with the existing value; TreeMap prints keys in alphabetical order.
A PriorityQueue hands out the smallest element (by natural order) first; peek looks at the next one without removing it.

prompt: You must drop every even number from an ArrayList<Integer> nums. Which line does it safely?
optionA: for (int x : nums) if (x % 2 == 0) nums.remove(x);
optionB: nums.forEach(x -> { if (x % 2 == 0) nums.remove(x); });
optionC: for (int i = 0; i < nums.size(); i++) nums.remove(i);
optionD: nums.removeIf(x -> x % 2 == 0);
correctAnswerText: nums.removeIf(x -> x % 2 == 0);
explanation: removeIf (Java 8+) removes matching elements in one safe pass. Removing through the list inside for-each or forEach fails fast, and the index loop removes the wrong items.

prompt: A registration form collects emails; duplicates must be dropped and the list shown in the order people signed up. Which type fits?
optionA: HashSet<String>
optionB: LinkedHashSet<String>
optionC: ArrayList<String>
optionD: TreeSet<String>
correctAnswerText: LinkedHashSet<String>
explanation: A Set removes duplicates and the linked variant preserves insertion order. TreeSet would sort alphabetically, HashSet has no order, and a List keeps duplicates.

optionA: equals cannot be called on items during a for-each
optionB: Strings cannot be removed while they are referenced
optionC: The list changed outside the loop's hidden iterator
optionD: ArrayList forbids removing any element except the last
correctAnswerText: The list changed outside the loop's hidden iterator
explanation: for-each uses an Iterator; l.remove bumps the modification count and the next call to next() detects it. Use Iterator.remove or removeIf.

prompt: Person is a record (Java 16+). After adding Asha (21), Bala (22) and Chitra (21) to new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age)), size() is 2. Why?
optionA: Compare says 0 for equal ages, so Chitra counts as present
optionB: TreeSet keeps only the first and the last item it is given
optionC: Records cannot be stored in sorted sets in any Java version
optionD: comparingInt drops odd numbers when it compares the ages
correctAnswerText: Compare says 0 for equal ages, so Chitra counts as present
explanation: A TreeSet uses compare, not equals, to decide duplicates. Add a tie-breaker such as thenComparing(Person::name) to keep both.

prompt: RollNo wraps a String and overrides neither equals nor hashCode. m.put(new RollNo("21CS07"), "Meena") then m.get(new RollNo("21CS07")) returns null. Why?
optionA: Two RollNo objects are only equal if they are the same one
optionB: HashMap cannot use user-defined classes as its key type
optionC: get returns null until the map has been resized at least once
optionD: The String inside is copied, so the two values now differ
correctAnswerText: Two RollNo objects are only equal if they are the same one
explanation: With Object's equals and hashCode, a new RollNo with the same text is a different key. Override both, or make RollNo a record.

prompt: A service builds List<String> tags = List.of(a, b); and later calls tags.add(c). Some requests also fail earlier with NullPointerException. What explains both?
optionA: List.of is fixed-size but does allow null as elements
optionB: tags.add only fails when two threads call it at once
optionC: List.of returns null whenever any argument is empty
optionD: List.of is unmodifiable and also rejects null elements
correctAnswerText: List.of is unmodifiable and also rejects null elements
explanation: add throws UnsupportedOperationException, and List.of(a, b) throws NPE when a or b is null. Use new ArrayList<>(...) when the list must change.
The view reads through to base, so it sees "y". The copy was taken before the add and is a separate unmodifiable list.

prompt: Why does static void fill(List<? extends Number> nums) { nums.add(1); } fail to compile?
optionA: Number is abstract, so nothing can be added to such a list
optionB: nums might be a List<Double>, so adding an Integer is unsafe
optionC: Methods with wildcard parameters must be declared generic
optionD: The literal 1 is an int and lists cannot hold primitives
correctAnswerText: nums might be a List<Double>, so adding an Integer is unsafe
explanation: With ? extends, the compiler does not know the exact element type, so it allows no adds except null. Use List<? super Integer> to add.

prompt: Sorting [5, Integer.MIN_VALUE, -3] with l.sort((x, y) -> x - y) leaves it as [5, -2147483648, -3]. What is the bug?
optionA: sort ignores comparators that are written as lambdas
optionB: Negative numbers are always sorted after positive ones
optionC: Lambdas cannot compare boxed Integer values correctly
optionD: x - y overflows for extreme values and flips the sign
correctAnswerText: x - y overflows for extreme values and flips the sign
explanation: 5 - MIN_VALUE overflows to a negative number, so 5 is judged smaller. Use Integer.compare(x, y) or Comparator.naturalOrder().

prompt: List<Integer> l = List.of(100, 100, 1000, 1000); prints true false for (l.get(0) == l.get(1)) and (l.get(2) == l.get(3)). Why the difference?
optionA: List.of stores values above 999 as Long objects
optionB: The second pair was added later and is a copy
optionC: == compares values but 1000 overflows the cache
optionD: == compares references; only -128..127 are cached
correctAnswerText: == compares references; only -128..127 are cached
explanation: Autoboxing reuses cached Integer objects for -128 to 127, so 100 matches by identity while 1000 does not. Compare boxed values with equals.

prompt: A job checks each of 200,000 incoming roll numbers with seenList.contains(roll) before adding it to an ArrayList, and it takes minutes. What is the cause?
optionA: contains scans the whole list, making the job quadratic
optionB: contains locks the list, so the calls are serialised
optionC: ArrayList resizes on every add, copying all the strings
optionD: Strings are hashed again on each call to contains
correctAnswerText: contains scans the whole list, making the job quadratic
explanation: List.contains is O(n), so n checks cost O(n squared). A HashSet gives O(1) average contains and add.

prompt: Class loading fails with IllegalArgumentException at static final Map<String,Integer> CODES = Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2, "a", 3);. Why?
optionA: Map.of accepts at most two key and value pairs in total
optionB: Map.of cannot be assigned to a static final field at all
optionC: Map.of throws on a duplicate key instead of replacing it
optionD: Integer values must be boxed explicitly for Map.of
correctAnswerText: Map.of throws on a duplicate key instead of replacing it
explanation: Unlike put, the Map.of factory treats a repeated key as a bug and throws IllegalArgumentException ("duplicate key").

prompt: A results page appends marks at the end and then reads them by index for paging. A teammate picks LinkedList "because inserts are O(1)". Your judgement?
optionA: LinkedList: inserts dominate, so it is always the winner
optionB: ArrayList: appends are amortised O(1) and get(i) is fast
optionC: Either: both have the same cost for get(i) in practice
optionD: LinkedList: it uses less memory per element than arrays
correctAnswerText: ArrayList: appends are amortised O(1) and get(i) is fast
explanation: Appending to ArrayList is amortised O(1) and indexing is O(1); LinkedList pays O(n) per get and more memory per node. LinkedList rarely wins in practice.

prompt: A contest leaderboard must show the top ten scores and "everyone between 70 and 80". Which map suits it best?
optionA: HashMap, since O(1) lookups beat everything else here
optionB: EnumMap, since scores fall into a fixed set of values
optionC: TreeMap, for sorted keys and range views like subMap
optionD: LinkedHashMap, since it remembers when scores arrived
correctAnswerText: TreeMap, for sorted keys and range views like subMap
explanation: The queries are about order and ranges, which TreeMap answers in O(log n) with headMap, tailMap and subMap. A HashMap would need a full scan and sort each time.

prompt: A Batch class exposes its students list. Callers must not change it and should see a stable result even if the batch changes later. What should the getter return?
optionA: students itself, so callers always see the latest data
optionB: A new ArrayList<>(students) that callers may freely edit
optionC: Collections.unmodifiableList(students), a live view
optionD: List.copyOf(students), a snapshot callers cannot change
correctAnswerText: List.copyOf(students), a snapshot callers cannot change
explanation: Both needs are met by an unmodifiable copy. A view still changes under the caller; a plain ArrayList copy is stable but invites confused edits that go nowhere.

prompt: Many request threads read and update a shared Map of session counts. Which choice is soundest?
optionA: HashMap, since reads far outnumber the writes here
optionB: Collections.synchronizedMap with get then put calls
optionC: TreeMap, because sorted maps are safe for threads
optionD: ConcurrentHashMap, using merge for atomic updates
correctAnswerText: ConcurrentHashMap, using merge for atomic updates
explanation: ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent access and merge/compute update a key atomically. A synchronized map still races on get-then-put; a plain HashMap can corrupt.

prompt: Old code uses List items = new ArrayList(); with casts on every get. A fresher says "it works, leave it". How do you judge it?
optionA: Use List<Item>: errors move from run time to compile time
optionB: Use List<Object>: that is what raw types already mean
optionC: Leave it: raw types run faster since nothing is checked
optionD: Leave it: generics are removed at run time, so no gain
correctAnswerText: Use List<Item>: errors move from run time to compile time
explanation: Raw types let any object in and fail later with ClassCastException far from the cause. Generics are erased at run time, but the compile-time checks are the whole benefit.

prompt: Each user has a set of permissions drawn from enum Permission { READ, WRITE, DELETE, ADMIN }. What is the best set implementation?
optionA: EnumSet, a compact bit set in declaration order
optionB: HashSet, since it suits any type equally well
optionC: TreeSet, since enums cannot be hashed safely
optionD: ArrayList, since there are only four values
correctAnswerText: EnumSet, a compact bit set in declaration order
explanation: EnumSet stores enum members as bits: tiny, very fast, and ordered by declaration. HashSet works but wastes space; a List allows duplicates.

prompt: A report joins 50,000 orders to 5,000 customers by looping over the customer list for every order. What is the better design?
optionA: Switch the customer list to a LinkedList instead
optionB: Sort the orders first so the loop can end earlier
optionC: Build a Map from id to customer once, then look up
optionD: Run the same nested loop on more threads at once
correctAnswerText: Build a Map from id to customer once, then look up
explanation: The nested loop is O(orders x customers). One pass to build a HashMap makes each lookup O(1), turning 250 million comparisons into about 55,000 operations.

prompt: Employee implements Comparable by salary, because one report sorts by salary. Others sort by name or joining date. How do you judge it?
optionA: Right: the first sort needed should become the natural one
optionB: Implement Comparable three times, once for each order
optionC: Fine, as long as equals also compares only the salary
optionD: Use Comparators per report; salary is no natural order
correctAnswerText: Use Comparators per report; salary is no natural order
explanation: Natural order should be the one obvious ordering and consistent with equals; two employees with the same salary are not equal. Report-specific orders belong in Comparators.

prompt: findCourses(studentId) returns null when a student has no courses. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Return an empty list so callers can loop without checks
optionB: Return a list holding one null element as a marker
optionC: Throw an exception, since no courses is always an error
optionD: Keep null, because it clearly signals "nothing found"
correctAnswerText: Return an empty list so callers can loop without checks
explanation: An empty collection is a valid answer that every loop handles; null forces a check at every call site, and the one that forgets throws NullPointerException.

prompt: A breadth-first search over a campus map needs a queue of nodes. Which declaration is the best choice?
optionA: Stack<Node> q = new Stack<>();
optionB: List<Node> q = new ArrayList<>();
optionC: Set<Node> q = new HashSet<>();
optionD: Deque<Node> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
correctAnswerText: Deque<Node> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
explanation: ArrayDeque gives O(1) offer and poll at both ends with less overhead than LinkedList. Removing from the front of an ArrayList is O(n), a Stack is LIFO, and a Set has no order.

prompt: What makes a Java interface a functional interface that a lambda can implement?
optionA: It has a single generic type parameter T
optionB: It is annotated with @FunctionalInterface
optionC: It declares only default and static methods
optionD: It declares exactly one abstract method
correctAnswerText: It declares exactly one abstract method
explanation: One abstract method is the whole rule. @FunctionalInterface only asks the compiler to check it; an interface without the annotation still qualifies.

prompt: Which java.util.function interface takes a value and returns a boolean?
optionA: Predicate<T>
optionB: Function<T, R>
optionC: Consumer<T>
optionD: Supplier<T>
correctAnswerText: Predicate<T>
explanation: Predicate.test(T) returns boolean, which is why filter() takes one. Function maps, Consumer returns nothing, Supplier takes nothing.

prompt: Which of these stream operations is a terminal operation?
optionA: collect
optionB: sorted
optionC: map
optionD: filter
correctAnswerText: collect
explanation: collect produces a result and ends the pipeline. map, filter and sorted are intermediate: they return another stream and do nothing on their own.

prompt: Which lambda is equivalent to the method reference String::length?
optionA: () -> String.length()
optionB: s -> s.length()
optionC: (s, n) -> s.length(n)
optionD: s -> String.length(s)
correctAnswerText: s -> s.length()
explanation: A reference to an instance method through the class name takes the object as its first argument: String::length means s -> s.length().

prompt: What is java.util.Optional<T>?
optionA: An annotation marking a parameter as optional
optionB: A wrapper that makes any field nullable safely
optionC: A list type that holds at most one element
optionD: A container that may or may not hold a value
correctAnswerText: A container that may or may not hold a value
explanation: Optional is a box that is either empty or holds one non-null value, so a method can say "there may be no result" in its return type.

prompt: Which stream operation turns each element into a stream and merges them into one?
optionA: reduce
optionB: concat
optionC: map
optionD: flatMap
correctAnswerText: flatMap
explanation: flatMap maps each element to a stream and flattens the results into a single stream; map would leave you with a stream of streams.

prompt: What does Collectors.groupingBy(classifier) return for a Stream<T> by default?
optionA: A Set<K> of keys
optionB: A Map<K, List<T>>
optionC: A List<List<T>>
optionD: A Map<K, Long>
correctAnswerText: A Map<K, List<T>>
explanation: Each key from the classifier maps to the list of elements that produced it. A downstream collector such as counting() changes the value type.

prompt: What does the compiler generate for record Point(int x, int y) {}  (Java 16+)?
optionA: Only a constructor; equality stays by reference
optionB: A no-argument constructor plus public fields

prompt: What does reduce(identity, accumulator) do with a stream?

correctAnswerText: Combines all elements into one result

prompt: Which functional interface fits the lambda () -> new ArrayList<String>()?

correctAnswerText: Supplier<List<String>>

prompt: Why does list.stream().filter(...).map(...) on its own do no work at all?

optionD: Intermediate steps only run once a terminal step asks
correctAnswerText: Intermediate steps only run once a terminal step asks
explanation: Intermediate operations are lazy: they build a recipe. Only a terminal operation such as collect or forEach pulls elements through it.

prompt: Why can a Stream object not be traversed a second time?

correctAnswerText: A stream is a one-shot view that is consumed as it runs
explanation: A stream is not a collection; it is a single pass over a source. Reusing it throws IllegalStateException, so create a fresh stream from the source instead.

prompt: Why must a local variable used inside a lambda be effectively final?
optionA: Lambdas run on another thread that cannot see the stack

optionC: The compiler inlines the lambda only for final values

correctAnswerText: The lambda captures a copy, so changes could never agree
explanation: The lambda gets a copy of the value, and it may run after the method returns. Allowing either side to change it would make the two copies silently disagree.

prompt: For a List<Order> where each order has a List<Item>, why use flatMap rather than map to get all items?
optionA: flatMap removes duplicate items across different orders
optionB: map gives one list per order; flatMap gives one item stream
optionC: map can only return primitives, not lists of objects

correctAnswerText: map gives one list per order; flatMap gives one item stream
explanation: map(Order::getItems) yields Stream<List<Item>>. flatMap(o -> o.getItems().stream()) yields Stream<Item>, the shape you actually want.

prompt: What is the difference between opt.orElse(load()) and opt.orElseGet(() -> load())?

optionB: orElse always calls load(); orElseGet only when empty

optionD: orElseGet always calls load(); orElse only when empty
correctAnswerText: orElse always calls load(); orElseGet only when empty
explanation: orElse takes a value, so its argument is evaluated before the call even when a value is present. orElseGet takes a Supplier and runs it only for an empty Optional.

prompt: Why can anyMatch return early on a stream of a million elements?
optionA: It samples elements randomly instead of checking all
optionB: It sorts the stream first and checks only the start
optionC: It runs in parallel by default and splits the work
optionD: It is short-circuiting and stops at the first match
correctAnswerText: It is short-circuiting and stops at the first match
explanation: anyMatch, findFirst, limit and similar are short-circuiting: once the answer is known no further elements are pulled, which also lets them finish on infinite streams.

prompt: Why does Collectors.toMap(keyFn, valueFn) need a third argument when keys can repeat?

correctAnswerText: Without a merge function a repeated key throws
explanation: The two-argument toMap throws IllegalStateException ("Duplicate key") on a clash. The third argument, a merge function such as Integer::sum, says how to combine the values.

prompt: Why is a parallel stream over a list of 50 numbers usually slower than a sequential one?
optionA: Parallel streams must sort elements before processing
optionB: The JVM limits parallel streams to a single core anyway
optionC: Splitting, scheduling and merging cost more than the work
optionD: Parallel streams always copy the list into an array first
correctAnswerText: Splitting, scheduling and merging cost more than the work
explanation: Parallelism has fixed overhead: splitting the source, handing tasks to the common ForkJoinPool and combining results. With tiny work per element that overhead dominates.

prompt: Why is Optional discouraged as the type of an entity field?

correctAnswerText: It was designed as a return type and is not Serializable
explanation: Optional exists to signal "maybe no result" from a method. It is not Serializable and frameworks such as JPA do not map it, so fields stay nullable and getters may return Optional.

prompt: A record Team(String name, List<String> members) is called immutable. Why is that only partly true?

correctAnswerText: Its fields are final, but the list itself can still change
explanation: Record fields are final, so members cannot be reassigned, but a mutable List can still be added to. Copy it with List.copyOf in a compact constructor for real immutability.

prompt: Which pipeline returns the three highest distinct salaries from a List<Integer> salaries?

prompt: A teammate adds .parallelStream() to a Spring controller that filters 200 products per request. Your judgement?

correctAnswerText: Remove it: tiny input, and every request shares one pool
explanation: Two hundred cheap filters gain nothing from parallelism, and all parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool, so concurrent requests contend for it. Measure before parallelising.

prompt: For a repository method that looks up a user by email, which return type is the better design?

prompt: A method is declared search(String term, Optional<String> city). What is the better design?

prompt: Code must walk a list, call a method that throws a checked IOException, and stop at the first failure. Loop or stream?

correctAnswerText: A plain for loop: checked exceptions and early exit are natural
explanation: Lambdas in java.util.function cannot throw checked exceptions, so a stream needs wrapping that hides the real error. A loop handles both the exception and the early stop directly.

prompt: Should a JPA @Entity in a Spring Boot 3 project be written as a Java record?

explanation: Hibernate instantiates entities through a no-arg constructor and sets fields, and records are final with final fields. Records suit DTOs and projections instead.

prompt: A pipeline uses .peek(o -> o.setStatus(SHIPPED)) to update orders before counting them. Your judgement?

correctAnswerText: Move the update out: peek is for debugging, not logic
explanation: peek may be skipped when the stream can compute the result without visiting elements (count() on a sized source does this since Java 9). Do the update in a forEach or a loop.

prompt: Summing ten million int scores, one version uses Stream<Integer>.reduce(0, Integer::sum), another mapToInt(...).sum(). Which is better?

optionB: mapToInt: it avoids boxing every value into an Integer

optionD: reduce: it is the general form, so the JIT favours it
correctAnswerText: mapToInt: it avoids boxing every value into an Integer
explanation: Stream<Integer> boxes and unboxes every element, creating garbage and indirection. IntStream works on primitives and is the right choice for numeric work.

prompt: A report groups sales by month and must list months in order. Which collector choice is best?
optionA: groupingBy(Sale::month, TreeMap::new, toList())

correctAnswerText: groupingBy(Sale::month, TreeMap::new, toList())
explanation: The default groupingBy builds a HashMap with no ordering promise. Passing TreeMap::new as the map factory keeps keys sorted where the map is built.

prompt: A filter lambda has grown to eight lines of business rules. What is the best way to improve the pipeline?
optionA: Convert the whole pipeline to a parallel stream instead
