correctAnswerText: Move the rules to a named method and use a method reference
explanation: filter(this::isEligible) reads as intent, and the named method can be unit-tested on its own. Long inline lambdas are where stream code stops being readable.

prompt: In which case is a parallel stream most likely to be worth trying?
optionA: A CPU-heavy pure function over a large ArrayList in a batch job
optionB: Calling a remote API for each element inside a web request
optionC: Reading lines from a LinkedList and adding them to a HashMap
optionD: Writing each element of a small list to the same log file
correctAnswerText: A CPU-heavy pure function over a large ArrayList in a batch job
explanation: Parallelism pays off for lots of independent CPU work over a source that splits well (arrays, ArrayList). Shared output, blocking I/O and poorly-splitting sources defeat it.

prompt: Which single method does the Runnable interface declare?
optionA: void start()
optionB: void execute()
optionC: Object call()
optionD: void run()
correctAnswerText: void run()
explanation: Runnable has one method, void run(), which holds the task. start() belongs to Thread, call() to Callable, execute() to Executor.

prompt: Which Thread method actually begins a new thread of execution?
optionA: run()
optionB: begin()
optionC: launch()
optionD: start()
correctAnswerText: start()
explanation: start() asks the JVM to create a new thread, which then calls run(). Calling run() yourself just runs it on the current thread.

prompt: What does the synchronized keyword guarantee for a block of code?
optionA: The block is retried if another thread fails
optionB: The block runs faster on a multi-core CPU
optionC: The block always runs on the main thread
optionD: Only one thread at a time holds its lock
correctAnswerText: Only one thread at a time holds its lock
explanation: synchronized takes an object's monitor lock, so threads using the same lock run the block one at a time; it also makes their changes visible to each other.

prompt: What does marking a field volatile guarantee?
optionA: The field can never be changed once it is set
optionB: Only one thread can modify the field at a time
optionC: The field is stored on the stack, not the heap
optionD: Every read sees the latest write by any thread
correctAnswerText: Every read sees the latest write by any thread
explanation: volatile is about visibility: writes are published to other threads and reads are not served from a stale cached copy. It does not make compound updates atomic.

prompt: What is a deadlock?
optionA: Two threads that write the same field at one time
optionB: A thread that is killed while still holding a lock
optionC: A thread that loops forever and never releases CPU
optionD: Threads each waiting for a lock another one holds
correctAnswerText: Threads each waiting for a lock another one holds
explanation: In a deadlock each thread holds something the other needs and waits for it, so none can proceed. A busy loop is livelock or starvation; concurrent writes are a race.

prompt: What is an ExecutorService?
optionA: A scheduler that runs the main method at JVM startup
optionB: A thread that executes SQL statements in the background
optionC: A class that converts a Runnable into a new process
optionD: A service that runs submitted tasks on managed threads
correctAnswerText: A service that runs submitted tasks on managed threads
explanation: You hand it tasks with submit or execute; it owns the threads, usually a reusable pool, and gives back Futures for results.

prompt: What can a Callable do that a Runnable cannot?
optionA: Repeat itself at a fixed interval of time
optionB: Run on the main thread instead of in a pool
optionC: Skip the executor queue and run immediately
optionD: Return a result and throw a checked exception
correctAnswerText: Return a result and throw a checked exception
explanation: Callable.call() returns a value and may throw checked exceptions; the Future from submit carries either back. Runnable.run() returns void and cannot throw checked ones.

prompt: What does AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() provide?
optionA: A counter that resets itself when it reaches the limit
optionB: An increment that is cached until the thread finishes
optionC: A thread-safe increment without a synchronized block
optionD: An integer that cannot be changed after it is created
correctAnswerText: A thread-safe increment without a synchronized block
explanation: Atomic classes use hardware compare-and-set so the read, add and write happen as one indivisible step, with no lock to take.

prompt: In the JVM, where do objects created with new live, and what does each thread get for itself?
optionA: Objects live in the metaspace; each thread has its own heap
optionB: Objects live in CPU registers; all threads share one stack
optionC: Objects live on the thread stack; the heap holds only classes
optionD: Objects live on the shared heap; each thread has its own stack
correctAnswerText: Objects live on the shared heap; each thread has its own stack
explanation: All threads share the heap, which is why shared objects need coordination. Local variables and call frames sit on each thread's private stack.

prompt: Which objects can the garbage collector reclaim?
optionA: Objects no longer reachable from any live reference
optionB: Objects that have not been used for a few minutes
optionC: Objects whose fields have all been set to null
optionD: Objects created inside a method that has returned
correctAnswerText: Objects no longer reachable from any live reference
explanation: Reachability is the rule: if nothing live (stack variables, static fields, other reachable objects) still points to it, it can go. Age and idleness do not matter.

prompt: Why does calling thread.run() instead of thread.start() give no concurrency?
optionA: run() creates a thread that the JVM then refuses to schedule
optionB: run() starts the thread but at the lowest possible priority
optionC: run() queues the task until the current thread has finished
optionD: run() is an ordinary call that executes on the current thread
correctAnswerText: run() is an ordinary call that executes on the current thread
explanation: Only start() creates a new thread. run() is just a method; calling it directly runs the body synchronously in the caller.

prompt: Why is count++ unsafe when two threads run it on a shared field?
optionA: Each thread gets its own copy of every field it touches
optionB: The JVM runs ++ on int fields only from the main thread
optionC: It is a read, an add and a write that can interleave
optionD: The ++ operator is not allowed on fields shared by threads
correctAnswerText: It is a read, an add and a write that can interleave
explanation: Both threads can read the same old value, add one, and write back the same result, so one increment is lost. That is a race condition.

prompt: Why does declaring a counter volatile not make count++ thread-safe?
optionA: volatile fixes visibility, but ++ is still three steps
optionB: volatile only works on boolean fields, not on int ones
optionC: volatile makes the field read-only for other threads
optionD: volatile slows writes down so increments are dropped
correctAnswerText: volatile fixes visibility, but ++ is still three steps
explanation: Each read sees the latest value, but two threads can still read, add and write in an interleaved way. Use AtomicInteger or synchronized for the compound update.

prompt: Why does main call worker.join() before printing a total the worker computed?
optionA: join merges the worker into main so that both share a stack
optionB: join waits for the worker to finish, so the total is complete
optionC: join copies the worker's variables back into the main thread
optionD: join restarts the worker if it has not produced a result yet
correctAnswerText: join waits for the worker to finish, so the total is complete
explanation: Without join, main may print before the worker finishes. join blocks until the thread ends, and everything the worker wrote is then visible to main.

prompt: Why use a thread pool rather than new Thread(...) for each incoming task?
optionA: Threads are reused and their number is bounded
optionB: Pooled threads never need any synchronization
optionC: A new Thread cannot run lambda expressions
optionD: Pool threads run with a higher CPU priority
correctAnswerText: Threads are reused and their number is bounded
explanation: Creating a thread is costly and each takes memory for its stack. A pool reuses a fixed set and queues extra work instead of creating thousands of threads.

prompt: What happens when you call future.get() on a task that is still running?
optionA: It returns null at once and fills it in later on
optionB: It throws because the task has not completed yet
optionC: It cancels the task and returns the partial result
optionD: The calling thread blocks until the result is ready
correctAnswerText: The calling thread blocks until the result is ready
explanation: get() waits. That is why calling it immediately after submit turns concurrent work back into sequential work; get(timeout, unit) bounds the wait.

prompt: Why does making every thread acquire locks in the same global order prevent deadlock?
optionA: The JVM detects the order and breaks any cycle automatically
optionB: Ordered locks are released faster, so waits never get long
optionC: No thread can hold a later lock while waiting on an earlier one
optionD: Only one lock can then be held by the program at any moment
correctAnswerText: No thread can hold a later lock while waiting on an earlier one
explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle: A waits for B while B waits for A. If everyone takes A before B, nobody can hold B while asking for A, so no cycle can form.

prompt: Why can a race condition pass every test on a developer laptop and still fail in production?
optionA: Production JVMs disable the locks that tests rely upon
optionB: Races only happen when the code is run on Linux servers
optionC: Tests run single-threaded, so races are compile errors there
optionD: Its result depends on thread timing, which changes under load
correctAnswerText: Its result depends on thread timing, which changes under load
explanation: A race is a bug whose outcome depends on how threads happen to interleave. Light test load rarely produces the bad interleaving; heavy production load eventually does.

prompt: Why should an ExecutorService created in main be shut down when the work is done?
optionA: Its pool threads are non-daemon and keep the JVM alive

prompt: Several threads count words into a shared ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> counts. Which line counts correctly?

prompt: main starts three Thread objects that each load one file, and must continue only after all three finish. What should it do?

prompt:

prompt: A service adds every response to a static Map<String, byte[]> cache and never removes entries. After two days it dies with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Diagnosis?
optionA: The garbage collector stopped running after the first day of uptime

correctAnswerText: The static map keeps every entry reachable, so the GC cannot free them
explanation: A static field is a GC root. Everything in the map stays reachable, so the heap grows until it is full. Bound the cache (size or TTL) or evict entries.

explanation: Without an executor argument runAsync uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), whose threads are daemon threads. Nothing keeps the JVM alive, so it exits first. Call join() on the future.

prompt: A web app shares one static SimpleDateFormat across requests. Under load some dates parse to nonsense or throw NumberFormatException. Cause and fix?
optionA: The pattern string is cached badly; build it with concat
optionB: SimpleDateFormat keeps mutable state; use DateTimeFormatter
optionC: Date parsing needs the main thread; parse in a constructor
optionD: Static fields are reset per request; use an instance field
correctAnswerText: SimpleDateFormat keeps mutable state; use DateTimeFormatter
explanation: SimpleDateFormat stores intermediate parse state in fields, so concurrent calls corrupt each other. java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter is immutable and safe to share.

prompt: For a single shared request counter, which is the better choice and why?
optionA: A volatile int, since volatile makes ++ atomic too
optionB: A ThreadLocal int, since each thread then has one
optionC: AtomicInteger: one variable, atomic update, no lock
optionD: A synchronized block, since atomics are often wrong
correctAnswerText: AtomicInteger: one variable, atomic update, no lock
explanation: For one variable an atomic class is simpler and cheaper than a lock. synchronized earns its place when several fields must change together; volatile and ThreadLocal do not count correctly.

prompt: An upload service uses Executors.newCachedThreadPool() for slow image processing. Traffic can spike to thousands of uploads. Your judgement?
optionA: Better to call new Thread() directly for each upload instead
optionB: Risky: it creates a thread per waiting task; use a bounded pool
optionC: Fine as long as each task calls Thread.yield() periodically
optionD: Ideal: cached pools reuse threads, so spikes are handled well
correctAnswerText: Risky: it creates a thread per waiting task; use a bounded pool
explanation: A cached pool has no upper limit: when all threads are busy it creates another. A spike can create thousands of threads and exhaust memory. A bounded pool with a queue degrades gracefully.

prompt: On an 8-core server, one pool does pure number-crunching and another mostly waits on HTTP calls. How should they be sized?
optionA: One thread each, as extra threads only add context switches
optionB: About 8 for the CPU work; noticeably more for the waiting work
optionC: About 8 for both, since cores limit every kind of task equally
optionD: More for the CPU work; about 8 for the waiting work instead
correctAnswerText: About 8 for the CPU work; noticeably more for the waiting work
explanation: CPU-bound threads beyond the core count just take turns. Threads blocked on I/O use no CPU while waiting, so more of them keep the cores busy.

prompt: A dashboard calls three independent services, 300 ms each, one after another. What is the best improvement?
optionA: Call each from its own new Thread and never join
optionB: Start all three with supplyAsync and wait with allOf
optionC: Run all three calls inside one synchronized block
optionD: Raise the JVM heap so each call completes faster
correctAnswerText: Start all three with supplyAsync and wait with allOf
explanation: Running them concurrently brings the wait to roughly the slowest call, about 300 ms. allOf (or joining each future) waits for all of them and still surfaces failures.

prompt: A product catalogue map is read by hundreds of threads and updated rarely. Collections.synchronizedMap or ConcurrentHashMap?
optionA: Either: both take one lock for every single read
optionB: ConcurrentHashMap: reads do not block each other
optionC: synchronizedMap: one lock makes reads much faster
optionD: synchronizedMap: ConcurrentHashMap loses updates
correctAnswerText: ConcurrentHashMap: reads do not block each other
explanation: synchronizedMap guards every call with one lock, so readers queue behind each other. ConcurrentHashMap reads without locking and is built for exactly this read-heavy load.

prompt: Many threads read a configuration object that changes once an hour. Which design is safest?
optionA: An immutable config object, swapped in via a volatile reference
optionB: A mutable config object with every getter made synchronized
optionC: A mutable config object copied into a ThreadLocal per request
optionD: A mutable config object whose setters are called in place
correctAnswerText: An immutable config object, swapped in via a volatile reference
explanation: An immutable object can be read by any number of threads without locks. Replacing the whole object through a volatile reference publishes the new version safely and atomically.

prompt: A developer proposes calling System.gc() every minute to stop an OutOfMemoryError. Your judgement?
optionA: Reject it: System.gc() deletes objects that are still used
optionB: Accept it: forcing GC is the standard fix for heap errors
optionC: Accept it, but call it every second for better coverage
optionD: Reject it: GC cannot free reachable objects; find the leak
correctAnswerText: Reject it: GC cannot free reachable objects; find the leak
explanation: The JVM already collects before throwing OutOfMemoryError. If memory is still full, something holds references; System.gc() is only a hint and adds pauses. Take a heap dump.

prompt: Heap usage climbs steadily for days until OutOfMemoryError. Someone doubles -Xmx and calls it fixed. Your judgement?
optionA: It is the right fix; heap errors mean the heap is too small
optionB: It only delays the crash; steady growth points to a leak
optionC: It makes things worse, since a bigger heap disables GC
optionD: It fixes it for good, since GC runs more often in big heaps
correctAnswerText: It only delays the crash; steady growth points to a leak
explanation: A heap that grows without levelling off means something keeps references. More heap buys time; a heap dump showing what fills it is what fixes it.

prompt: When is ReentrantLock a better choice than a synchronized block?
optionA: Whenever the protected code is shorter than ten lines
optionB: When you need tryLock with a timeout or a fair lock
optionC: Always, because synchronized is deprecated in Java 17
optionD: Never, because ReentrantLock cannot be released early
correctAnswerText: When you need tryLock with a timeout or a fair lock
explanation: synchronized is simpler and releases automatically. ReentrantLock adds tryLock (give up instead of waiting forever), interruptible waits and fairness, at the cost of an unlock in finally.

prompt: Audit records are written to disk by a daemon thread so it "never blocks shutdown". Your judgement?

optionC: Good: daemon threads write to disk faster than others do
optionD: Risky: daemon threads cannot write files under Java 17
correctAnswerText: Risky: daemon threads are cut off at exit, losing records
explanation: The JVM exits without waiting for daemon threads, so queued audit records can be lost. Important work needs a non-daemon thread or executor that is shut down and awaited.

prompt: Which JDBC interface represents an open session with the database?

prompt: Which character marks a parameter placeholder in PreparedStatement SQL?

prompt: In "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", which index refers to the ? in ps.setInt(index, 42)?

prompt: What is the autoCommit setting of a new JDBC connection by default?
optionA: true: each statement commits on its own

correctAnswerText: true: each statement commits on its own
explanation: A new connection is in auto-commit mode, so every statement is its own transaction. setAutoCommit(false) is how you group several statements into one.

prompt: What is a javax.sql.DataSource?
optionA: A ResultSet that can be scrolled both ways
optionB: A cache of query results kept in the JVM

correctAnswerText: A factory that hands out database connections
explanation: DataSource is the standard way to obtain connections; the implementation behind it, such as HikariDataSource, can pool them. It replaces DriverManager in applications.

prompt: What is HikariCP, the default in Spring Boot 3?
optionA: A SQL query builder
optionB: An ORM like Hibernate
optionC: A JDBC connection pool
optionD: A MySQL JDBC driver
correctAnswerText: A JDBC connection pool
explanation: HikariCP keeps a pool of open connections and lends them out through a DataSource. The driver (Connector/J) and the ORM (Hibernate) are separate layers.

prompt: What is a DAO (Data Access Object)?
optionA: A database view used to restrict data access

correctAnswerText: A class that hides the SQL for one kind of data
explanation: A DAO such as UserDao exposes findById, save and so on, and keeps the JDBC code behind them, so the rest of the application deals in objects rather than SQL.

prompt: Why does a PreparedStatement with ? parameters prevent SQL injection?
optionA: It strips quote characters out of every string value

correctAnswerText: Bound values are sent as data and never parsed as SQL
explanation: The SQL text is fixed before any value arrives; a parameter can only ever be a value, so input like ' OR '1'='1 is just an odd string, not extra SQL.

prompt: Why must every Connection be closed once you are done with it?
optionA: The JVM refuses to start a new thread until it closes
optionB: Connections are limited, and unclosed ones run out
optionC: Unclosed connections roll back all earlier commits

correctAnswerText: Connections are limited, and unclosed ones run out
explanation: Both the database and the pool allow a limited number of connections. Each one not closed stays checked out, and eventually new requests have none to use.

prompt: Why must rs.next() be called before reading the first row of a ResultSet?
optionA: next() is what sends the query to MySQL
optionB: The first row is reserved for the column count

correctAnswerText: The cursor starts before the first row
explanation: A fresh ResultSet's cursor sits before row one. next() moves it forward and returns false when no rows remain, which is why while (rs.next()) is the reading loop.

prompt: Why can rs.getInt("bonus") not tell you whether the bonus column was NULL?

prompt: Why does a web application use a connection pool instead of DriverManager.getConnection per request?
optionA: DriverManager connections cannot run PreparedStatements
optionB: Opening a connection is slow; a pool reuses open ones
optionC: A pool lets one connection serve many threads at once
optionD: DriverManager only allows a single connection per JVM
correctAnswerText: Opening a connection is slow; a pool reuses open ones
explanation: Each new connection costs a network handshake and authentication. A pool pays that once and lends connections out; it also caps how many the app can open.

prompt: Inside a manual transaction, why call conn.rollback() in the catch block?
optionA: It closes the connection and returns it to the pool
optionB: It undoes the statements that already ran in it

correctAnswerText: It undoes the statements that already ran in it
explanation: If the second of two updates fails, the first has run but is uncommitted. rollback discards it so the database never shows half the change.

prompt: With HikariCP, what does conn.close() do to a connection borrowed from the pool?
optionA: Ends the network session with the database
optionB: Nothing; pooled connections are never closed
optionC: Removes it from the pool and opens a new one
optionD: Returns it to the pool rather than ending it
correctAnswerText: Returns it to the pool rather than ending it
explanation: The pool hands out a wrapper whose close() gives the real connection back for reuse. That is why closing is still mandatory with a pool.

prompt: Why is try-with-resources preferred over closing JDBC objects at the end of the try block?
optionA: It closes them even when an exception is thrown

correctAnswerText: It closes them even when an exception is thrown
explanation: A close() at the end of try is skipped when a statement throws. try-with-resources always closes, in reverse order of declaration, and keeps the original exception.

prompt: Why is addBatch() plus executeBatch() faster than calling executeUpdate() for each of 5,000 inserts?

correctAnswerText: Many rows travel per round trip instead of one each
explanation: Most of the cost of small inserts is network round trips. A batch sends many at once. (With MySQL, rewriteBatchedStatements=true lets Connector/J merge them further.)

prompt: Why keep SQL inside a DAO instead of writing it in the service or controller classes?
optionA: Business code stays free of SQL and can be tested alone

correctAnswerText: Business code stays free of SQL and can be tested alone
explanation: The DAO is the one place that knows tables and columns. Services call methods like findByEmail, can be tested with a fake DAO, and survive a schema change untouched.

prompt: A login form gives you an email string. Which code looks the user up safely?

prompt: A transfer debits one account and credits another. Which sequence makes the two updates all-or-nothing?
optionA: setAutoCommit(false); first update; commit(); second; commit()

prompt: The column age is nullable. Which line keeps a NULL age as null in your Java object?

prompt: After inserting an order into a table with an AUTO_INCREMENT id, you need the new id. How?

prompt: You must insert 1,000 students with one PreparedStatement ps. Which loop is right?

prompt: The customers table has 3 rows with city 'Pune' and 5 with 'Chennai'. What does executeUpdate return for UPDATE customers SET tier = 'GOLD' WHERE city = 'Pune'?

optionA: In whatever order the GC picks

prompt: A search box should find products whose name contains the typed term. How do you bind it safely?

optionB: SQL "name LIKE '%?%'" with setString(1, term)

prompt: Which loop turns every row of a ResultSet rs into a Student in a list?

optionC: if (rs.next()) { list.add(new Student(rs.getInt("id"), rs.getString("name"))); }
optionD: for (int i = 0; i < rs.size(); i++) { list.add(new Student(rs.getInt(i), rs.getString(i))); }
correctAnswerText: while (rs.next()) { list.add(new Student(rs.getInt("id"), rs.getString("name"))); }
explanation: while (rs.next()) advances before each read and stops after the last row. if reads one row; ResultSet has no size(); do-while reads before the first next() and fails.

optionA: It binds userId to the first placeholder anyway
optionB: SQLException: parameter index 0 is out of range
optionC: It binds nothing, so every cart row gets deleted
optionD: It compiles to a warning and deletes no rows
correctAnswerText: SQLException: parameter index 0 is out of range
explanation: Parameter indexes start at 1, so 0 is rejected with an SQLException. The statement never runs; setLong(1, userId) is the fix.

prompt:
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "' AND pin = '" + pin + "'";
An attacker types x for name and ' OR '1'='1 for pin. What happens?
optionA: MySQL escapes the quote automatically and the attack is ignored
optionB: The WHERE clause becomes always true and every user is returned
optionC: The query fails with a syntax error because of the extra quote
optionD: No rows return, because no user has the name x in the table
correctAnswerText: The WHERE clause becomes always true and every user is returned
explanation: The SQL becomes ... name = 'x' AND pin = '' OR '1'='1'. AND binds tighter than OR, so the final OR '1'='1' is true for every row.

prompt: A DAO method does Connection c = dataSource.getConnection(); ... and returns without closing c. After about ten requests every call hangs, then fails with a timeout. Why?
optionA: MySQL blocks a client that runs more than ten queries per minute
optionB: The JDBC driver caches results and stops after ten distinct queries
optionC: The garbage collector closes connections, but only every ten calls
optionD: Each call keeps a pooled connection, until none are left to borrow
correctAnswerText: Each call keeps a pooled connection, until none are left to borrow
explanation: Unclosed connections stay checked out. Once the pool (HikariCP's default maximum is 10) is empty, getConnection waits, then times out. Use try-with-resources.

prompt: Code calls conn.setAutoCommit(false), runs an INSERT that returns 1, then closes the connection. The row never shows up in the table. Why?
optionA: executeUpdate returning 1 means the insert was queued, not run
optionB: commit() was never called, so the insert was not made permanent
optionC: Closing the connection deletes the rows that it inserted
optionD: Inserts are only visible after the server is restarted
correctAnswerText: commit() was never called, so the insert was not made permanent
explanation: With auto-commit off, changes stay in an open transaction until commit(). Other sessions never see them, and they are discarded when the connection goes away.

optionA: The query must be closed before its rows can be read
optionB: getString cannot read a column by its name, only index
optionC: A ResultSet is empty until the transaction is committed
optionD: rs.next() was not called, so no row is current yet
correctAnswerText: rs.next() was not called, so no row is current yet
explanation: The cursor starts before the first row, so there is no current row to read. Call if (rs.next()) first; reading by column name is fine.

prompt: A DAO method opens a connection in try-with-resources and returns the ResultSet to the service, which then calls rs.next(). It fails with "ResultSet is closed". Why?
optionA: rs.next() may only be called once per ResultSet
optionB: Leaving the try closed the connection and its ResultSet
optionC: The service is on another thread and cannot read it
optionD: A ResultSet can only be read inside a static method
correctAnswerText: Leaving the try closed the connection and its ResultSet
explanation: The ResultSet lives only as long as its statement and connection, which closed when the method returned. Map rows into objects inside the DAO and return those.

prompt: A marks report shows 0 for students who have not taken the exam yet; their marks column is NULL. The code uses int m = rs.getInt("marks"). What is going on?
optionA: The SELECT replaced NULL with 0 because of the int column
optionB: MySQL stores NULL integers as 0 in the table itself
optionC: A NULL column makes getInt fall back to the previous row
optionD: getInt maps NULL to 0, so "not taken" looks like a zero
correctAnswerText: getInt maps NULL to 0, so "not taken" looks like a zero
explanation: Primitive getters cannot return null, so SQL NULL becomes 0. Read it with getObject("marks", Integer.class) or check rs.wasNull() and show "absent".

optionA: Placeholders stand for values, never for a table name
optionB: Table names must be bound with setObject, not setString
optionC: setString cannot bind values to the first placeholder
optionD: Only one placeholder is allowed per SQL statement
correctAnswerText: Placeholders stand for values, never for a table name
explanation: The server must know which table to read when it parses the statement, so ? can only stand for values. Table and column names have to be in the SQL text, chosen from a fixed list.

prompt: A transfer runs the debit UPDATE, then the credit UPDATE throws because the target account does not exist. autoCommit was left at its default. What is the state?
optionA: Neither ran, since the error stopped the batch
optionB: The debit is committed; the money has vanished
optionC: Both updates are rolled back by the driver
optionD: The debit is held until the credit is retried
correctAnswerText: The debit is committed; the money has vanished
explanation: With auto-commit on, the debit committed the moment it ran. Nothing ties it to the failed credit, so the database is left inconsistent. Group both in one transaction.

prompt: An orders page loads 500 orders, then for each one calls customerDao.findById(order.customerId()). It takes seconds. What is the problem?
optionA: Orders must be loaded one at a time for correctness
optionB: 501 separate queries; one join or IN query would do
optionC: findById is slow because it uses a PreparedStatement
optionD: The pool is too small, so it should be raised to 500
correctAnswerText: 501 separate queries; one join or IN query would do
explanation: This is the N+1 query problem: one query for the list plus one per row, each paying a round trip. Fetch customers with a JOIN, or one IN (...) query for all ids.

prompt: With a pool of 10, a report endpoint runs a 40-second query. When a few users open it, even the fast login endpoint starts failing with "Connection is not available, request timed out". Why?
optionA: HikariCP gives report queries a higher priority than logins
optionB: The slow reports hold the connections, so logins wait and time out
optionC: Login queries are cancelled whenever a report query is running
optionD: The database locks the users table while any report is running
correctAnswerText: The slow reports hold the connections, so logins wait and time out
explanation: All endpoints share one pool. Long-running queries keep connections checked out, and other requests wait past the connection timeout (30 s by default in HikariCP) and fail.

prompt: A student project calls DriverManager.getConnection in every servlet request. It is going live for a college fest. Your advice?
optionA: Use one static Connection shared by every request
optionB: Switch to a pooled DataSource such as HikariCP
optionC: Keep it, but open a second connection per request
optionD: Keep it: DriverManager pools connections already
correctAnswerText: Switch to a pooled DataSource such as HikariCP
explanation: Opening a connection per request is slow and uncapped under load. A pool reuses connections and limits them. One shared Connection is unsafe, as connections are not meant to be shared by concurrent requests.

prompt: Requests are timing out waiting for connections, and someone proposes raising the pool from 10 to 500. Your judgement?
optionA: Lower it to 1 instead so queries never compete at all
optionB: Do it: more connections always means more throughput
optionC: Find what holds connections first; a huge pool overloads the DB
optionD: Do it, and set the connection timeout to zero as well
correctAnswerText: Find what holds connections first; a huge pool overloads the DB
explanation: A database does useful work on only a limited number of connections at once; hundreds just contend. Waiting usually means leaks or slow queries, which a bigger pool hides.

prompt: A product list lets users sort by a column chosen from a query parameter, ?sort=price. How should the SQL be built?
optionA: Concatenate sort after escaping any single quotes in it
optionB: Bind sort as a ? placeholder in the ORDER BY clause
optionC: Concatenate sort, since ORDER BY cannot be injected
optionD: Map sort to a fixed set of allowed columns, reject anything else
correctAnswerText: Map sort to a fixed set of allowed columns, reject anything else
explanation: A placeholder in ORDER BY binds a constant string, so it does not sort by the column. Concatenation is injectable whatever is escaped. A whitelist is the only safe option.

prompt: A checkout opens a transaction, reserves stock, calls a payment gateway over HTTP (up to 20 s), then inserts the order and commits. Your judgement?
optionA: Good, but raise the transaction isolation to SERIALIZABLE
optionB: Good design: the transaction protects the payment call too
optionC: Keep the remote call outside the transaction; keep it short
optionD: Commit after every statement so the HTTP call is quicker
correctAnswerText: Keep the remote call outside the transaction; keep it short
explanation: A rollback cannot undo an HTTP payment, and the open transaction holds locks and a pooled connection for the full 20 s. Do the remote work outside it and keep database work short.

prompt: A DAO method catches SQLException, prints the stack trace and returns null. Is that a good choice?
optionA: No: rethrow with context so callers cannot miss the failure
optionB: No: it should return an empty list for every SQL error
optionC: Yes: callers should never have to deal with database errors
optionD: Yes, as long as the stack trace is printed to System.out
correctAnswerText: No: rethrow with context so callers cannot miss the failure
explanation: Returning null turns "the database is down" into "not found" and fails later somewhere unrelated. Wrap it in an unchecked exception (Spring uses DataAccessException) and let it surface.

prompt: What should a StudentDao.findByBatch(batchId) method return to the service layer?
optionA: A List<Student> built from the rows inside the DAO
optionB: The Connection, so the service can run follow-up queries
optionC: The open ResultSet, so the service reads only what it needs
optionD: The SQL string, so the service can choose when to run it
correctAnswerText: A List<Student> built from the rows inside the DAO
explanation: Returning domain objects keeps JDBC types inside the DAO and lets it close everything before returning. Handing out a ResultSet or Connection leaks both the resource and the abstraction.

prompt: An import loads two million rows from a CSV. What batching approach is best?
optionA: executeBatch every few thousand rows, committing per chunk
optionB: executeBatch after every single row is added to it
optionC: One addBatch for all two million, then one executeBatch
optionD: executeUpdate for each row with autoCommit left on
correctAnswerText: executeBatch every few thousand rows, committing per chunk
explanation: Chunks keep memory bounded and round trips few, and committing per chunk keeps transactions short and makes a failed import restartable. One giant batch can exhaust memory.

prompt: A Spring Boot app uses JPA, but one monthly report needs a complex SQL aggregate over many tables. What is reasonable?
optionA: Drop JPA from the whole project and rewrite it in JDBC
optionB: Load all the entities with JPA and aggregate them in Java
optionC: Write that one query in plain SQL via JDBC or JdbcTemplate
optionD: Create a JPA entity for every intermediate result row
correctAnswerText: Write that one query in plain SQL via JDBC or JdbcTemplate
explanation: An ORM is for loading and saving objects. A set-based report is plain SQL's job, and mixing the two in one app is normal. Pulling every entity into memory to sum them is the slow path.

prompt: A DAO maps rows with SELECT * and reads columns by position (rs.getString(2)). Your judgement?
optionA: Fine: column positions in a table never change over time
optionB: Better than names, since positions make queries faster
optionC: Fine, as long as every column is read with getString
optionD: Fragile: name the columns in SELECT and read them by name
correctAnswerText: Fragile: name the columns in SELECT and read them by name
explanation: Adding or reordering a column silently shifts positions, and SELECT * fetches data you do not use. Listing columns and reading by name keeps the mapping correct as the schema grows.

prompt: Sign-up runs SELECT to check a username is free, then INSERTs it. Two users occasionally get the same name. What is the best fix?
optionA: Mark the Java sign-up method synchronized on every app server
optionB: Run the SELECT twice before inserting to double-check the name
optionC: Add Thread.sleep between the SELECT and INSERT to space them
optionD: A UNIQUE constraint on username, handling the duplicate-key error
correctAnswerText: A UNIQUE constraint on username, handling the duplicate-key error
explanation: Two requests can both pass the check before either inserts. Only the database sees every insert, so a UNIQUE constraint is the real guard; a Java lock fails once there are two servers.

prompt: Which annotation turns a plain Java class into a JPA entity?
optionA: @Component from Spring context
optionB: @Entity from jakarta.persistence
optionC: @Repository from Spring Data
optionD: @Table from jakarta.persistence
correctAnswerText: @Entity from jakarta.persistence
explanation: @Entity makes the class managed by JPA. @Table only customises the table name and is optional; Spring stereotypes have nothing to do with mapping.

prompt: Which annotation marks the field that holds an entity's primary key?
optionA: @Column(unique = true)
optionB: @Key
optionC: @Id
optionD: @PrimaryKey
correctAnswerText: @Id
explanation: Every entity needs exactly one @Id (or an embedded id). A unique column is not the identifier Hibernate uses to track the instance.

prompt: With MySQL, which generation strategy lets the AUTO_INCREMENT column assign the id?
optionA: GenerationType.SEQUENCE
optionB: GenerationType.TABLE
optionC: GenerationType.IDENTITY
optionD: GenerationType.UUID
correctAnswerText: GenerationType.IDENTITY
explanation: IDENTITY delegates the id to the database column, which on MySQL is AUTO_INCREMENT. MySQL has no sequences, and TABLE emulates them slowly.

prompt: In a bidirectional one-to-many, which @OneToMany attribute names the field on the other side that owns the relation?
optionA: joinColumn
optionB: inverseSide
optionC: mappedBy
optionD: targetEntity
correctAnswerText: mappedBy
explanation: mappedBy points at the field in the child (usually the @ManyToOne) that owns the foreign key, marking the collection as the inverse side.

prompt: Which setting deletes a child row when the child is removed from its parent's collection?
optionA: orphanRemoval = true
optionB: cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST
optionC: optional = false
optionD: fetch = FetchType.EAGER
correctAnswerText: orphanRemoval = true
explanation: orphanRemoval deletes a child that is no longer referenced by the collection. PERSIST only cascades saving; it never deletes anything.

prompt: What is the default fetch type of a @ManyToOne association?
optionA: SUBSELECT
optionB: LAZY
optionC: JOIN
optionD: EAGER
correctAnswerText: EAGER
explanation: To-one associations default to EAGER and to-many to LAZY. That default is why many teams set @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) explicitly.

prompt: In a JPQL query, what does the FROM clause name?
optionA: The entity class name
optionB: The repository interface
optionC: The database table name
optionD: The schema and table pair
correctAnswerText: The entity class name
explanation: JPQL queries the object model: entity names and their fields. Hibernate translates them to the tables and columns of the mapping.

prompt: An entity has been created with new and never persisted. Which state is it in?
optionA: Managed
optionB: Detached
optionC: Removed
optionD: Transient (new)
correctAnswerText: Transient (new)
explanation: A new object is unknown to any persistence context. It becomes managed on persist, and detached once its context closes.

prompt: Which annotation turns on optimistic locking for an entity?
optionA: @Lock
optionB: @Version
optionC: @Transactional
optionD: @Timestamp
correctAnswerText: @Version
explanation: A @Version field is checked and incremented on every update. @Lock on a repository method requests a lock mode for one query, which is different.

prompt: Which JPQL construct loads an association in the same query as its parent?
optionA: LEFT JOIN
optionB: JOIN FETCH
optionC: INNER SELECT
optionD: EAGER JOIN
correctAnswerText: JOIN FETCH
explanation: JOIN FETCH initialises the association from the joined rows. A plain JOIN can filter on the association but leaves it unloaded.

prompt: Why does it matter which side of a relationship is the owning side?
optionA: The owning side decides which table is created first
optionB: Only the owning side can be navigated from Java code
optionC: The owning side is always loaded first by every query
optionD: Only owning-side changes are written to the foreign key
correctAnswerText: Only owning-side changes are written to the foreign key
explanation: Hibernate reads the owning side to decide the foreign key value. Changes made only on the mappedBy side are ignored when writing.

prompt: What does LAZY fetching mean for a collection association?
optionA: It is never loaded unless a JPQL query asks for it
optionB: It is loaded by a background thread after the parent
optionC: It is queried from the database on first access
optionD: It is loaded with the parent but kept out of memory
correctAnswerText: It is queried from the database on first access
explanation: Hibernate puts a proxy collection in place and runs the query the first time the collection is touched, which needs an open session.

prompt: What is dirty checking in Hibernate?
optionA: At flush, changed managed entities are written automatically
optionB: Detached entities are compared with the database on read
optionC: Fields are validated against constraints before each insert
optionD: Modified entities are rejected outside of a transaction
correctAnswerText: At flush, changed managed entities are written automatically
explanation: Hibernate keeps a snapshot of each managed entity and, at flush, issues UPDATEs for whatever changed, with no save() needed.

prompt: What is the persistence context?
optionA: The managed entities of a session, one instance per id
optionB: The schema metadata Hibernate reads during startup
optionC: The connection pool shared by every repository bean
optionD: The cache of query results shared across transactions
correctAnswerText: The managed entities of a session, one instance per id
explanation: It is the first-level cache and unit of work of an EntityManager: it guarantees one Java object per database row and tracks changes.

prompt: What does cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST on a parent's collection do?
optionA: Removing the parent also removes every child row
optionB: Children are loaded whenever the parent is loaded
optionC: Persisting the parent also persists new children in it
optionD: Children are saved only when persisted on their own
correctAnswerText: Persisting the parent also persists new children in it
explanation: Cascades propagate entity operations along the association. PERSIST spreads persist only; REMOVE and orphanRemoval are separate choices.

prompt: What is the N+1 select problem?
optionA: One query is repeated N+1 times inside a transaction
optionB: A join returns N+1 rows because a parent repeats
optionC: A batch insert sends one statement more than needed
optionD: One query loads a list, then one more runs for each row
correctAnswerText: One query loads a list, then one more runs for each row
explanation: Loading N parents and then touching an association on each issues N extra queries. It hides in development and hurts with real data.

prompt: Why is LazyInitializationException thrown?
optionA: A query returned more rows than a collection can hold
optionB: An eager association failed to load due to a null key
optionC: A lazy association is touched after its session closed
optionD: A lazy association is loaded twice in one transaction
correctAnswerText: A lazy association is touched after its session closed
explanation: The proxy needs an open persistence context to run its query. Once the transaction ends, touching an unloaded proxy fails.

prompt: How does optimistic locking with @Version detect a conflicting update?
optionA: The database refuses any two writes in the same second
optionB: The UPDATE checks the version it read; zero rows means conflict
optionC: Hibernate compares every column against the current row
optionD: The first reader locks the row until its transaction ends
correctAnswerText: The UPDATE checks the version it read; zero rows means conflict
explanation: Hibernate adds "where version = ?" to the UPDATE. If another transaction already bumped the version, no row matches and it throws.

prompt: How does JPQL differ from SQL?
optionA: It runs in memory against entities that are already loaded
optionB: It is compiled into bytecode instead of into database SQL
optionC: It queries entities and their fields, not tables and columns
optionD: It cannot filter, join or sort; it only loads rows by id
correctAnswerText: It queries entities and their fields, not tables and columns
explanation: JPQL is translated to SQL for the database, but it is written against the mapped model, so it navigates fields like o.customer.city.

prompt: Why does GenerationType.IDENTITY stop Hibernate from batching inserts?
optionA: IDENTITY columns cannot be written inside a transaction
optionB: The id is known only after each row has been inserted
optionC: IDENTITY forces each insert to open a new connection
optionD: The id is generated in Java and must be checked first
correctAnswerText: The id is known only after each row has been inserted
explanation: Hibernate must insert immediately on persist to learn the id, so it cannot hold inserts back and send them as one JDBC batch.

prompt: OrderItem has @ManyToOne @JoinColumn(name = "order_id") private Order order. How should Order map its List<OrderItem> items?
optionA: @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "order")
optionB: @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order")
optionC: @OneToMany @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")
optionD: @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order_id")
correctAnswerText: @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order")
explanation: mappedBy names the Java field "order", not the column. A second @JoinColumn would make both sides try to own the same foreign key.

prompt: Which repository query loads authors together with their books in one SQL statement?
optionA: @Query("select a from Author a left join a.books b")
optionB: @Query("select a from Author a where a.books is not empty")
optionC: @Query("select distinct a from Author a join fetch a.books")
optionD: @Query("select a, count(b) from Author a join a.books b")
correctAnswerText: @Query("select distinct a from Author a join fetch a.books")
explanation: Only a fetch join initialises the collection. A plain left join can filter or count but leaves books as a lazy proxy, so N+1 remains.

prompt: Which JPQL query returns products cheaper than a given maximum price?
optionA: select p from Product where Product.price < :max
optionB: select p from product p where price < max
optionC: select * from product where price < :max
optionD: select p from Product p where p.price < :max
correctAnswerText: select p from Product p where p.price < :max
explanation: JPQL uses the entity name, an alias for its fields and a named parameter bound with :max. select * is SQL, not JPQL.

prompt: Order.items is mapped with cascade = ALL and orphanRemoval = true. Inside a transaction, code calls order.getItems().remove(item). What happens at commit?
optionA: Nothing, unless repository.delete is called
optionB: An exception, since the item is still referenced
optionC: The item row stays with order_id set to null
optionD: The item row is deleted from the table
correctAnswerText: The item row is deleted from the table
explanation: orphanRemoval treats an item dropped from the collection as an orphan and deletes it at flush, with no explicit delete call.

prompt: In a @Transactional service method: User u = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); u.setName("Ravi"); and nothing else. What happens?
optionA: The new name is written to the database at commit
optionB: The change is saved only if flush() is called
optionC: An exception is thrown for the unsaved change
optionD: Nothing is saved because save() was never called
correctAnswerText: The new name is written to the database at commit
explanation: u is managed, so dirty checking finds the change at flush before commit and issues an UPDATE. save() is not needed for managed entities.

prompt: spring.jpa.open-in-view is false. A controller gets an Order from a @Transactional service, then reads order.getItems() and gets LazyInitializationException. Best fix?
optionA: Change every association in the model to EAGER
optionB: Call Hibernate.initialize in the controller method
optionC: Load the items in the service query with join fetch
optionD: Catch the exception and return an empty item list
correctAnswerText: Load the items in the service query with join fetch
explanation: Load what the response needs while the transaction is open, ideally mapped to a DTO. Hibernate.initialize in the controller still has no session.

prompt: Two admins open Product 9 at version 3. The first saves, making it version 4. The second then saves its copy carrying version 3. What happens?
optionA: The second waits until the first transaction ends
optionB: The second save silently overwrites the first one
optionC: An optimistic locking failure; the second save is rejected
optionD: Both saves are merged column by column
correctAnswerText: An optimistic locking failure; the second save is rejected
explanation: The second UPDATE says "where version = 3", matches nothing, and Spring surfaces ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException instead of losing an edit.

prompt: Within one transaction: User a = em.find(User.class, 1L); User b = em.find(User.class, 1L); What is a == b?
optionA: false, unless equals and hashCode are overridden
optionB: false; each find builds a new object from a new query
optionC: true, but only when the second-level cache is enabled
optionD: true; the persistence context returns the same instance
correctAnswerText: true; the persistence context returns the same instance
explanation: The first-level cache guarantees one instance per id per context, so the second find is served from memory with no SQL.

prompt: Order has a default @ManyToOne Customer customer. The query "select o from Order o" loads 100 orders. What happens to customers?
optionA: They never load unless join fetch is written
optionB: They load through one automatic SQL join
optionC: They load eagerly, often by extra selects per customer
optionD: They stay as lazy proxies until first touched
correctAnswerText: They load eagerly, often by extra selects per customer
explanation: The default EAGER must be honoured, but JPQL does not add the join, so Hibernate issues follow-up selects: an eager N+1.

prompt: In JPA 3.1 (Hibernate 6.2+), which mapping makes the provider generate a UUID for a field "UUID id"?
optionA: @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
optionB: @Id @Column(columnDefinition = "uuid auto")
optionC: @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)
optionD: @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.TABLE)
correctAnswerText: @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)
explanation: JPA 3.1 added GenerationType.UUID. IDENTITY needs a numeric auto-increment column, and a column definition does not generate anything.

prompt: An orders page logs one "select … from orders" and then fifty "select … from customer where id=?". What is going on?
optionA: A missing index on customer.id slows each lookup
optionB: The second-level cache lacks the customer table
optionC: Each order's customer is loaded by a separate query
optionD: The orders query is re-run once per rendered row
correctAnswerText: Each order's customer is loaded by a separate query
explanation: That log shape is N+1: one list query then one per row. The fix is a fetch join, an entity graph or batch fetching for this use case.

prompt: Comment has @ManyToOne Post post; Post has @OneToMany(mappedBy = "post") comments. Code does post.getComments().add(c); em.persist(c); and post_id is null. Why?
optionA: mappedBy makes the comments list read-only in memory
optionB: The list must be a Set for the key to be written
optionC: persist must be called on the post, not on the comment
optionD: c.setPost(post) was never called; only the owner writes
correctAnswerText: c.setPost(post) was never called; only the owner writes
explanation: Comment.post owns the foreign key. Adding to the inverse list changes nothing in SQL; a helper like addComment should set both sides.

prompt: A controller returns an Order entity whose items each refer back to the order. Writing the JSON fails with infinite recursion. Why?
optionA: The transaction is committed twice in the response
optionB: Hibernate reloads the items for each serialisation
optionC: The lazy proxy cannot be converted to a JSON value
optionD: Jackson follows order to items to order without end
correctAnswerText: Jackson follows order to items to order without end
explanation: Bidirectional links form a cycle that Jackson walks forever. Returning a DTO avoids both this and accidental lazy loading.

prompt: A @Transactional method loads a User, calls user.setEmail(candidate) to test it, finds it invalid, and returns without saving or throwing. What is stored?
optionA: Nothing changes until the entity is loaded again
optionB: The original email, since the method returned early
optionC: The original email, since save() was never called
optionD: The invalid email, written by dirty checking at commit
correctAnswerText: The invalid email, written by dirty checking at commit
explanation: The entity was managed, so the change is flushed at commit. Validate on a DTO or a copy, never by mutating a managed entity.

prompt: Student has @ManyToMany(cascade = CascadeType.ALL) Set<Course> courses. Deleting one student fails on a foreign key or deletes courses others take. Why?
optionA: CascadeType.ALL skips the delete of join table rows
optionB: The join table is owned by Course, so it is never cleared
optionC: REMOVE cascades to shared Course rows, not just the links
optionD: A many-to-many cannot be mapped with a Set collection
correctAnswerText: REMOVE cascades to shared Course rows, not just the links
explanation: ALL includes REMOVE, which deletes the Course entities themselves. Many-to-many targets are shared, so cascade REMOVE is almost always wrong.

prompt: The query "select o from Order o join fetch o.items" with setMaxResults(20) logs a warning that pagination is being applied in memory. What is happening?
optionA: Only the first twenty items of each order are fetched
optionB: The database pages the item rows rather than the orders
optionC: The limit is dropped and an exception follows at commit
optionD: Hibernate loads every matching row and pages in memory
correctAnswerText: Hibernate loads every matching row and pages in memory
explanation: A collection fetch multiplies rows, so SQL LIMIT cannot page parents. Page the order ids first, then fetch their items.

prompt: An endpoint builds a User from the request body (id 7, only name set) and calls repo.save(user). Afterwards email and phone are null in the table. Why?
optionA: save inserts a new row and keeps the old row as well
optionB: dirty checking skips fields that were never loaded
optionC: save merges the detached copy, null fields included
optionD: Hibernate clears fields when no version is given
correctAnswerText: save merges the detached copy, null fields included
explanation: With an id present, save() calls merge, which copies every field of the detached object onto the managed one, nulls and all.

prompt: An entity's equals and hashCode use its generated id. A new instance added to a HashSet before persist cannot be found in that set afterwards. Why?
optionA: Its hashCode changed once the id was assigned
optionB: The id is assigned at commit, not during persist
optionC: HashSet stores a copy of the entity on insert
optionD: persist swaps the object for a different proxy
correctAnswerText: Its hashCode changed once the id was assigned
explanation: The set filed it under the hash of a null id. When persist assigned the id the hash moved and the lookup checks the wrong bucket.

prompt: A Product has @Version, but concurrent edits never conflict. The update copies DTO fields onto a freshly loaded entity and saves it. Why is the conflict missed?
optionA: Spring Data disables versioning for save() on entities
optionB: The fresh load reads the latest version, so the check passes
optionC: The version field must be a timestamp to be compared
optionD: @Version only takes effect when pessimistic locks are on
correctAnswerText: The fresh load reads the latest version, so the check passes
explanation: The check only protects the version the user actually saw. Carry the version in the DTO and compare it, or set it on the entity.

prompt: Inside one transaction, code persists a new Order and then runs a JPQL count of orders. The count includes the new order before commit. Why?
optionA: The persist call committed its own small separate transaction
optionB: Hibernate flushes pending changes before a query that sees them
optionC: JPQL counts only the entities held in the persistence context
optionD: MySQL reads uncommitted rows from all other transactions
correctAnswerText: Hibernate flushes pending changes before a query that sees them
explanation: In AUTO flush mode Hibernate flushes before a query whose result could depend on pending changes; the row is visible inside this transaction.

prompt: A team proposes making every association EAGER so LazyInitializationException never happens again. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Reject: it loads graphs nobody asked for; fetch per use case
optionB: Accept, but only for the @OneToMany collections in the model
optionC: Accept: eager loading always costs less than lazy loading
optionD: Reject: EAGER is not permitted on a @ManyToOne association
correctAnswerText: Reject: it loads graphs nobody asked for; fetch per use case
explanation: Global EAGER drags large graphs into every query and cannot be undone per query. Keep associations lazy and fetch what each use case needs.

prompt: Spring Boot enables spring.jpa.open-in-view by default and warns about it at startup. For a REST API, which position is sounder?
optionA: Turn it off and mark every association as FetchType.EAGER
optionB: Keep it on, since it removes the need to design queries at all
optionC: Turn it off and load what each response needs in the service
optionD: Keep it on, because it makes database connections short-lived
correctAnswerText: Turn it off and load what each response needs in the service
explanation: Open-in-view holds a connection for the whole request and hides lazy loading in serialisation. Explicit fetching keeps queries visible.

prompt: Should a REST API return JPA entities directly in its responses?
optionA: Prefer DTOs: entities leak lazy state, cycles and schema
optionB: Prefer entities: DTOs only duplicate the same fields
optionC: Prefer DTOs only when the database is not MySQL
optionD: Prefer entities, as long as every relation is EAGER
correctAnswerText: Prefer DTOs: entities leak lazy state, cycles and schema
explanation: Entities couple the API to the table design and serialise proxies and cycles. A DTO is the contract; the entity can change behind it.

prompt: A seat-booking feature sees heavy contention on a few hot rows during a sale. Which locking choice deserves serious consideration?
optionA: Optimistic locking with the version check switched off
optionB: Pessimistic locks (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) on the hot rows
optionC: No locking, since transactions already serialise writes
optionD: Optimistic locking alone, retrying each conflict forever
correctAnswerText: Pessimistic locks (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) on the hot rows
explanation: Optimistic locking suits rare conflicts; under constant contention most attempts fail and retry. Briefly locking hot rows is often cheaper.

prompt: An Invoice always loads its lines, and nothing ever navigates from a line back to its invoice. Which mapping judgement fits?
optionA: Map it one-way from Invoice with @JoinColumn on the list
optionB: Map only Line to Invoice; collections cannot be mapped
optionC: Map both sides, since JPA requires a bidirectional pair
optionD: Use @ManyToMany so that either side can own the link
correctAnswerText: Map it one-way from Invoice with @JoinColumn on the list
explanation: A back-reference nobody uses is extra state to keep in sync. Hibernate 6 maps a unidirectional @OneToMany with @JoinColumn efficiently.

prompt: A nightly job inserts two million rows through JPA on MySQL with IDENTITY ids and is slow. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Use JDBC batching or a bulk loader; IDENTITY blocks batching
optionB: Call flush after every single row to keep memory stable
optionC: Wrap every row in a transaction of its own to save memory
optionD: Switch every fetch type to LAZY to speed up the inserts
correctAnswerText: Use JDBC batching or a bulk loader; IDENTITY blocks batching
explanation: Row-by-row JPA inserts with IDENTITY cannot batch and fill the persistence context. Bulk work belongs in JDBC batches or LOAD DATA.

prompt: When is a native SQL query the right choice over JPQL?
optionA: When it needs a database feature JPQL cannot express
optionB: Whenever speed matters, since JPQL is interpreted
optionC: Never, because native queries are not supported
optionD: Whenever a query joins more than two entities at once
correctAnswerText: When it needs a database feature JPQL cannot express
explanation: Window functions, vendor hints or JSON operators may need native SQL. JPQL is translated to SQL once, so it is not slower by nature.

prompt: Which association most deserves cascade = ALL together with orphanRemoval = true?
optionA: Order to the Customer who placed it in the first place
optionB: Order to its OrderLines, which exist only inside the order
optionC: Employee to the Department in which the employee works
optionD: OrderLine to the catalogue Product that the line refers to
correctAnswerText: Order to its OrderLines, which exist only inside the order
explanation: Cascade suits composition: children whose life is owned by the parent. Products, customers and departments are shared and outlive any order.

prompt: Listing twenty posts per page with their tags shows N+1. Which fix suits a paged list best?
optionA: Page the posts, then batch-load their tags in one query
optionB: Cache each post's tags in a static HashMap field
optionC: Add join fetch for the tags in the paged query itself
optionD: Mark the tags collection as EAGER on the Post entity
correctAnswerText: Page the posts, then batch-load their tags in one query
explanation: Fetch-joining a collection breaks SQL paging. Page the parents, then load the children with an IN query, @BatchSize or an entity graph.

prompt: How should a JPA entity with a generated id implement equals and hashCode?
optionA: Lombok @Data, generating both from all of the fields
optionB: A natural key, or id equality with a constant hashCode
optionC: Every field, so that two copies compare equal by value
optionD: Id equality and an id hash, even before the persist
correctAnswerText: A natural key, or id equality with a constant hashCode
explanation: The id is null until persist and fields change over time. A stable business key, or id-based equals with a fixed hash, survives both.

prompt: In Spring, what does Inversion of Control mean?
optionA: The caller decides when the JVM loads each of its classes
optionB: The container creates objects and wires their dependencies
optionC: Control passes from the database layer to the web layer
optionD: Each object creates its own dependencies with the new keyword
correctAnswerText: The container creates objects and wires their dependencies
explanation: Objects declare what they need and the container supplies it. That inversion is what lets a test or another environment swap a dependency.

prompt: What is the default scope of a Spring bean?
optionA: request
optionB: session
optionC: prototype
optionD: singleton
correctAnswerText: singleton
explanation: Unless told otherwise, the container creates one shared instance per bean definition and hands the same object to every injection point.

prompt: Which annotation marks a method in a @Configuration class as producing a bean?
optionA: @Bean
optionB: @Component
optionC: @Autowired
optionD: @Service
correctAnswerText: @Bean
explanation: A @Bean method returns the object to register; its parameters are injected. @Component goes on a class found by scanning instead.

prompt: Which annotation, placed at the injection point, selects one bean by name when several share a type?
optionA: @Value
optionB: @Profile
optionC: @Primary
optionD: @Qualifier
correctAnswerText: @Qualifier
explanation: @Qualifier("name") narrows the candidates at that injection point. @Primary is declared on the bean and sets a default for every injection point.

prompt: Which annotation injects the property app.timeout into a field?
optionA: @Config("${app.timeout}")
optionB: @Property("app.timeout")
optionC: @Inject("app.timeout")
optionD: @Value("${app.timeout}")
correctAnswerText: @Value("${app.timeout}")
explanation: @Value with a ${...} placeholder resolves the property from the environment (properties, YAML, environment variables).

prompt: Which annotation registers a bean only when the "dev" profile is active?
optionA: @Primary("dev")
optionB: @Profile("dev")
optionC: @Lazy("dev")
optionD: @Scope("dev")
correctAnswerText: @Profile("dev")
explanation: @Profile on a class or @Bean method makes the definition conditional on the active profiles.

prompt: Which annotation marks a method to run once a bean's dependencies have been injected?
optionA: @PostConstruct
optionB: @PostLoad
optionC: @AfterInject
optionD: @PreDestroy
correctAnswerText: @PostConstruct
explanation: jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct runs after injection and before the bean is used. @PreDestroy runs at shutdown; @PostLoad is a JPA callback.

prompt: In Spring AOP, what is "advice"?
optionA: The proxy class that is generated at runtime
optionB: The code that runs at a matched join point
optionC: The expression that chooses which methods match
optionD: The object whose methods are being intercepted
correctAnswerText: The code that runs at a matched join point
explanation: Advice is the behaviour (before, after, around); the pointcut selects where; the target is the original bean; the proxy applies it.

prompt: Which classes does component scanning register as beans?
optionA: Only the classes listed in application.properties
optionB: Every class on the classpath with a public constructor
optionC: Only the classes that are returned from @Bean methods
optionD: Classes marked @Component or a stereotype such as @Service
correctAnswerText: Classes marked @Component or a stereotype such as @Service
explanation: @Service, @Repository, @Controller and @Configuration are meta-annotated with @Component, so scanning finds them all under the base package.

prompt: By default, how does Spring apply @Transactional behaviour to a bean?
optionA: By rewriting the class bytecode at compile time
optionB: By registering the method with the JDBC driver
optionC: By wrapping the bean in a runtime proxy object
optionD: By editing the method body through reflection
correctAnswerText: By wrapping the bean in a runtime proxy object
explanation: Callers receive a proxy that starts and ends the transaction around the real call. AspectJ weaving is possible but not the default.

prompt: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
optionA: It is the only style that allows circular dependencies
optionB: Field injection was removed from Spring Framework 6
optionC: Dependencies are explicit, final and testable without Spring
optionD: It lets beans start faster because reflection is skipped
correctAnswerText: Dependencies are explicit, final and testable without Spring
explanation: A constructor states what a class needs, allows final fields, and lets a test call new with fakes. Field injection still works but hides all of that.

prompt: What does @Primary on a bean do?
optionA: Gives the bean priority over properties files
optionB: Makes it the default when several beans match a type
optionC: Makes the bean initialise before all other beans
optionD: Makes it the only bean of its type that is allowed
correctAnswerText: Makes it the default when several beans match a type
explanation: When one type has several candidates, the @Primary one wins unless an injection point asks for another by @Qualifier.

prompt: What does the prototype scope mean?
optionA: One instance for each HTTP request handled
optionB: A new instance each time the context restarts
optionC: One instance shared across the whole context
optionD: A new instance each time the bean is requested
correctAnswerText: A new instance each time the bean is requested
explanation: Every getBean or injection of a prototype creates a fresh object. Spring does not manage its destruction afterwards.

prompt: When do you need a @Bean method instead of @Component?
optionA: To register a class you cannot annotate, such as a library type
optionB: To make the class visible to component scanning at all
optionC: To let Spring inject dependencies into the class fields
optionD: To make the bean a singleton rather than a prototype one
correctAnswerText: To register a class you cannot annotate, such as a library type
explanation: You cannot put @Component on a library class, and some objects need configuring when built. A @Bean method covers both.

prompt: Why must a singleton bean hold no per-request mutable state?
optionA: One instance serves every concurrent request
optionB: Spring clones each singleton for every thread
optionC: The container erases singleton fields on idle
optionD: Singletons are recreated after every request
correctAnswerText: One instance serves every concurrent request
explanation: Concurrent requests run through the same object on different threads, so a field written by one request is visible to another.

prompt: What does a pointcut define in Spring AOP?
optionA: What code runs when an advised method is called
optionB: Which proxy type Spring will generate for a bean
optionC: When the aspect bean itself gets instantiated
optionD: Which method executions the advice applies to
correctAnswerText: Which method executions the advice applies to
explanation: A pointcut is a predicate over join points, such as execution(* com.cb.service..*(..)). The advice is what runs there.

prompt: What does starting an application with spring.profiles.active=prod do?
optionA: Disables every bean that has no @Profile annotation
optionB: Switches Spring to a faster, non-reflective container
optionC: Adds prod-only beans and loads application-prod properties
optionD: Compiles the application with production optimisations
correctAnswerText: Adds prod-only beans and loads application-prod properties
explanation: Profile-specific beans and property files join the defaults; beans without @Profile stay registered in every profile.

prompt: Why does @Transactional not apply when a bean calls its own annotated method through this?
optionA: this refers to a copy of the bean, not itself
optionB: The inner method is excluded by default rules
optionC: The call skips the proxy, so no advice runs
optionD: Spring forbids transactions on inner calls
correctAnswerText: The call skips the proxy, so no advice runs
explanation: Advice lives in the proxy. A call on this goes straight to the target object, so whatever annotation the method carries is never seen.

prompt: Why put initialisation logic in a @PostConstruct method rather than the constructor?
optionA: It runs at shutdown, so cleanup is always guaranteed
optionB: It runs before the constructor and can prepare the fields
optionC: It runs once per request, unlike the bean constructor
optionD: It runs after all injection, including fields and setters
correctAnswerText: It runs after all injection, including fields and setters
explanation: Field and setter injection happen after construction, so only @PostConstruct is sure to see every dependency in place.

prompt: What is the ApplicationContext?
optionA: The object holding the active database session
optionB: A thread-local map of the current request's data
optionC: A registry mapping each controller to its URLs
optionD: The container holding bean definitions and instances
correctAnswerText: The container holding bean definitions and instances
explanation: It is Spring's IoC container: it reads configuration, creates and wires beans, and adds events, resources and environment access.

prompt: Beans razorpayGateway and stripeGateway both implement PaymentGateway. A constructor takes PaymentGateway gateway, with no qualifiers. What happens at startup?
optionA: The first bean found on the classpath is injected
optionB: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException; the context fails
optionC: Both are injected into a list automatically
optionD: Startup works; the error comes on first payment
correctAnswerText: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException; the context fails
explanation: Two candidates, no @Primary, no @Qualifier and no matching parameter name: Spring cannot choose and refuses to start.

prompt: Which constructor parameter receives every bean that implements PaymentGateway?
optionA: List<PaymentGateway> gateways
optionB: Set<Class<PaymentGateway>> gateways
optionC: ObjectFactory<PaymentGateway> gateways
optionD: Optional<PaymentGateway> gateways
correctAnswerText: List<PaymentGateway> gateways
explanation: Spring injects all matching beans into a List (ordered by @Order) or a Map keyed by bean name, a common strategy-pattern setup.

prompt: A singleton ReportService receives a prototype ReportBuilder in its constructor, and each generate() call uses this.builder. How many builders are used?
optionA: None; prototypes cannot be injected
optionB: One for each thread that calls generate()
optionC: A new one for every call to generate()
optionD: One, created when ReportService was built
correctAnswerText: One, created when ReportService was built
explanation: Injection happens once, when the singleton is built. The prototype scope only says each lookup is new, and there was only one lookup.

prompt: Which change gives each generate() call in that singleton a fresh ReportBuilder?
optionA: Inject ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> and call getObject()
optionB: Annotate the injected builder with @Primary instead
optionC: Give ReportBuilder the singleton scope instead
optionD: Mark ReportService itself as @Lazy for startup
correctAnswerText: Inject ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> and call getObject()
explanation: ObjectProvider (or a lookup method or scoped proxy) asks the container each time, so a prototype bean is created per call.

prompt: How do you inject app.retries with a default of 3 when the property is absent?
optionA: @Value("${app.retries:3}")
optionB: @Value("${app.retries}=3")
optionC: @Value("app.retries ?: 3")
optionD: @Value("#{app.retries:3}")
correctAnswerText: @Value("${app.retries:3}")
explanation: A colon inside the placeholder supplies the default. #{...} is SpEL, not property resolution.

prompt: @Configuration class AppConfig { @Bean Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); } } and @Service class Billing { Billing(Clock clock) { … } }. What happens?
optionA: Billing receives the Clock returned by clock()
optionB: Billing gets a new Clock.systemDefaultZone()
optionC: Startup fails because Clock lacks @Component
optionD: Startup fails: @Bean methods must be static
correctAnswerText: Billing receives the Clock returned by clock()
explanation: The @Bean method registers a Clock bean, and constructor injection resolves it by type, which also lets a test pass a fixed clock.

prompt: Non-transactional placeAll() loops and calls this.placeOne(o); placeOne is @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW). How do placeOne's writes run?
optionA: Each placeOne call in a fresh transaction of its own
optionB: All orders in one transaction started by placeAll
optionC: Not at all; startup fails because of the self-call
optionD: Without its own transaction, since the proxy is skipped
correctAnswerText: Without its own transaction, since the proxy is skipped
explanation: The self-call never reaches the proxy, so REQUIRES_NEW is ignored; each repository call commits on its own, and a failure leaves partial orders.

prompt: Which pointcut matches every public method of classes directly in package com.cb.service?
optionA: call(public com.cb.service.*)
optionB: execution(public * com.cb.service.*.*(..))
optionC: execution(* com.cb.service(..))
optionD: within(com.cb.service.*.public())
correctAnswerText: execution(public * com.cb.service.*.*(..))
explanation: execution(modifiers return-type package.Class.method(args)): .*.* means any class in the package and any method; (..) means any arguments.

prompt: MockSms is @Profile("dev") and TwilioSms is @Profile("!dev"); both implement SmsSender. The app runs with no active profile. Which is injected?
optionA: TwilioSms, because dev is not active
optionB: MockSms, as dev is the default profile
optionC: Both, so startup fails on ambiguity
optionD: Neither one until a profile is set
