correctAnswerText: TwilioSms, because dev is not active
explanation: With no profile set only "default" is active, so "!dev" matches and "dev" does not. Exactly one SmsSender exists.

prompt: A @Scope("prototype") bean has a @PreDestroy method. What happens to it when the context closes?
optionA: It is not called; Spring does not track prototypes
optionB: It is called once for each instance created
optionC: It is called as each instance is garbage collected
optionD: It is called once, for the latest instance only
correctAnswerText: It is not called; Spring does not track prototypes
explanation: The container hands prototypes over and forgets them. Releasing their resources is the caller's job.

prompt: A needs B in its constructor and B needs A in its constructor. What happens when a Spring Boot 3 app starts?
optionA: It starts, injecting a proxy into one of the two
optionB: It starts, injecting null into the second bean
optionC: It fails: the circular reference cannot be resolved
optionD: It starts, but the first method call throws
correctAnswerText: It fails: the circular reference cannot be resolved
explanation: Neither can be built first. Boot also forbids circular references by default; the fix is a redesign, not allow-circular-references.

prompt: A public method calls a private @Transactional method in the same class, and no transaction starts. Why?
optionA: Proxies cannot intercept private methods or self-calls
optionB: The private method must be static to be advised
optionC: Private methods need REQUIRES_NEW to be intercepted
optionD: Transactions start only inside @Repository classes
correctAnswerText: Proxies cannot intercept private methods or self-calls
explanation: Two reasons stack: the call is on this, and a proxy cannot override a private method. Move the boundary to a public method of another bean.

prompt: A @Service's @Transactional method is declared final. It runs with no transaction and its injected fields look null inside it. Why?
optionA: final methods run before dependency injection is done
optionB: The transaction manager refuses to handle final methods
optionC: CGLIB cannot override final, so the proxy runs it itself
optionD: final methods are skipped by component scanning rules
correctAnswerText: CGLIB cannot override final, so the proxy runs it itself
explanation: The class-based proxy is an uninitialised subclass instance. A final method cannot be overridden, so it executes on the proxy, whose fields are null.

prompt: A unit test does new PriceService().quote() and gets NullPointerException on taxService, an @Autowired private field. Why?
optionA: The field must be public to be injected at all
optionB: @Autowired fields are set on the first call only
optionC: Nothing injected it; new bypasses the container
optionD: TaxService needs @Primary to be found in tests
correctAnswerText: Nothing injected it; new bypasses the container
explanation: Only the container processes @Autowired. With constructor injection the test would be forced to pass a TaxService and could not forget.

prompt: @Component class Cfg { @Value("${app.name}") String name; Cfg() { System.out.println(name.length()); } } throws NullPointerException at startup. Why?
optionA: The property app.name is missing from the file
optionB: The constructor runs twice, once with a null value
optionC: @Value cannot be used on package-private fields
optionD: Field injection happens after the constructor runs
correctAnswerText: Field injection happens after the constructor runs
explanation: Fields are populated after the object exists. Inject the value as a constructor parameter, or use it in @PostConstruct.

prompt: Two @Configuration classes each declare @Bean ObjectMapper objectMapper(). What happens when Spring Boot 3 starts?
optionA: It uses whichever definition registered first
optionB: It fails: bean definition overriding is disabled
optionC: It uses whichever definition registered last
optionD: It keeps both under two generated bean names
correctAnswerText: It fails: bean definition overriding is disabled
explanation: Same bean name twice is an override, which Boot turns off by default so one definition cannot silently replace another.

prompt: A @RequestScope bean is injected into a singleton controller and each request still sees its own data. Why?
optionA: The controller is converted to request scope as well
optionB: Request beans are copied into the controller per call
optionC: The injected object is a scoped proxy for the current one
optionD: Spring rebuilds the singleton controller per request
correctAnswerText: The injected object is a scoped proxy for the current one
explanation: @RequestScope defaults to a class-based scoped proxy, which looks up the bean bound to the current request on every call.

prompt: An @Async method is called from another method in the same bean and runs on the caller's thread. Why?
optionA: @Async works only on methods that return void and no value
optionB: The default executor was full, so it ran the task inline
optionC: The self-call skips the proxy that submits it to an executor
optionD: @Async works only on methods that take no parameters
correctAnswerText: The self-call skips the proxy that submits it to an executor
explanation: @Async is proxy-based like @Transactional. Calling it on this runs it synchronously; call it through another bean.

prompt: The @SpringBootApplication class is in com.cb.app; a @Service in com.cb.billing causes NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. Why?
optionA: The service class must implement an interface first
optionB: @Service beans must be declared in a @Bean method
optionC: Scanning covers only classes in the same Maven module
optionD: Scanning covers com.cb.app and its sub-packages only
correctAnswerText: Scanning covers com.cb.app and its sub-packages only
explanation: The main class's package is the scan root. Move it to com.cb, or list base packages explicitly.

prompt: A constructor has @Qualifier("smsSender") Sender s. The only match is @Component class SmsSender with no explicit name. Does it resolve?
optionA: Yes: the default bean name is smsSender
optionB: Yes, but only if SmsSender is @Primary
optionC: No: default names keep the capital letter
optionD: No: @Qualifier works only with @Bean
correctAnswerText: Yes: the default bean name is smsSender
explanation: Scanned beans are named after the simple class name with a lower-case first letter, and @Qualifier falls back to matching that name.

prompt: A class needs eight constructor-injected dependencies and the team wants field injection to tidy it. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Use a static service locator to look up each dependency
optionB: Switch to setters, so dependencies can be left out freely
optionC: Keep constructors; the long list says the class does too much
optionD: Switch to fields; the dependency count then stops mattering
correctAnswerText: Keep constructors; the long list says the class does too much
explanation: Field injection hides the smell without removing it. Eight collaborators usually means the class should be split.

prompt: Must every Spring service have an interface so that it can be proxied?
optionA: No; CGLIB proxies classes, so add interfaces for real seams
optionB: No, but then the bean cannot be injected anywhere else
optionC: Yes; Spring 6 can proxy beans only through an interface
optionD: Yes; without one, @Transactional is ignored completely
correctAnswerText: No; CGLIB proxies classes, so add interfaces for real seams
explanation: Boot uses class-based proxies by default. Introduce an interface where there are several implementations or a boundary, not by ritual.

prompt: placeOne must run in its own transaction when called from placeAll in the same service. Which fix is cleanest?
optionA: Inject the service into itself with field @Autowired
optionB: Make placeOne static so that the proxy can reach it
optionC: Move placeOne into a separate bean and call it there
optionD: Annotate the whole service with @Scope("prototype")
correctAnswerText: Move placeOne into a separate bean and call it there
explanation: A separate bean means the call goes through a proxy and the boundary is visible. Self-injection works but hides it; static cannot be proxied.

prompt: A team uses @Profile("featureX") to switch a business feature on for some customers. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Prefer a property condition; profiles describe environments
optionB: Put @Primary on the feature bean so it wins when it is present
optionC: Hard-code the switch, since configuration adds failure points
optionD: Profiles are ideal; they can be switched per request at runtime
correctAnswerText: Prefer a property condition; profiles describe environments
explanation: Profiles are fixed at startup and mean dev, test or prod. Feature switches belong in properties, @ConditionalOnProperty or a flag service.

prompt: A singleton service stores the current user in a field for convenience. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Wrong: concurrent requests overwrite each other's user
optionB: Fine, because each request gets its own singleton
optionC: Wrong only when the app runs on several servers
optionD: Fine, as long as the field is declared private
correctAnswerText: Wrong: concurrent requests overwrite each other's user
explanation: Per-request data in a shared object leaks between users. Pass it as a parameter or read it from the request's security context.

prompt: Which job is Spring AOP the right tool for?
optionA: Changing the arguments of every JDK library call
optionB: Making private helper methods run in a transaction
optionC: Replacing the ordinary business logic of one method
optionD: Timing or logging around many service methods at once
correctAnswerText: Timing or logging around many service methods at once
explanation: AOP fits cross-cutting concerns repeated across many beans. Spring AOP only advises public calls through proxies on Spring beans.

prompt: Several services need one RestClient configured with a base URL and timeouts. Which way is best?
optionA: A public static final field holds one RestClient
optionB: Each service copies the URL and timeouts locally
optionC: A @Bean method in a @Configuration class builds it
optionD: Each service builds its own RestClient on every call
correctAnswerText: A @Bean method in a @Configuration class builds it
explanation: One configured bean, injected where needed, keeps settings in one place and lets tests replace it. Static fields defeat both.

prompt: When is the prototype scope a sound choice?
optionA: For stateful helpers that must not be shared
optionB: For controllers, to keep request data separate
optionC: For repositories, so each query gets a new one
optionD: For every service, to avoid thread-safety bugs
correctAnswerText: For stateful helpers that must not be shared
explanation: Prototype suits short-lived stateful objects. Stateless services and repositories should stay singletons; prototypes do not fix shared state.

prompt: A module reads twelve related settings. Which way of binding them is soundest?
optionA: Read them with System.getenv inside each method body
optionB: Use twelve @Value fields, as they are easier to validate
optionC: Hard-code the defaults and skip external configuration
optionD: Bind them into one typed @ConfigurationProperties class
correctAnswerText: Bind them into one typed @ConfigurationProperties class
explanation: A typed properties class groups related settings, supports validation and relaxed binding, and is injected like any bean.

prompt: A developer calls context.getBean(X.class) inside services instead of injecting X. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Prefer it: it is the only way to reach prototypes
optionB: Avoid it only because getBean is now deprecated
optionC: Prefer it: it is faster than constructor injection
optionD: Avoid it: dependencies become hidden and tests harder
correctAnswerText: Avoid it: dependencies become hidden and tests harder
explanation: Service location couples code to the container and hides what a class needs. Injection, or ObjectProvider for late lookup, keeps it explicit.

prompt: What does spring-boot-starter-web bring into a project?
optionA: Spring Data JPA and a MySQL JDBC driver
optionB: Spring Security with a default login form
optionC: Thymeleaf with a set of HTML templates
optionD: Spring MVC, Jackson and an embedded Tomcat
correctAnswerText: Spring MVC, Jackson and an embedded Tomcat
explanation: A starter is a curated dependency set. The web starter gives you MVC, JSON via Jackson and a server to run inside the jar.

prompt: Which annotation combines @Controller and @ResponseBody?
optionA: @RestController
optionB: @ControllerAdvice
optionC: @ResponseEntity
optionD: @RequestMapping
correctAnswerText: @RestController
explanation: Every handler in a @RestController writes its return value to the response body, usually as JSON.

prompt: Which files does Spring Boot read for configuration by default?
optionA: boot.config or boot.yaml at the root
optionB: spring.properties or spring.yml
optionC: application.properties or application.yml
optionD: config.xml beside the main class
correctAnswerText: application.properties or application.yml
explanation: Boot loads application.properties/.yml from the classpath and the config directories, plus profile-specific variants.

prompt: Which annotation on a @RequestBody parameter triggers bean validation of the DTO?
optionA: @Required
optionB: @Checked
optionC: @Valid
optionD: @NotNull
correctAnswerText: @Valid
explanation: @Valid (or @Validated) asks Spring to run the jakarta.validation constraints declared on the DTO before the handler runs.

prompt: Which annotation marks a class whose @ExceptionHandler methods apply to all controllers and write a response body?
optionA: @ErrorHandler
optionB: @ControllerHandler
optionC: @RestControllerAdvice
optionD: @ExceptionMapper
correctAnswerText: @RestControllerAdvice
explanation: @RestControllerAdvice is @ControllerAdvice plus @ResponseBody, the usual home for API-wide error handling.

prompt: Which Spring Data interface provides CRUD plus paging and sorting for JPA entities?
optionA: JpaRepository<T, ID>
optionB: CrudOperations<T, ID>
optionC: JdbcTemplate<T, ID>
optionD: EntityManager<T, ID>
correctAnswerText: JpaRepository<T, ID>
explanation: JpaRepository extends ListCrudRepository and ListPagingAndSortingRepository and adds JPA operations such as flush.

prompt: Which annotation binds the {id} part of /users/{id} to a method parameter?
optionA: @RequestHeader
optionB: @RequestBody
optionC: @RequestParam
optionD: @PathVariable
correctAnswerText: @PathVariable
explanation: @PathVariable reads URI template segments; @RequestParam reads query string parameters such as ?page=2.

prompt: Which Actuator endpoint reports whether the application is up?
optionA: /actuator/ping
optionB: /actuator/health
optionC: /actuator/status
optionD: /actuator/alive
correctAnswerText: /actuator/health
explanation: health aggregates indicators (database, disk space and so on) and is what load balancers and Kubernetes probes call.

prompt: Which test annotation loads only the MVC layer for testing a controller?
optionA: @WebMvcTest
optionB: @SpringBootTest
optionC: @DataJpaTest
optionD: @JsonTest
correctAnswerText: @WebMvcTest
explanation: @WebMvcTest builds controllers, advice, filters and MockMvc, but not services or repositories, which you mock.

prompt: Which annotation on the main class enables auto-configuration, component scanning and configuration?
optionA: @EnableWebMvc
optionB: @ComponentScan
optionC: @SpringBootApplication
optionD: @Configuration
correctAnswerText: @SpringBootApplication
explanation: It combines @SpringBootConfiguration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan rooted at the main class's package.

prompt: What does Spring Boot auto-configuration do?
optionA: Copies a default application.yml into the project during build
optionB: Generates a REST controller for each entity found in the app
optionC: Adds beans for what is on the classpath, unless you define your own
optionD: Downloads any missing library dependencies when the app starts
correctAnswerText: Adds beans for what is on the classpath, unless you define your own
explanation: Auto-configuration classes are conditional: on a class being present, a property, and no user bean of that type already existing.

prompt: Why use @RestControllerAdvice?
optionA: To log every request and response body automatically
optionB: To turn exceptions into one consistent error response format
optionC: To validate request bodies before they reach a controller
optionD: To add a common prefix to every controller URL in the app
correctAnswerText: To turn exceptions into one consistent error response format
explanation: Centralising exception-to-response mapping keeps controllers clean and gives clients one predictable error shape.

prompt: Why accept a DTO in a request body rather than the JPA entity?
optionA: Because @Valid works only on classes named DTO
optionB: To make Hibernate load the entities more quickly
optionC: Because Jackson cannot serialise entity classes
optionD: To control which fields a client can see and set
correctAnswerText: To control which fields a client can see and set
explanation: Binding straight to an entity lets a client set fields such as role or id (mass assignment) and ties the API to the table design.

prompt: What does @Transactional on a service method give you?
optionA: All its database work commits or rolls back together
optionB: The method is retried automatically on any failure
optionC: Its results are cached for the rest of the request
optionD: Each query inside it runs on a separate new thread
correctAnswerText: All its database work commits or rolls back together
explanation: The proxy opens a transaction before the method and commits after it, or rolls back if it throws an exception that triggers rollback.

prompt: By default, which exceptions make a @Transactional method roll back?
optionA: Any exception at all, checked or unchecked
optionB: Unchecked exceptions and errors, not checked ones
optionC: Checked exceptions only, not runtime exceptions
optionD: None, unless rollbackFor is set explicitly
correctAnswerText: Unchecked exceptions and errors, not checked ones
explanation: RuntimeException and Error roll back; checked exceptions commit unless you add rollbackFor. Many silent partial saves come from this rule.

prompt: How does Spring Data implement findByEmailAndActive(String email, boolean active)?
optionA: It parses the method name into a query at startup
optionB: It builds SQL by calling every getter on the entity
optionC: It needs a @Query written by the developer
optionD: It loads the whole table and filters it in Java
correctAnswerText: It parses the method name into a query at startup
explanation: Method names are parsed against entity properties when the repository is created; a misspelt property fails startup rather than at runtime.

prompt: Why return 201 Created for a successful POST that creates a resource?
optionA: It is required for the browser to render JSON
optionB: It means the body was accepted but not stored
optionC: It tells the client to retry the request later
optionD: It tells the client a new resource now exists
correctAnswerText: It tells the client a new resource now exists
explanation: 201, usually with a Location header pointing at the new resource, is more precise than 200 for creation.

prompt: With the dev profile active, what happens to application-dev.yml?
optionA: It declares beans that only dev code can inject
optionB: Its values are loaded on top of application.yml
optionC: It replaces application.yml and its values entirely
optionD: It is loaded only by tests, never at runtime
correctAnswerText: Its values are loaded on top of application.yml
explanation: Profile-specific files override matching keys from the base file; anything they do not mention keeps its base value.

prompt: What does @DataJpaTest set up by default?
optionA: Only the controllers, with every repository mocked out
optionB: JPA pieces on an embedded database, rolled back per test
optionC: A MySQL container started fresh for each test class
optionD: The full application context with a real running server
correctAnswerText: JPA pieces on an embedded database, rolled back per test
explanation: It loads entities, repositories and the EntityManager, swaps in an embedded database if one is available, and rolls back after each test.

prompt: Why is /actuator/env not reachable over HTTP by default?
optionA: Only the health endpoint is exposed over HTTP by default
optionB: The env endpoint needs a MySQL database configured
optionC: Actuator endpoints can only be called from a terminal
optionD: The env endpoint was removed from Spring Boot 3
correctAnswerText: Only the health endpoint is exposed over HTTP by default
explanation: Endpoints are opt-in over HTTP because some reveal configuration and secrets. management.endpoints.web.exposure.include widens it.

prompt: A GET /users/{id} handler finds no user. Which return gives the client a 404?
optionA: return new ResponseEntity<>(HttpStatus.OK);
optionB: return ResponseEntity.ok().body(null);
optionC: return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
optionD: return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
correctAnswerText: return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
explanation: notFound() builds 404 with no body. 204 means success with nothing to return, which tells the client the wrong thing.

prompt: A DTO field must be a non-blank email address. Which declaration does that?
optionA: @Column(nullable = false) String email;
optionB: @NotBlank @Email private String email;
optionC: @Pattern(regexp = ".*") String email;
optionD: @NotNull @Size(min = 0) String email;
correctAnswerText: @NotBlank @Email private String email;
explanation: @Email alone accepts null and blank, so @NotBlank is added. @Column is a database mapping, not input validation.

prompt: GET /products?page=2&size=20&sort=price,desc must return a page of products. Which controller signature fits?
optionA: List<ProductDto> list(Sort sort, String size)
optionB: Page<ProductDto> list(Pageable pageable)
optionC: Page<ProductDto> list(@RequestBody Pageable p)
optionD: List<ProductDto> list(int page, int size)
correctAnswerText: Page<ProductDto> list(Pageable pageable)
explanation: Spring MVC resolves Pageable from page, size and sort parameters; pass it to the repository and map the page to DTOs.

prompt: With Spring Data defaults, which rows does ?page=2&size=20 return?
optionA: Rows 1–40, two pages combined
optionB: Rows 41–60, as pages are zero-based
optionC: Rows 21–40, as pages are one-based
optionD: Rows 2–21, as page is an offset
correctAnswerText: Rows 41–60, as pages are zero-based
explanation: Page numbers start at 0, so page=2 is the third page. Frontends written for one-based pages are off by one unless configured.

prompt: In a @RestControllerAdvice, how do you map ProductNotFoundException to 404?
optionA: @ControllerAdvice(ProductNotFoundException.class) @ResponseBody(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
optionB: @ExceptionHandler(ProductNotFoundException.class) @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
optionC: @ExceptionHandler(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) @ResponseStatus(ProductNotFoundException.class)
optionD: @RequestMapping(ProductNotFoundException.class) @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
correctAnswerText: @ExceptionHandler(ProductNotFoundException.class) @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
explanation: @ExceptionHandler names the exception type; @ResponseStatus (or a ResponseEntity return) sets the status of the response.

prompt: The server must listen on 8081 only when the prod profile is active. Where does server.port go?
optionA: port: 8081 in pom.xml under a prod profile
optionB: server.port: 8081 in application.yml only
optionC: server.port: 8081 in application-prod.yml
optionD: spring.port.prod: 8081 in application.yml
correctAnswerText: server.port: 8081 in application-prod.yml
explanation: Profile-specific files override the base file only when that profile is active; Maven profiles do not affect runtime properties.

prompt: A default @Transactional method saves an order, then throws java.io.IOException. What happens to the order?
optionA: It rolls back because Spring wraps the exception
optionB: It commits, as checked exceptions do not roll back
optionC: It rolls back, like for any exception thrown
optionD: It stays pending until the next service call
correctAnswerText: It commits, as checked exceptions do not roll back
explanation: Checked exceptions commit by default. Use @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) or throw an unchecked exception.

prompt: Which repository method finds active users in a city, sorted by name?
optionA: List<User> findByCityOrderByNameAndActive(String city)
optionB: List<User> queryCityWhereActiveSortedName(String city)
optionC: List<User> findByCityAndActiveTrueOrderByNameAsc(String city)
optionD: List<User> findAllCityActiveSortName(String city)
correctAnswerText: List<User> findByCityAndActiveTrueOrderByNameAsc(String city)
explanation: Property names joined with And, a True keyword for booleans and OrderBy…Asc form a valid derived query.

prompt: A @WebMvcTest(UserController.class) test needs the controller's UserService. How is it usually supplied?
optionA: A @MockitoBean field (@MockBean before Boot 3.4)
optionB: A UserService bean declared in application.yml
optionC: An @Autowired field, since slices load services
optionD: A second @DataJpaTest on the same test class
correctAnswerText: A @MockitoBean field (@MockBean before Boot 3.4)
explanation: The MVC slice does not create services, so a Mockito mock is registered in the context. @MockitoBean replaced @MockBean in Boot 3.4.

prompt: A @Valid @RequestBody fails validation and no custom handler exists. What status does Spring Boot return?
optionA: 409 Conflict
optionB: 422 Unprocessable Entity
optionC: 400 Bad Request
optionD: 500 Internal Server Error
correctAnswerText: 400 Bad Request
explanation: MethodArgumentNotValidException maps to 400. Override it in @RestControllerAdvice to return field-level messages.

prompt: A developer defines their own DataSource @Bean and now spring.datasource.url is ignored. Why?
optionA: Boot's DataSource auto-configuration backs off for it
optionB: spring.datasource.url works only in properties files
optionC: application.yml is read only when no @Bean exists
optionD: The custom bean is replaced by the default at runtime
correctAnswerText: Boot's DataSource auto-configuration backs off for it
explanation: Auto-configuration creates its DataSource only when none exists. Your bean wins, and it is up to you to bind those properties.

prompt: A @Transactional(readOnly = true) method loads a User and changes its name. No error occurs, yet nothing is written. Why?
optionA: Read-only transactions always roll back when they finish
optionB: readOnly makes Hibernate skip the flush, so no UPDATE runs
optionC: The change needed an explicit repository.save() call
optionD: MySQL drops writes on read-only connections silently
correctAnswerText: readOnly makes Hibernate skip the flush, so no UPDATE runs
explanation: With JPA, readOnly sets Hibernate's flush mode to manual, so dirty checking never issues the UPDATE. Use it only for genuine reads.

prompt: create(@RequestBody UserDto dto) saves users with blank names even though UserDto.name has @NotBlank. Why?
optionA: The DTO must extend a Spring validation base class
optionB: The parameter lacks @Valid, so no validation runs
optionC: Validation runs only for GET and DELETE requests
optionD: @NotBlank is checked only on JPA entity classes
correctAnswerText: The parameter lacks @Valid, so no validation runs
explanation: Constraints are only declarations. Validation runs when @Valid is present and spring-boot-starter-validation is on the classpath.

prompt: Clients get 500 for EntityNotFoundException though a @RestControllerAdvice maps it to 404. The advice is in com.cb.common; the main class is in com.cb.app. Why?
optionA: Spring maps entity exceptions to 500 first
optionB: The advice sits outside the scanned packages
optionC: The handler must live inside the controller
optionD: @RestControllerAdvice handles checked ones only
correctAnswerText: The advice sits outside the scanned packages
explanation: The advice is never registered because scanning starts at com.cb.app. Moving the main class up to com.cb fixes both this and similar cases.

prompt: A @Transactional method saves an order, then catches a RuntimeException thrown by another @Transactional bean it called. Commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException. Why?
optionA: Two @Transactional beans cannot share one transaction
optionB: The inner call marked the shared transaction rollback-only
optionC: The catch block quietly re-threw the exception later
optionD: The order was saved twice and broke a unique key
correctAnswerText: The inner call marked the shared transaction rollback-only
explanation: The inner method joined the outer transaction (REQUIRED); its exception marked it rollback-only, and catching it cannot undo that.

prompt: A @SpringBootTest suite takes three minutes, and each test class declares a different set of mocked beans. Why is it slow?
optionA: JUnit 5 runs all Spring tests on a single thread only
optionB: Mocked beans run much slower than real ones at runtime
optionC: Each distinct mock set forces a new context to be built
optionD: @SpringBootTest restarts the database before each test
correctAnswerText: Each distinct mock set forces a new context to be built
explanation: Spring caches contexts by configuration, and mocked beans are part of it. Sharing one mock setup lets classes reuse a context.

prompt: findByName("ravi") returns nothing though a row named "Ravi" exists. The column uses the utf8mb4_bin collation. Why?
optionA: findBy methods search only the primary key column
optionB: The binary collation makes comparison case-sensitive
optionC: Derived queries always lower-case their parameters
optionD: Spring Data cached an earlier empty result set
correctAnswerText: The binary collation makes comparison case-sensitive
explanation: MySQL 8's default collation is case-insensitive, but _bin compares bytes. Use findByNameIgnoreCase or a case-insensitive collation.

prompt: A POST body {"user_name":"ravi"} binds to a DTO field userName, which arrives as null. Why?
optionA: @RequestBody reads only from query string parameters
optionB: Jackson skips every field whose name has an underscore
optionC: Jackson matches names exactly; user_name is not userName
optionD: The DTO needs a no-argument constructor to bind at all
correctAnswerText: Jackson matches names exactly; user_name is not userName
explanation: Unknown properties are ignored by Boot's default mapper. Use @JsonProperty("user_name") or a snake_case naming strategy.

prompt: In production, management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* was set and /actuator/heapdump downloads without login. What is the problem?
optionA: Only the health endpoint can ever be exposed over HTTP
optionB: The setting has no effect unless Spring Security is used
optionC: Every endpoint is exposed, including a full memory dump
optionD: Heap dumps are blocked by Actuator in production anyway
correctAnswerText: Every endpoint is exposed, including a full memory dump
explanation: A heap dump can contain passwords, tokens and user data. Expose only what is needed and secure the rest.

prompt: A paged repository method on a large table is slow, and the log shows two SQL queries per page. Why the second one?
optionA: Hibernate loads the next page early in the background
optionB: The sort clause is applied in a second separate query
optionC: Spring Data re-runs the page query to verify results
optionD: Page<T> runs a count query to report the total pages
correctAnswerText: Page<T> runs a count query to report the total pages
explanation: A Page knows its total, which costs a count. Return Slice<T> when the client needs only "is there a next page".

prompt: Should a team pin the version of every library a Spring Boot starter brings in?
optionA: Yes; Boot ignores the versions given by its parent POM
optionB: Yes; starters pick a different version on every build
optionC: No; Maven always resolves the newest version anyway
optionD: No; let Boot's dependency management pick, override rarely
correctAnswerText: No; let Boot's dependency management pick, override rarely
explanation: Boot's BOM ships versions tested together. Overriding one is sometimes needed for a fix, but pinning everything invites mismatches.

prompt: A team runs spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update in production. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Fine, provided the team takes manual backups each week
optionB: Prefer create-drop, so the schema always starts clean
optionC: Fine: Hibernate changes schemas safely in every situation
optionD: Avoid it: use migrations such as Flyway, with validate or none
correctAnswerText: Avoid it: use migrations such as Flyway, with validate or none
explanation: update never drops or renames safely and leaves no history. Versioned migrations are reviewed, repeatable and reversible.

prompt: Which error response design is best for a public API?
optionA: The default stack trace, so clients debug faster
optionB: One ProblemDetail-style body, with no stack traces
optionC: A plain text message that varies per controller
optionD: Always 200, with an error flag in the JSON body
correctAnswerText: One ProblemDetail-style body, with no stack traces
explanation: Spring 6 supports RFC 7807 ProblemDetail. A consistent body with the right status is easy to handle and leaks nothing internal.

prompt: Where should @Transactional usually be placed?
optionA: On the entity classes the service will change
optionB: On every controller method that handles requests
optionC: On service methods that form one unit of work
optionD: On each repository method the service calls
correctAnswerText: On service methods that form one unit of work
explanation: The service knows which writes belong together. Repository methods are already transactional individually, which is not enough.

prompt: Which test gives the best value for checking a controller's validation and status codes?
optionA: Plain unit tests that call the method directly
optionB: @WebMvcTest with MockMvc and a mocked service
optionC: @SpringBootTest with real MySQL for every case
optionD: Manual Postman checks before each release
correctAnswerText: @WebMvcTest with MockMvc and a mocked service
explanation: The MVC slice exercises binding, validation, advice and serialisation quickly. Calling the method directly skips all of that.

prompt: Where should input validation live for a create-user endpoint?
optionA: On the request DTO, plus business rules in the service
optionB: Only in database constraints, so the code stays simple
optionC: In entity setters, so that Jackson triggers the checks
optionD: Only in the frontend form, where the user types data
correctAnswerText: On the request DTO, plus business rules in the service
explanation: DTO constraints reject malformed input early; rules such as "email not taken" need the service; database constraints stay as a backstop.

prompt: A well-formed request tries to create a user whose email already exists. Which status fits best?
optionA: 409 Conflict
optionB: 200 OK with an error message
optionC: 500 Internal Server Error
optionD: 400 Bad Request
correctAnswerText: 409 Conflict
explanation: The request is valid but clashes with the current state of the resource; 409 says exactly that. 500 suggests a server bug.

prompt: A list endpoint returns all 80,000 products in one response. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Keep it; gzip makes the response size irrelevant here
optionB: Paginate with a capped size; never return unbounded lists
optionC: Cache the full list on every client when it starts up
optionD: Keep it, but switch the response format over to XML
correctAnswerText: Paginate with a capped size; never return unbounded lists
explanation: Unbounded lists grow with the data, slowing the database, the server and the client. Pages with a maximum size stay predictable.

prompt: Where should the production database password live?
optionA: In an environment variable or a secret store
optionB: In application.yml, committed with the source
optionC: In a Java constant so that it cannot change
optionD: In application-prod.yml, committed but encoded
correctAnswerText: In an environment variable or a secret store
explanation: Committed secrets live forever in git history. Boot reads environment variables and external config, so nothing sensitive is in the repo.

prompt: Which Actuator exposure suits a production deployment?
optionA: Every endpoint, served on the same port as the API
optionB: Nothing; Actuator never belongs on the classpath
optionC: Every endpoint, since Actuator data is read-only
optionD: health, plus chosen endpoints, secured where sensitive
correctAnswerText: health, plus chosen endpoints, secured where sensitive
explanation: Health is needed for probes and metrics for monitoring; env, heapdump and similar should stay closed or behind authentication.

prompt: In Spring Security 6, how is HTTP security configured?
optionA: By declaring a SecurityFilterChain @Bean
optionB: By implementing a HandlerInterceptor bean
optionC: By extending WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter
optionD: By listing rules in application.yml only
correctAnswerText: By declaring a SecurityFilterChain @Bean
explanation: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was removed in Security 6. You build the chain with HttpSecurity in a @Bean method.

prompt: Which interface loads a user's details by username for authentication?
optionA: UserDetailsService
optionB: PasswordEncoder
optionC: AuthenticationManager
optionD: SecurityContext
correctAnswerText: UserDetailsService
explanation: loadUserByUsername returns UserDetails (username, password hash, authorities), which the authentication provider checks.

prompt: Which PasswordEncoder is a standard choice for storing user passwords?
optionA: Base64PasswordEncoder
optionB: NoOpPasswordEncoder
optionC: Md5PasswordEncoder
optionD: BCryptPasswordEncoder
correctAnswerText: BCryptPasswordEncoder
explanation: BCrypt is salted and deliberately slow. NoOp stores plain text and exists only for legacy tests.

prompt: Which HTTP status means the request is not authenticated?
optionA: 404 Not Found
optionB: 403 Forbidden
optionC: 401 Unauthorized
optionD: 400 Bad Request
correctAnswerText: 401 Unauthorized
explanation: Despite its name, 401 means "who are you?" — missing or invalid credentials. 403 means known but not allowed.

prompt: Which annotation enables @PreAuthorize checks in Spring Security 6?
optionA: @EnableWebSecurity
optionB: @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity
optionC: @EnableMethodSecurity
optionD: @EnableAuthorization
correctAnswerText: @EnableMethodSecurity
explanation: @EnableMethodSecurity turns on pre/post annotations by default. The older @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity is deprecated.

prompt: What are the three parts of a JWT?
optionA: Header, payload and signature
optionB: Header, body and session id
optionC: Key, value and expiry time
optionD: Username, password and role
correctAnswerText: Header, payload and signature
explanation: Three Base64URL parts separated by dots: algorithm header, claims payload, and a signature over the first two.

prompt: What does CSRF stand for?
optionA: Cross-Site Response Framing
optionB: Cross-Site Request Forgery
optionC: Cross-Server Resource Fetch
optionD: Client-Side Request Filter
correctAnswerText: Cross-Site Request Forgery
explanation: Another site makes the victim's browser send a request to yours, with the cookies the browser attaches automatically.

prompt: Where does Spring Security keep the authenticated user for the current request?
optionA: HttpSessionRegistry
optionB: SecurityContextHolder
optionC: AuthenticationStore
optionD: PrincipalRepository
correctAnswerText: SecurityContextHolder
explanation: SecurityContextHolder holds the SecurityContext, whose Authentication carries the principal and authorities, thread-local by default.

prompt: Which authority does hasRole("ADMIN") check for?
optionA: ADMIN_ROLE
optionB: ROLE_ADMIN
optionC: AUTH_ADMIN
optionD: ADMIN only
correctAnswerText: ROLE_ADMIN
explanation: hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix. hasAuthority("ADMIN") checks the string exactly as written.

prompt: What does CORS control?
optionA: Which users are allowed to log in to the app
optionB: Which servers may connect to your database
optionC: Which HTTP methods a controller may declare
optionD: Which other origins a browser lets call your API
correctAnswerText: Which other origins a browser lets call your API
explanation: CORS is a browser rule: a page from another origin may read your responses only if your server says so in headers.

prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
optionA: Authorization happens first and authentication comes after
optionB: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides access
optionC: Authentication sets permissions; authorization checks passwords
optionD: Both mean checking the password, only at different layers
correctAnswerText: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides access
explanation: First establish who the caller is, then decide what that caller may do. Many bugs come from doing the first and skipping the second.

prompt: Why use BCrypt rather than plain SHA-256 to store passwords?
optionA: It produces shorter hashes that save database space
optionB: It is salted and deliberately slow, resisting brute force
optionC: It is faster, so logins under heavy load stay quick
optionD: It can be decrypted when a user forgets the password
correctAnswerText: It is salted and deliberately slow, resisting brute force
explanation: Fast hashes let attackers try billions of guesses per second. BCrypt's cost factor and per-password salt make that impractical.

prompt: Why can a JWT not easily be revoked before it expires?
optionA: JWTs are encrypted, so the server cannot read them
optionB: Revoking a token requires the user's current password
optionC: The server accepts any validly signed, unexpired token
optionD: The token lives only in the server's database session
correctAnswerText: The server accepts any validly signed, unexpired token
explanation: Stateless validation checks signature and expiry only. Revocation needs extra state such as a denylist or short expiry with refresh.

prompt: What does a valid JWT signature guarantee?
optionA: The user is still active in the database now
optionB: The contents were not altered after signing
optionC: The payload is hidden from whoever holds it
optionD: The token can be used from one device only
correctAnswerText: The contents were not altered after signing
explanation: Signing gives integrity, not secrecy: anyone can Base64-decode the payload, so never put secrets in it.

prompt: Why is CSRF protection often disabled for a stateless API that takes a JWT in the Authorization header?
optionA: Spring Security 6 removed CSRF support for every kind of REST endpoint
optionB: JWT tokens are encrypted end to end, so a forged request is impossible
optionC: CSRF only affects GET requests, which a JSON API normally avoids anyway
optionD: Browsers attach cookies automatically, but not Authorization headers
correctAnswerText: Browsers attach cookies automatically, but not Authorization headers
explanation: CSRF abuses credentials the browser sends by itself. A header added by your own JavaScript cannot be added by another site.

prompt: What is a SecurityFilterChain?
optionA: A list of controllers that require a logged-in user to call
optionB: A sequence of redirects that ends at the login page
optionC: A chain of database queries used to load the current user
optionD: An ordered set of filters each request passes before the servlet
correctAnswerText: An ordered set of filters each request passes before the servlet
explanation: Security runs as servlet filters before any controller: reading credentials, authenticating, translating exceptions, then authorizing.

prompt: When should a secured API return 403?
optionA: The token is malformed or has already expired
optionB: The requested resource does not exist at all
optionC: The request carries no credentials of any kind
optionD: The caller is known but lacks permission for this
correctAnswerText: The caller is known but lacks permission for this
explanation: 403 means authenticated but not allowed. Missing or bad credentials are 401, so the client knows to log in again.

prompt: Why is @PreAuthorize("hasRole('USER')") not enough protection for GET /orders/{id}?
optionA: USER is not a valid role name in Security 6
optionB: Any user could read any other user's order
optionC: It also blocks admins from reading the order
optionD: hasRole works only on class-level annotations
correctAnswerText: Any user could read any other user's order
explanation: The role says what kind of caller this is, not whose order it is. An ownership check must compare the order's owner with the caller.

prompt: With Spring Security on, why must CORS also be enabled in the chain with http.cors(…)?
optionA: Spring MVC ignores all CORS settings in Boot 3
optionB: Without it the browser skips the preflight step
optionC: CORS headers may only be added to 401 responses
optionD: Preflight OPTIONS requests would be rejected before MVC
correctAnswerText: Preflight OPTIONS requests would be rejected before MVC
explanation: The browser's preflight carries no credentials, so the security filters reject it before Spring MVC's CORS handling is reached.

prompt: Why give access tokens a short expiry time?
optionA: It forces users to pick stronger passwords
optionB: It lets the server read it without any key
optionC: It makes the token smaller and quicker to send
optionD: It limits how long a stolen token stays usable
correctAnswerText: It limits how long a stolen token stays usable
explanation: Since a JWT cannot be cheaply revoked, its lifetime is the window an attacker gets. Refresh tokens restore convenience.

prompt: Allow /api/auth/** to everyone and require authentication for everything else. Which rule chain is right?
optionA: auth.requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll().anyRequest().authenticated()
optionB: auth.requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").authenticated().anyRequest().permitAll()
optionC: auth.requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").denyAll().anyRequest().authenticated()
optionD: auth.anyRequest().authenticated().requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
correctAnswerText: auth.requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll().anyRequest().authenticated()
explanation: Rules match in order, specific first. Spring refuses to start if anyRequest() is followed by more matchers.

prompt: At registration, how should the password be stored? (encoder is the injected PasswordEncoder.)
optionA: user.setPassword(raw.toUpperCase().strip())
optionB: user.setPassword(String.valueOf(raw.hashCode()))
optionC: user.setPassword(encoder.encode(raw))
optionD: user.setPassword(Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(raw.getBytes()))
correctAnswerText: user.setPassword(encoder.encode(raw))
explanation: encode produces a salted BCrypt hash. hashCode collides easily and Base64 is reversible encoding, not hashing.

prompt: At login, how do you check a raw password against the stored BCrypt hash?
optionA: encoder.encode(raw).equals(user.getPassword())
optionB: encoder.decode(user.getPassword()).equals(raw)
optionC: raw.equals(user.getPassword())
optionD: encoder.matches(raw, user.getPassword())
correctAnswerText: encoder.matches(raw, user.getPassword())
explanation: matches re-hashes using the salt stored inside the hash. Encoding again creates a new salt, so equals always fails.

prompt: getOrder(Long id) returns an Order with an ownerUsername field. Which rule lets only the owner receive it?
optionA: @Secured("returnObject.ownerUsername")
optionB: @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerUsername == authentication.name")
optionC: @PreAuthorize("returnObject.ownerUsername == authentication.name")
optionD: @PreAuthorize("hasRole(returnObject.ownerUsername)")
correctAnswerText: @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerUsername == authentication.name")
explanation: returnObject exists only after the method runs, so the check must be @PostAuthorize. A service-level check is an equally good option.

prompt: Authorities are stored as ROLE_ADMIN and ROLE_USER. Which annotation restricts a method to admins?
optionA: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
optionB: @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('ADMIN')")
optionC: @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
optionD: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ROLE_USER')")
correctAnswerText: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
explanation: hasRole('ADMIN') looks for ROLE_ADMIN. hasAuthority('ADMIN') wants the bare string, which these users do not have.

prompt: Which configuration stops Spring Security creating HTTP sessions for a JWT API?
optionA: securityContext(c -> c.requireExplicitSave(false)).httpBasic(withDefaults())
optionB: sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionFixation(f -> f.migrateSession()))
optionC: sessionManagement(s -> s.maximumSessions(1).maxSessionsPreventsLogin(true))
optionD: sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
correctAnswerText: sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
explanation: STATELESS means no session is created or used for the security context; every request must carry its token.

prompt: Where should a custom JWT authentication filter be registered?
optionA: As a @RestController that every incoming request is forwarded to first
optionB: Called by hand at the start of every controller method that needs it
optionC: http.addFilterAfter(jwtFilter, AuthorizationFilter.class) at the chain end
optionD: http.addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
correctAnswerText: http.addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
explanation: The filter must set the Authentication before authorization runs; placing it before the username/password filter is the usual spot.

prompt: Besides verifying the signature, which check must a JWT filter make before trusting a token?
optionA: Reject the token if its payload is not encrypted
optionB: Reject the token if its exp time has passed
optionC: Accept it if the header names any algorithm
optionD: Accept it if a username is present in the payload
correctAnswerText: Reject the token if its exp time has passed
explanation: A correctly signed token is still invalid after exp. Libraries check exp when parsing; hand-rolled code often forgets it.

prompt: A React app at http://localhost:5173 calls the API with credentials. Which CORS configuration works?
optionA: allowedOrigins("http://localhost:5173") with allowCredentials(true)
optionB: allowedHeaders("Origin") with allowCredentials(false) set
optionC: allowedOrigins("*") with allowCredentials(true) on all paths
optionD: allowedMethods("*") with no allowed origins configured
correctAnswerText: allowedOrigins("http://localhost:5173") with allowCredentials(true)
explanation: With credentials, the origin must be named exactly; Spring rejects "*" with allowCredentials(true), as browsers would.

prompt: A logged-in user with only ROLE_USER calls DELETE /api/admin/users/5, which requires ADMIN. Which status should come back?
optionA: 401 Unauthorized
optionB: 403 Forbidden
optionC: 404 Not Found
optionD: 405 Method Not Allowed
correctAnswerText: 403 Forbidden
explanation: The caller is authenticated, so this is not 401; they are refused permission, which is 403.

prompt: A new Spring Boot 3 app with session login: GET requests work, but every POST from the client returns 403 even for an ADMIN. Likely cause?
optionA: CSRF protection is on and the POST carries no token
optionB: The ADMIN role cannot perform write operations
optionC: Login credentials are not sent on POST requests
optionD: POST endpoints need @PreAuthorize to be reachable
correctAnswerText: CSRF protection is on and the POST carries no token
explanation: CSRF is on by default for state-changing methods. Send the token with each POST, or disable it only for a header-token API.

prompt: Users have the authority "ADMIN" (no prefix), and hasRole("ADMIN") rejects them with 403. Why?
optionA: hasRole is case-insensitive and fails on capitals
optionB: Authorities only work when loaded from a JWT
optionC: hasRole looks for ROLE_ADMIN, not ADMIN
optionD: 403 means the password check itself failed
correctAnswerText: hasRole looks for ROLE_ADMIN, not ADMIN
explanation: Either store ROLE_ADMIN, or use hasAuthority("ADMIN"). Mixing the two conventions is the usual cause.

prompt: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on a service method has no effect; any user can call it. Why?
optionA: @PreAuthorize works only on @RestController methods
optionB: Roles must be declared in application.yml before use
optionC: The method must also be annotated with @Transactional
optionD: @EnableMethodSecurity is missing from the configuration
correctAnswerText: @EnableMethodSecurity is missing from the configuration
explanation: Method security is opt-in. Without it the annotation is ignored; it is also proxy-based, so self-calls skip it too.

prompt: An admin is demoted to USER, but for hours they still pass admin checks. Roles are read from the JWT. Why?
optionA: Their old token still says ADMIN until it expires
optionB: Spring caches each role in the database connection
optionC: The BCrypt hash still contains the old role inside
optionD: The filter chain was built once at startup time
correctAnswerText: Their old token still says ADMIN until it expires
explanation: Claims are a snapshot taken at login. Short expiry, re-checking the user, or a token version bump handles role changes.

prompt: A browser shows a CORS error on POST, while Postman works. The preflight OPTIONS request gets 401. Why?
optionA: Postman skips HTTPS checks, so the API rejects browsers
optionB: The JSON body is too large for a cross-origin request
optionC: The server must answer 200 to every request it receives
optionD: The chain requires auth for the preflight, which carries none
correctAnswerText: The chain requires auth for the preflight, which carries none
explanation: Preflights never include credentials. Enabling http.cors() lets the CORS filter answer them before authorization.

prompt: A JWT filter Base64-decodes the payload and trusts its sub claim without verifying the signature. What follows?
optionA: The payload will fail to decode for most users
optionB: Tokens will expire sooner than configured
optionC: Anyone can forge a token that names any user
optionD: Only the expiry claim then needs verification
correctAnswerText: Anyone can forge a token that names any user
explanation: Without verification the payload is just text the client wrote. Always parse with the key and a fixed expected algorithm.

prompt: GET /api/orders/{id} checks only that the caller is logged in. A student changes 101 to 102 in the URL and sees another student's order. What is wrong?
optionA: The endpoint should use POST instead
optionB: Nothing ties the order to the caller
optionC: The JWT should list every order owned
optionD: The id should be a UUID to stop guessing
correctAnswerText: Nothing ties the order to the caller
explanation: This is an insecure direct object reference. Hard-to-guess ids reduce exposure but are not authorization; check the owner.

prompt: Registration saved encoder.encode(raw); login compares encoder.encode(raw).equals(stored), and login always fails. Why?
optionA: BCrypt salts each hash, so two encodings differ
optionB: equals() is case-sensitive for BCrypt hash text
optionC: BCrypt hashes change when the database restarts
optionD: The encoder must be a new instance for each call
correctAnswerText: BCrypt salts each hash, so two encodings differ
explanation: Each encode picks a random salt. Use encoder.matches(raw, stored), which reads the salt from the stored hash.

prompt: /api/auth/login is permitAll, yet a request that carries an expired token in its header gets 401 even on login. Why?
optionA: Expired tokens make Spring restart the HTTP session
optionB: Login endpoints must be served by a separate app
optionC: permitAll is ignored for POST requests by design
optionD: The JWT filter rejects the bad token before any rules apply
correctAnswerText: The JWT filter rejects the bad token before any rules apply
explanation: Filters run before authorization rules. A JWT filter should skip invalid tokens and let the rules decide, not end the request itself.

prompt: With no form login or HTTP Basic configured, requests that carry no token get 403, and the frontend says "no permission" instead of asking to log in. Why?
optionA: The frontend must send OPTIONS before every request
optionB: 403 is the only status Spring can use for security
optionC: The token header must be named X-Auth for Spring
optionD: No entry point returns 401 when authentication is missing
correctAnswerText: No entry point returns 401 when authentication is missing
explanation: Without a configured entry point Spring falls back to 403. Register one, such as HttpStatusEntryPoint(UNAUTHORIZED), to send 401.

prompt: A server-rendered app on one domain with one backend needs login. JWT or a server session?
optionA: JWT always, since sessions never scale
optionB: A session cookie: simpler and revocable here
optionC: JWT in localStorage, the safest storage
optionD: Neither; send the password every time
correctAnswerText: A session cookie: simpler and revocable here
explanation: JWT pays off across services and domains. For one app, sessions are revocable on logout and need no token handling.

prompt: How should a team judge storing the access token in localStorage?
optionA: Any XSS script can read it; weigh httpOnly cookies with CSRF
optionB: Fine, as long as the token is issued with no expiry
optionC: Ideal: the browser encrypts localStorage on disk for you
optionD: Ideal: JavaScript code has no way to read localStorage
correctAnswerText: Any XSS script can read it; weigh httpOnly cookies with CSRF
explanation: localStorage is readable by any script on the page. An httpOnly cookie hides the token from scripts but brings CSRF back.

prompt: A team disables CSRF for an app that authenticates with session cookies because it "breaks our forms". What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Fine: CSRF matters only for JWT-based REST APIs
optionB: Fine, as long as the cookies are marked Secure
optionC: Fine: HTTPS on its own already prevents CSRF
optionD: Wrong: cookie auth needs CSRF; send the token instead
correctAnswerText: Wrong: cookie auth needs CSRF; send the token instead
explanation: Cookie sessions are exactly what CSRF exploits. Include the CSRF token in forms and AJAX calls rather than turning protection off.

prompt: Where should "only the author may edit a post" be enforced?
optionA: On the server, in the service or a method rule
optionB: In MySQL, with one database user per student
optionC: Only in React, by hiding the edit button
optionD: Only in the JWT, by listing editable posts
correctAnswerText: On the server, in the service or a method rule
explanation: Anything in the browser can be bypassed with a crafted request. The UI can hide the button; the server must refuse.

prompt: An app grows from USER/ADMIN to many actions such as refund, export and ban. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Create a separate role for every user who needs access
optionB: Map roles to fine-grained authorities and check those
optionC: Move every permission check into the frontend router
optionD: Keep two roles and add if-checks on specific usernames
correctAnswerText: Map roles to fine-grained authorities and check those
explanation: Checking permissions such as order:refund lets roles change without code changes and keeps rules readable.

prompt: A team sets access tokens to expire after 30 days to avoid writing refresh logic. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Prefer no expiry, so tokens stay even simpler
optionB: Fine, if the signing key is rotated monthly
optionC: Fine: long tokens are safer as they change less
optionD: Prefer short access tokens plus refresh tokens
correctAnswerText: Prefer short access tokens plus refresh tokens
explanation: A stolen 30-day token works for a month and cannot be revoked. Short access tokens bound the damage; refresh tokens can be revoked.

prompt: A login endpoint replies "user not found" or "wrong password" separately. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Return the stored hash so users can compare it
optionB: Return 404 for unknown users, following REST
optionC: Use one generic message to avoid user enumeration
optionD: Keep both; specific messages help attackers less
correctAnswerText: Use one generic message to avoid user enumeration
explanation: Different answers let an attacker discover which emails are registered, then target them. One message reveals nothing.

prompt: The JWT signing secret "secret123" is hard-coded in the source. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Fine, since the key is compiled into bytecode
optionB: Fine, if the GitHub repository is kept private
optionC: Use a long random key from env or a secret store
optionD: Use each user's password as the signing key
correctAnswerText: Use a long random key from env or a secret store
explanation: Anyone with the key can mint admin tokens. A short guessable key can also be brute-forced from a single token.

prompt: To make the frontend work anywhere, a team sets allowedOriginPatterns("*") with credentials allowed. What is the soundest judgement?
optionA: Accept: CORS is only a browser convenience
optionB: Reject: any website could make credentialed calls
optionC: Reject: patterns are unsupported in Security 6
optionD: Accept: authentication already protects the API
correctAnswerText: Reject: any website could make credentialed calls
explanation: Patterns bypass the "*" with credentials safeguard. List the real frontend origins per environment instead.

prompt: Should all authorization rules live only in the URL rules of the filter chain?
optionA: Use URL rules broadly and method rules for detail
optionB: No; URL rules are ignored once methods are secured
optionC: Yes; services must never know who the caller is
optionD: Yes; method security is deprecated in Security 6
correctAnswerText: Use URL rules broadly and method rules for detail
explanation: URL rules are good coarse gates; method rules sit next to the logic and survive new endpoints calling the same service.

prompt: Which kind of function can be called on a line above the place where it is written?
optionA: An arrow function in a const
optionB: A function declaration
optionC: A method inside a class body
optionD: A function expression in let
correctAnswerText: A function declaration
explanation: A function declaration is hoisted whole, name and body, so it can be called before its line. A const or let binding is hoisted but stays uninitialised until its line runs.

prompt: Where does an arrow function get its value of `this` from?
optionA: The object it was called on
optionB: A new empty object per call
optionC: The scope it was written in
optionD: Always the global object
correctAnswerText: The scope it was written in
explanation: Arrows have no `this` of their own; they read it from the surrounding scope exactly like any other outer variable. That is why they suit callbacks and do not suit object methods.

prompt: In JavaScript, what is a closure?
optionA: A function that has finished running and returned
optionB: A function together with the variables it can reach
optionC: A function that is called with no arguments at all
optionD: A function stored as a property inside an object
correctAnswerText: A function together with the variables it can reach
explanation: A closure is a function plus the scope it was created in. The inner function keeps those outer variables alive after the outer function has returned.

prompt: What is a callback function?
optionA: A function that calls itself until it is done
optionB: A function that returns a second function
optionC: A function the browser runs on page load
optionD: A function passed in to be called by other code
correctAnswerText: A function passed in to be called by other code
explanation: A callback is handed to other code — map, addEventListener, setTimeout — which decides when to call it. It may be called at once or much later.

prompt: What makes a function "higher-order"?
optionA: It runs before any other function
optionB: It has more than three parameters
optionC: It is declared at the top of a file
optionD: It takes or returns another function
correctAnswerText: It takes or returns another function
explanation: Higher-order means functions are its inputs or outputs. map, filter and a function that returns a configured function are all higher-order.

prompt: In `function sum(...nums) {}`, what is `nums`?
optionA: Only the first argument passed in
optionB: A real array of the passed arguments
optionC: A copy of the caller's variables
optionD: An array-like arguments object
correctAnswerText: A real array of the passed arguments
explanation: A rest parameter collects the remaining arguments into a genuine Array, so map, reduce and the rest work on it — unlike the older array-like `arguments` object.

prompt: When does a default parameter value such as `b = 10` get used?
optionA: When the argument is undefined or missing
optionB: When the argument is any falsy value
optionC: When the argument is null or missing
optionD: Only when no arguments are passed at all
correctAnswerText: When the argument is undefined or missing
explanation: Defaults apply only for `undefined`, whether passed explicitly or left out. Passing 0, an empty string or null keeps that value.

prompt: Which description fits a pure function?
optionA: Written as an arrow with no braces or return keyword
optionB: Uses only const variables and never let inside it
optionC: Same output for the same input, and no side effects
optionD: Declared once at module level and never reassigned
correctAnswerText: Same output for the same input, and no side effects
explanation: Purity is about behaviour: the result depends only on the arguments, and nothing outside is changed or read. Syntax and declaration style have nothing to do with it.

prompt: What is an IIFE?
optionA: A function hoisted to the top of its scope
optionB: A function the browser calls on each event
optionC: A function imported from another module
optionD: A function expression run where it is defined
correctAnswerText: A function expression run where it is defined
explanation: Immediately Invoked Function Expression: `(function () { ... })()`. Before modules and block scope, it was the standard way to keep variables out of the global scope.

prompt: Which keyword declares a variable that is scoped to the whole function rather than to the block it sits in?
optionA: class
optionB: var
optionC: const
optionD: let
correctAnswerText: var
explanation: `var` is function-scoped and ignores blocks such as if and for. `let`, `const` and `class` are block-scoped, which is why they replaced var in modern code.

prompt: Why does calling a function stored in a `const` throw when the call comes before that const line?
optionA: The engine compiles expressions after declarations have run
optionB: A const can only hold primitives such as strings or numbers
optionC: The const is in its temporal dead zone until the line runs
optionD: Function expressions are hoisted only in strict-mode files
correctAnswerText: The const is in its temporal dead zone until the line runs
explanation: The binding exists from the start of the scope but is uninitialised until its declaration runs, so touching it earlier is a ReferenceError. Only declarations carry their body up.

prompt: Why is an arrow function a poor choice for an object method that reads `this.name`?
optionA: It makes `this` point at the method instead of the object
optionB: Arrow functions cannot be stored as properties of objects
optionC: It takes `this` from the outer scope, not from the object
optionD: Arrow functions run more slowly than methods when called
correctAnswerText: It takes `this` from the outer scope, not from the object
explanation: Written in an object literal, the arrow sees the `this` of the code around the literal — often the module or global — so `this.name` is not the object's name.

prompt: Why does a counter built with a closure keep its count between calls?
optionA: The inner function keeps a live reference to the outer variable
optionB: The outer function keeps running in the background until exit
optionC: JavaScript copies the variable into a global on each new call
optionD: The count is saved onto the function's prototype after a call
correctAnswerText: The inner function keeps a live reference to the outer variable
explanation: The returned function holds the scope that contains the variable, so the variable survives the outer call and every invocation updates the same one.

prompt: Is every callback in JavaScript called asynchronously?
optionA: Yes; callbacks only exist for network and timer APIs
optionB: No; but any callback inside a loop becomes asynchronous
optionC: No; map calls its callback at once, setTimeout calls later
optionD: Yes; every callback waits until the call stack is empty
correctAnswerText: No; map calls its callback at once, setTimeout calls later
explanation: Callback describes how a function is passed, not when it runs. Array methods call theirs synchronously during the call; timers and I/O call theirs later from the event loop.

prompt: For a regular (non-arrow) function, what decides the value of `this`?
optionA: Which variable the function is stored in
optionB: Where the function was written in the file
optionC: How the function is called at that moment
optionD: The first object created after it loads
correctAnswerText: How the function is called at that moment
explanation: `obj.f()` gives obj, a bare `f()` gives undefined in strict code, `new f()` gives a fresh object, and call/apply/bind set it explicitly. The definition site does not matter.

prompt: What does `fn.bind(obj)` return?
optionA: A new function whose `this` is fixed to obj
optionB: A copy of obj with fn added as a method
optionC: The same fn, now changed permanently
optionD: The result of calling fn with obj as `this`
correctAnswerText: A new function whose `this` is fixed to obj
explanation: bind does not call anything; it returns a new bound function. Use call or apply when you want to invoke immediately with a chosen `this`.

prompt: How do `call` and `apply` differ?
optionA: call fixes `this` for good; apply only for one invocation
optionB: call runs the function later; apply runs it straight away
optionC: call works on arrows; apply works on regular functions
optionD: call takes arguments one by one; apply takes an array
correctAnswerText: call takes arguments one by one; apply takes an array
explanation: Both invoke the function once with the `this` you give. The only difference is argument shape: a list for call, an array for apply (A for array).

prompt: Why are pure functions easy to unit test?
optionA: The engine caches their results, so each test runs only once
optionB: They run faster, so the suite finishes before it can time out
optionC: The output depends only on inputs, so no setup or mocks are needed
optionD: They cannot throw, so every failure is an assertion failure
correctAnswerText: The output depends only on inputs, so no setup or mocks are needed
explanation: With no hidden inputs and no side effects, a test is just "given these arguments, expect this value". Nothing has to be faked or reset between tests.

prompt: What does it mean that functions are first-class values in JavaScript?
optionA: They are compiled to machine code ahead of time
optionB: They are the only values allowed to be exported
optionC: They always run before other statements in a file
optionD: They can be stored, passed and returned like any value
correctAnswerText: They can be stored, passed and returned like any value
explanation: A function is an ordinary value: it can sit in a variable, an array or an object, be an argument, or be returned. Callbacks and closures both depend on this.

prompt: Why can an arrow function not use its own `arguments` object?
optionA: Arrows pass arguments by reference so none are recorded
optionB: Arrows receive arguments only through their default values
optionC: The arguments object is removed entirely in strict mode
optionD: Arrows have no arguments object; they see the outer one
correctAnswerText: Arrows have no arguments object; they see the outer one
explanation: Like `this`, `arguments` is not created for arrows; the name resolves to the enclosing function's. Use a rest parameter (`...args`) instead.

optionB: A ReferenceError on line 1
optionC: function, then function
optionD: undefined, then undefined
correctAnswerText: function, then undefined
explanation: The declaration greet is hoisted with its body. Only the `var hello` binding is hoisted, initialised to undefined; the function is assigned when that line runs.
Each makeCounter call creates a new `n`. a has been called three times by the log, b once — they do not share a counter.
With var there is one `i` for the whole loop, and every arrow reads it after the loop has left it at 3. With let each pass would get its own binding and print 0,1,2.

optionD: 11 null 11
explanation: The default replaces only undefined. null is a real value, and 1 + null is 1 because null converts to 0 in arithmetic.

explanation: The rest parameter is always an array, empty when nothing is left over. The first argument goes to `first`, so only the arguments after it are counted.

optionA: Asha undefined
optionB: Asha no this
optionC: A TypeError from hi()
optionD: Asha Asha
correctAnswerText: Asha no this
explanation: Class bodies are strict, so a bare call `hi()` gets `this === undefined`. Pulling a method off its object loses the object; the guard turns that into the string.

prompt: Given `function adder(n) { return x => x + n; }`, which expression produces a function `add5` such that `add5(2) === 7`?
optionA: adder(5)(2)
optionB: adder
optionC: adder.bind(5)
optionD: adder(5)
correctAnswerText: adder(5)
explanation: adder(5) returns the arrow with n fixed at 5. `adder` itself needs n first, adder(5)(2) is already the number 7, and bind(5) sets `this`, not n.
A bound function's `this` cannot be changed again — binding it a second time only creates another wrapper around the first binding, so both see { v: 2 }.

optionB: A TypeError reading name
optionC: a@undefined b@undefined
optionD: a@ b@
correctAnswerText: a@Core b@Core
explanation: list is a regular method called as team.list(), so its `this` is team; the arrow inside map borrows that `this`. This is the case arrows were designed for.

optionB: It prints undefined
optionC: It prints 2
optionD: It prints 1
correctAnswerText: It throws a ReferenceError
explanation: The inner `let x` shadows the outer one for the whole function body, and before its line it is in the temporal dead zone, so the read throws instead of falling back to 1.

prompt: `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100);` logs 3, 3, 3. What is the smallest correct fix?
optionA: Move console.log above the setTimeout call itself
optionB: Wrap console.log in a second nested arrow function
optionC: Declare the loop variable with let instead of var

prompt: An API uses callbacks nested four levels deep. What is the strongest reason to move it to promises with async/await?

prompt: Inside a component that renders a list of 50 rows, an inline arrow is created for each row on every render. Is that worth fixing?

prompt: A recursive function walking a linked list of a million nodes crashes with "Maximum call stack size exceeded". What is the best judgement?

prompt: For 50 items shown in a UI, a reviewer asks to replace a filter/map chain with a hand-written for loop "for speed". Judge it.

prompt: Should a shared utility module export functions that read their data from `this`?

prompt: What does `array.map(fn)` return?

prompt: What does `filter` return when no element passes the test?

prompt: A teammate writes every transformation with `reduce`, including simple maps and filters. Fair review?

prompt: An API returns order dates to a React app. How should they travel?

prompt: A list kept in React state needs to be shown sorted by name. What is the soundest approach?

optionB: Re-fetch from the server each time to avoid sorting
optionC: Sort a copy ([...list] or toSorted) and render that
optionD: Sort the state array in place; React sees the change
correctAnswerText: Sort a copy ([...list] or toSorted) and render that
explanation: In-place sort mutates state behind React's back and may not trigger a render. Sorting a copy (or deriving it with useMemo) keeps state untouched.

prompt: API data has optional nested fields that the app reads in many places. Which strategy holds up best?
optionA: Use JSON.stringify to test whether fields are present
optionB: Assume fields exist and let production reveal gaps
optionC: Wrap every property read in its own try/catch block
optionD: Validate and normalise the shape once at the boundary
correctAnswerText: Validate and normalise the shape once at the boundary
explanation: Checking once where data enters — and filling defaults — lets the rest of the code trust the shape. Scattered checks drift and miss cases.

prompt: Someone proposes `Object.freeze(config)` to stop accidental edits to app config. Judge it.
optionA: Dangerous, since freeze locks every variable in scope
optionB: Ideal, since it deep-freezes every nested level too
optionC: Useful, but shallow: nested objects remain mutable
optionD: Pointless, since frozen objects can still be edited
correctAnswerText: Useful, but shallow: nested objects remain mutable
explanation: freeze blocks changes to the object's own properties only. Nested objects need freezing too, or a deep-freeze helper; in strict mode a blocked write throws, which is helpful.

prompt: Which declaration keyword creates a binding that can never be reassigned?
optionA: static
optionB: var
optionC: const
optionD: let
correctAnswerText: const
explanation: const forbids reassignment of the binding (the object it points to can still change). let and var can be reassigned; static is a class keyword.

prompt: Which kind of string literal supports `${expression}` interpolation?
optionA: Double-quoted string literals
optionB: Single-quoted string literals
optionC: JSON string literals in code
optionD: Backtick template literals
correctAnswerText: Backtick template literals
explanation: Only backtick strings interpolate ${...}, and they may also span several lines. In quotes, ${x} is just those characters.

prompt: What does `const { email } = user;` do?
optionA: Reads user.email into a new constant email
optionB: Deletes the email property from the user
optionC: Copies the whole user into a constant email
optionD: Creates user.email if it does not exist yet
correctAnswerText: Reads user.email into a new constant email
explanation: Object destructuring pulls properties out by name into variables; the source object is not changed. A missing property gives undefined.

prompt: In `Math.max(...nums)`, what does `...` do?
optionA: Sorts nums before passing it to the call
optionB: Collects the arguments into a new array
optionC: Wraps nums inside another nested array
optionD: Expands the array into separate arguments
