correctAnswerText: Expands the array into separate arguments
explanation: In a call or literal, ... is spread: it unpacks the iterable. In a parameter list or destructuring pattern, the same dots are rest, which gathers.

prompt: Which keyword makes a value available to other ES modules?
optionA: export
optionB: import
optionC: module
optionD: require
correctAnswerText: export
explanation: export exposes a binding; import pulls it in. require and module.exports are the older CommonJS system Node also supports.

prompt: If `user.address` is undefined, what does `user.address?.city` evaluate to?
optionA: null
optionB: A TypeError
optionC: An empty string
optionD: undefined
correctAnswerText: undefined
explanation: ?. (ES2020) stops and returns undefined when the value on its left is null or undefined, instead of throwing a TypeError.

prompt: When does `a ?? b` evaluate to `b`?
optionA: Whenever a is any falsy value
optionB: Only when a is an empty string
optionC: Only when a is null or undefined
optionD: Only when both sides are defined
correctAnswerText: Only when a is null or undefined
explanation: ?? (ES2020) falls back only on null and undefined. 0, "" and false are kept — that is exactly its difference from ||.

prompt: Which built-in collection stores each value at most once?
optionA: Array
optionB: WeakRef
optionC: Set
optionD: Map
correctAnswerText: Set
explanation: A Set ignores additions of a value it already holds (using SameValueZero comparison). new Set(arr) is the standard dedupe.

prompt: In an ES6 class, which method runs automatically when you call `new`?
optionA: constructor
optionB: create
optionC: super
optionD: init
correctAnswerText: constructor
explanation: The constructor method initialises the new instance. super is how a subclass calls its parent's constructor or methods.

prompt: What does an `async` function always return?
optionA: The raw value
optionB: A Promise
optionC: A callback
optionD: undefined
correctAnswerText: A Promise
explanation: Whatever it returns is wrapped in a resolved promise, and anything it throws becomes a rejection. Callers must await it or call .then.

prompt: What does the temporal dead zone of a let or const binding refer to?
optionA: The time a promise waits before it is finally resolved
optionB: The gap between an import and its module finishing
optionC: The span before a let/const line where using it throws
optionD: The part of a loop in which var values are frozen
correctAnswerText: The span before a let/const line where using it throws
explanation: let, const and class bindings exist from the start of their block but are uninitialised until their declaration runs; any access before then is a ReferenceError.

prompt: Why does using `let` in a `for` loop fix the classic "every callback sees the last value" bug?
optionA: let values are copied into each closure
optionB: let makes the loop wait for each callback
optionC: let stops the loop running asynchronously
optionD: Each iteration gets its own fresh binding
correctAnswerText: Each iteration gets its own fresh binding
explanation: The spec creates a new `i` per iteration for let in a for header, so each closure captures a different variable. var has one variable for the whole loop.

prompt: How do default exports and named exports differ?
optionA: Default exports can only be functions and never values
optionB: Named exports must always be imported under a new name
optionC: A module has at most one default but can have many named
optionD: Named exports load lazily while defaults load eagerly
correctAnswerText: A module has at most one default but can have many named
explanation: export default marks one main value, imported under any name you choose. Named exports are imported by their exact names inside braces, and there can be many.

prompt: The same `...` syntax is called spread in one place and rest in another. What is the difference?
optionA: Spread copies deeply; rest copies only the top level
optionB: Spread works on objects only; rest works on arrays only
optionC: Spread is from ES5, while rest was added in ES2020
optionD: Spread expands values out; rest gathers them into one
correctAnswerText: Spread expands values out; rest gathers them into one
explanation: f(...args) and [...a, ...b] spread; function f(...args) and const [first, ...others] = arr gather the remainder. Both work for arrays, and objects since ES2018.

prompt: Why does `() => { id: 1 }` return undefined rather than an object?
optionA: The braces are read as a function body, not an object
optionB: Arrow functions cannot return objects of any kind
optionC: id: 1 is a syntax error inside any arrow function
optionD: Objects need the new keyword before they are returned
correctAnswerText: The braces are read as a function body, not an object
explanation: After =>, { opens a block; `id:` becomes a label and 1 an expression statement, with no return. Wrap the literal in parentheses: () => ({ id: 1 }).

prompt: Why is `qty ?? 1` usually better than `qty || 1` for a quantity field?
optionA: ?? also replaces empty strings and false with 1
optionB: || replaces a real 0 with 1, while ?? keeps the 0
optionC: || throws when qty is undefined, but ?? does not
optionD: ?? runs faster because it skips type conversion
correctAnswerText: || replaces a real 0 with 1, while ?? keeps the 0
explanation: || falls back on any falsy value, so a deliberate 0 becomes 1. ?? only falls back on null/undefined, which is what "no value given" means.

prompt: What are ES6 classes, underneath?
optionA: A way to make each object copy its own methods
optionB: Clearer syntax over prototype-based inheritance
optionC: A new object model that fully replaces prototypes
optionD: A TypeScript-only feature, not plain JavaScript
correctAnswerText: Clearer syntax over prototype-based inheritance
explanation: Methods still live on the prototype, and instanceof still walks the prototype chain. Classes add clearer syntax plus rules like strict mode and required new.

prompt: What does a `Map` offer over a plain object used as a dictionary?
optionA: Keys that expire after a configurable time
optionB: Only string keys, sorted in alphabet order
optionC: Only number keys, kept in ascending order
optionD: Keys of any type, kept in insertion order
correctAnswerText: Keys of any type, kept in insertion order
explanation: Map keys can be objects, numbers or strings without conversion, iteration follows insertion order, and size is a property. Object keys are always strings or symbols.

prompt: What does `await` do inside an async function?
optionA: Blocks the whole thread until the data arrives
optionB: Turns the promise into a callback function
optionC: Runs the promise on a separate CPU thread
optionD: Pauses that function until the promise settles
correctAnswerText: Pauses that function until the promise settles
explanation: Only the async function is suspended; the rest of the program and the event loop keep running. When the promise settles, the function resumes with its value.

prompt: What is true of a binding you get from `import { count } from './store.js'`?
optionA: It is a snapshot taken once and never updated
optionB: It is live and read-only in the importing module
optionC: It becomes a global variable shared by all scripts
optionD: It is a copy that the importer may reassign freely
correctAnswerText: It is live and read-only in the importing module
explanation: ES module imports are live views of the exporter's variable: if store.js changes count, importers see it. Assigning to count in the importer is a TypeError.

optionA: undefined 18 undefined
optionB: Kiran undefined undefined
optionC: Kiran 18 undefined
optionD: A ReferenceError for name
correctAnswerText: Kiran 18 undefined
explanation: name is renamed to n, age falls back to its default because the value is undefined, and city is simply missing, so undefined.
The right side builds [2, 1] first, then destructuring assigns it — a swap without a temporary variable.

optionA: dark l
optionB: dark m
optionC: light m
optionD: light l
correctAnswerText: dark l
explanation: Object spread applies left to right, and a later key overwrites an earlier one. That is how "defaults first, overrides after" is written.

optionA: ${n} items = 60
optionB: 3 items = n * 20
optionC: 3 item = 60
optionD: 3 items = 60
correctAnswerText: 3 items = 60
explanation: Every ${} holds a full expression, including a ternary and arithmetic, evaluated when the literal is evaluated.

optionC: 3 3 "none"
explanation: ?? keeps 0 and "" because they are not null/undefined; || throws away the falsy 0 and uses 3.

optionA: undefined undefined undefined
optionB: It throws a TypeError
optionC: undefined null undefined
optionD: null undefined undefined
correctAnswerText: undefined undefined undefined
explanation: ?. returns undefined (never null) when it short-circuits, ?.() skips calling a missing function, and once a chain short-circuits the rest of it (.length) is skipped too.

optionA: 3 js,css,JS
optionB: 2 js,css
optionC: 4 js,css,js,JS
optionD: 3 css,js,JS
correctAnswerText: 3 js,css,JS
explanation: The second "js" is dropped; "JS" differs by case so it stays. A Set keeps first-insertion order.

optionA: 1 str
optionB: 1 num
optionC: 2 str
optionD: 2 num
correctAnswerText: 2 num
explanation: Map does not convert keys, so the number 1 and the string "1" are different keys. A plain object would turn both into "1" and keep one.

optionA: Rex makes a sound (woof)
optionB: undefined makes a sound (woof)
optionC: Rex (woof)
optionD: A TypeError: Dog has no constructor
correctAnswerText: Rex makes a sound (woof)
explanation: A subclass without a constructor gets one that passes its arguments to super, so n is set. super.speak() calls the parent method with the same this.

optionA: C, A, B
optionB: A, B, C
optionC: C, B, A
optionD: A, C, B
correctAnswerText: A, C, B
explanation: An async function runs synchronously until its first await, so A prints first. The await yields, C prints, and B follows once the microtask runs.

optionA: let variables are hoisted as undefined, just like var
optionB: The first line throws as well but its error is hidden
optionC: typeof always throws for variables declared further down
optionD: later exists but is in its TDZ; undeclared never existed
correctAnswerText: later exists but is in its TDZ; undeclared never existed
explanation: typeof is safe for a name that does not exist at all, but a let binding in its temporal dead zone throws even under typeof.

optionA: await only works on the first item of any array it is in
optionB: async arrows run on a different thread from the forEach
optionC: forEach does not wait for the promises its callback returns
optionD: console.log always runs before any await can complete
correctAnswerText: forEach does not wait for the promises its callback returns
explanation: forEach calls each async callback and ignores the promise it returns. Use for...of with await for sequence, or await Promise.all(items.map(save)) for parallel.

optionA: catch cannot handle errors that come from fetch calls
optionB: Async functions turn every error into a warning
optionC: A return inside try always skips the catch block
optionD: Without await, the promise rejects after try has exited
correctAnswerText: Without await, the promise rejects after try has exited
explanation: return fetchData() hands back the pending promise and leaves the try immediately. `return await fetchData()` keeps the rejection inside the try.

prompt: `ids.map(i => { id: i })` produces an array of undefined. What is the fix?
optionA: Add the new keyword before the object's braces
optionB: Use a function expression, since arrows cannot
optionC: Wrap the object in parentheses: i => ({ id: i })
optionD: Add a semicolon after i inside the object literal
correctAnswerText: Wrap the object in parentheses: i => ({ id: i })
explanation: The braces were parsed as a block body with a label, so nothing was returned. Parentheses force them to be read as an object literal expression.

prompt: utils.js has `export function format() {}`. app.js has `import format from './utils.js'` and fails to load. Why?
optionA: Import paths in modules cannot begin with ./ at all
optionB: format is a named export, so import it as { format }
optionC: The file needs a .mjs extension to export functions
optionD: Functions must be exported using export const only
correctAnswerText: format is a named export, so import it as { format }
explanation: A default import asks for the module's default export, which utils.js does not have. Named exports must be imported by name in braces.

optionA: role must be declared as a static class field first
optionB: super must be called inside a separate init method
optionC: A subclass may not use `this` before super() has run
optionD: Subclasses cannot add properties the parent lacks
correctAnswerText: A subclass may not use `this` before super() has run
explanation: In a derived class the parent constructor creates the object, so `this` does not exist until super() returns. Call super(n) first.

optionA: Objects cannot be keys, so one was dropped
optionB: Plain objects keep only the newest key added
optionC: The second object overwrote the first by id
optionD: Both keys become the string "[object Object]"
correctAnswerText: Both keys become the string "[object Object]"
explanation: Object keys are converted to strings, and every plain object stringifies the same way. A Map (or a Set of objects) uses the object itself as the key.

prompt:
Calling `show()` with no argument throws a TypeError. What is the fix?
function show({ name }) { return name; }
optionA: Default the parameter: function show({ name } = {})
optionB: Add return before name so it can be read first
optionC: Declare name with let before destructuring it
optionD: Move the destructuring out of the parameter list
correctAnswerText: Default the parameter: function show({ name } = {})
explanation: Destructuring undefined throws. Giving the whole pattern a default of {} makes a missing argument yield name === undefined instead.

prompt: Three independent requests run in `Promise.all`; one fails and the page shows nothing. Why, and what fits better?
optionA: all rejects on the first failure; allSettled keeps each result
optionB: all ignores failures, so the empty result must be a later bug
optionC: all runs them in sequence; race would run them all in parallel
optionD: all retries failures forever; any stops after the first failure
correctAnswerText: all rejects on the first failure; allSettled keeps each result
explanation: Promise.all is all-or-nothing. Promise.allSettled (ES2020) reports each outcome, so the two good sections can render and the failed one can show its error.

prompt: Why does `for (const x of arr)` work while `for (const i = 0; i < 3; i++)` throws?
optionA: for...of copies arr first, so x is never really assigned
optionB: const is only allowed in the header of for...of loops
optionC: The classic loop needs var in order to read the length
optionD: for...of makes a new binding per pass; i++ reassigns one
correctAnswerText: for...of makes a new binding per pass; i++ reassigns one
explanation: Each for...of iteration declares a fresh const x. The counting loop must change i after the first pass, which is an assignment to a constant.

prompt: A team adds a lint rule banning `var`. Judge it.
optionA: Unsound: let breaks closures, so var is safer there
optionB: Sound: engines removed var support after ES2015
optionC: Sound: block scope and the TDZ catch reuse bugs early
optionD: Unsound: var runs faster, so hot loops should keep it
correctAnswerText: Sound: block scope and the TDZ catch reuse bugs early
explanation: let/const scope to the block and fail loudly on early use, which removes whole classes of bugs. var is still supported; it is just never the better choice in new code.

prompt: A style guide says "use const by default; use let only when you reassign". Judge it.
optionA: Good: const values are stored faster in the engine's memory
optionB: Bad: const makes every object immutable, so updates will fail
optionC: Bad: const cannot be used inside loops or nested functions
optionD: Good: reassignment then stands out, though objects stay mutable
correctAnswerText: Good: reassignment then stands out, though objects stay mutable
explanation: The value is in signalling: a let tells the reader to watch for reassignment. Readers must still remember that const objects and arrays can be mutated.

prompt: A codebase is choosing between default exports and named exports as its convention. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Prefer default; only defaults allow many exports per file
optionB: Prefer named; default exports are not part of ES2015
optionC: Prefer named; names then stay consistent across imports
optionD: Prefer default; named exports can never be tree-shaken
correctAnswerText: Prefer named; names then stay consistent across imports
explanation: Named exports are imported by their real name, so search, rename and auto-import tools stay accurate. Defaults let every importer pick a different name. Both are standard.

prompt: Code reads `order?.items?.[0]?.price?.amount` everywhere, even where an order must always have items. Judge it.
optionA: Overuse hides bugs; a missing required field should fail loudly
optionB: Overuse slows the page, as each ?. triggers a network call
optionC: Ideal; optional chaining has no cost and prevents every bug
optionD: Ideal; the chain also validates the type of every field
correctAnswerText: Overuse hides bugs; a missing required field should fail loudly
explanation: ?. is for data that is genuinely optional. On required data it turns a clear crash into a silent undefined that surfaces much later, far from the cause.

prompt: For a small app's shopping-cart model, judge a class versus a factory function returning an object.
optionA: Either fits; classes suit many instances, factories suit closures
optionB: Only classes; factories cannot return objects with methods
optionC: Only factories; classes cannot hold any private state at all
optionD: Only classes; factory functions were deprecated in modern JS
correctAnswerText: Either fits; classes suit many instances, factories suit closures
explanation: Both are legitimate. Classes share methods on a prototype and read familiarly; factories give privacy through closures and avoid `this`. Team convention decides.

prompt: When is async/await the better choice over chained `.then()` calls?
optionA: Never, since await blocks the browser's main thread
optionB: Only with callbacks, since promises cannot report errors
optionC: Only inside loops, since it always runs items in parallel
optionD: For sequential steps; with Promise.all for parallel ones
correctAnswerText: For sequential steps; with Promise.all for parallel ones
explanation: await reads like ordinary sequential code and pairs with try/catch. For independent work, start everything and await Promise.all; then is equivalent underneath.

prompt: A page awaits three independent API calls one after another, and takes about three times longer than any single call. Best change?
optionA: Keep them in sequence; the engine overlaps them anyway
optionB: Start all three, then await Promise.all to overlap them
optionC: Use three setTimeout calls so each one gets a thread
optionD: Wrap each in its own async function to make it faster
correctAnswerText: Start all three, then await Promise.all to overlap them
explanation: Each await waits for its call before the next one starts. Starting them together and awaiting Promise.all makes the total roughly the slowest single call.

prompt: A list of 5,000 rows checks "is this id selected?" for every row on every render. Which structure holds the selected ids best?
optionA: A comma-joined string searched with indexOf
optionB: A Set of ids, giving quick has() checks per row
optionC: An array with includes, which uses an index
optionD: A Map of each id to itself, which is required
correctAnswerText: A Set of ids, giving quick has() checks per row
explanation: Set.has is effectively constant time; includes rescans the array for each of the 5,000 rows. A Map would also work, but it is not required.

prompt: A reducer over 50,000 items grows its result with `acc = [...acc, x]`. Judge it.
optionA: Fine; engines turn spread into push internally
optionB: Risky only because spread drops undefined items
optionC: Ideal; spread is the fastest way to grow arrays
optionD: Quadratic copying; push into one array instead
correctAnswerText: Quadratic copying; push into one array instead
explanation: Each spread copies the whole accumulator, so total work grows with the square of n. Immutability matters for shared state, not for a local accumulator.

prompt: An old site loads ten script tags that share globals. Judge moving it to ES modules.
optionA: Not worth it: modules force every function into a class
optionB: Not worth it: globals load faster with no import step
optionC: Worth it: each file gets its own scope and explicit imports
optionD: Worth it: modules make the whole page run on many threads
correctAnswerText: Worth it: each file gets its own scope and explicit imports
explanation: Modules end accidental global collisions and make dependencies visible in the import lines, which also enables bundling and tree-shaking.

prompt: How many columns does the default Bootstrap 5 grid divide a row into?
explanation: Twelve divides evenly into halves, thirds, quarters and sixths, which is why col-6, col-4 and col-3 all work. The count is a Sass variable ($grid-columns).

prompt: Which Bootstrap class gives a container that is full width at every screen size?
optionA: .row
optionB: .container
optionC: .container-fluid
optionD: .col
correctAnswerText: .container-fluid
explanation: .container-fluid is always 100% wide. .container snaps to a fixed max-width at each breakpoint; .row and .col are grid parts, not containers.

prompt: At what minimum width does Bootstrap 5's md breakpoint begin?
optionB: 768px
optionC: 576px
optionD: 992px
correctAnswerText: 768px
explanation: sm 576px, md 768px, lg 992px, xl 1200px, xxl 1400px. The md tier is the usual "tablet and up" switch.

prompt: What does the class `col-md-6` do?
optionA: Six columns wide on small screens only
optionB: Six pixels of gutter from the md tier up
optionC: Half width only at md; full width above it
optionD: Half width from md up; full width below md
correctAnswerText: Half width from md up; full width below md
explanation: Breakpoint classes apply from that width upward. Below md the column falls back to the default, which for a plain .row child is full width.

prompt: Which classes produce Bootstrap's standard primary button?
optionA: btn primary
optionB: button primary
optionC: btn-blue
optionD: btn btn-primary
correctAnswerText: btn btn-primary
explanation: Every button needs the base .btn plus a variant such as .btn-primary or .btn-outline-secondary. The variant alone lacks the base padding and border rules.

prompt: Which attribute lets a button open a Bootstrap 5 modal without writing any JavaScript?
optionA: modal-toggle="true"
optionB: data-bs-modal="show"
optionC: data-bs-toggle="modal"
optionD: data-open="modal"
correctAnswerText: data-bs-toggle="modal"
explanation: data-bs-toggle="modal" with data-bs-target="#id" is picked up by Bootstrap's bundled JS. v4 used data-toggle without the bs prefix.

prompt: What does the utility class `mt-3` do?
optionA: Sets the element's top to three pixels
optionB: Adds top margin from the spacing scale
optionC: Moves the element down three grid rows
optionD: Adds three columns' worth of padding
correctAnswerText: Adds top margin from the spacing scale
explanation: m = margin, t = top, 3 = step three of the spacer scale (1rem by default). p is padding; x and y cover both sides of an axis.

prompt: Which Bootstrap class hides an element at every screen size?
optionA: d-none
optionB: display-0
optionC: hidden-all
optionD: hide-all
correctAnswerText: d-none
explanation: d-none sets display: none. Combined with d-{breakpoint}-block it shows the element again from that breakpoint up.

prompt: Which class gives text inputs Bootstrap's standard form styling?
optionA: form-control
optionB: input-field
optionC: form-input
optionD: control-text
correctAnswerText: form-control
explanation: .form-control styles inputs and textareas; .form-select styles selects, and .form-check wraps checkboxes and radios.

prompt: Where is Bootstrap's brand colour defined so a project can change it at the source?
optionA: In the $primary Sass variable
optionB: In the class list of each button
optionC: In bootstrap.min.css only, line 1
optionD: In a primary attribute on <html>
correctAnswerText: In the $primary Sass variable
explanation: $primary feeds buttons, links, alerts, utilities and more. Changing it once in Sass rebuilds all of them consistently.

prompt: Why does an element with `col-6 col-lg-3` show two per row on a phone and four per row on a laptop?
optionA: Classes apply from their breakpoint up, so lg overrides
optionB: lg classes apply below lg and col-6 applies above it
optionC: The class written last always wins, at every screen size
optionD: Bootstrap always picks the narrower of the two widths
correctAnswerText: Classes apply from their breakpoint up, so lg overrides
explanation: col-6 holds at all sizes; from 992px the col-lg-3 media query also matches and overrides it. That is mobile-first in practice.

prompt: Why should columns be direct children of a `.row`?
optionA: Columns outside a row are removed from the page
optionB: Rows load the JavaScript that columns depend on
optionC: Columns read their widths from the row's id value
optionD: The row is the flex container that sets up gutters
correctAnswerText: The row is the flex container that sets up gutters
explanation: .row is display:flex with wrap and negative margins that balance the columns' gutter padding. Without it the columns have no flex parent to size against.

prompt: In Bootstrap 5, a dropdown fails when only bootstrap.min.js is loaded. Why does the bundle file fix it?
optionA: The bundle loads the CSS that dropdowns require
optionB: Dropdowns need Popper, and the bundle includes it
optionC: Dropdowns need jQuery, and the bundle includes it
optionD: Dropdowns only work inside a .navbar element
correctAnswerText: Dropdowns need Popper, and the bundle includes it
explanation: Dropdowns, tooltips and popovers position themselves with Popper. bootstrap.bundle.min.js ships Popper; bootstrap.min.js expects you to load it yourself. v5 needs no jQuery.

prompt: What does adding `.was-validated` to a form do?
optionA: Blocks submission until every field holds some value
optionB: Adds the required attribute to every input in the form
optionC: Shows valid/invalid styles from the browser's checks
optionD: Runs the server-side validation for the form on submit
correctAnswerText: Shows valid/invalid styles from the browser's checks
explanation: It switches on styling driven by :valid and :invalid, so constraints like required and type="email" colour the fields. It validates nothing itself.

prompt: What is the main benefit of Bootstrap's utility classes such as `d-flex`, `gap-2` and `text-end`?
optionA: They make the page download its JavaScript faster
optionB: Small single-purpose classes compose without new CSS
optionC: They are the only way to set margins with Bootstrap
optionD: They replace the grid on screens narrower than 576px
correctAnswerText: Small single-purpose classes compose without new CSS
explanation: Utilities let you adjust spacing, alignment and display in markup without writing a one-off CSS rule for each small variation.

prompt: How does a plain `.container` behave as the screen widens?
optionA: Always 1140px wide, scrolling on phones
optionB: Always 100% wide at every size of screen
optionC: Width set by how many columns it contains
optionD: Fixed max-width at each breakpoint, fluid below sm
correctAnswerText: Fixed max-width at each breakpoint, fluid below sm
explanation: Below 576px it fills the width; from each breakpoint up it snaps to that tier's max-width (540, 720, 960, 1140, 1320px) and centres itself.

prompt: Why customise Bootstrap through Sass variables instead of overriding its compiled CSS?
optionA: Sass variables make the CSS file download faster
optionB: CSS overrides are ignored by Bootstrap's JavaScript
optionC: Compiled CSS cannot be overridden by any selector
optionD: One variable feeds every rule that uses it, in one place
correctAnswerText: One variable feeds every rule that uses it, in one place
explanation: Changing $primary or $border-radius once regenerates every component consistently. Overrides must chase each selector and break when Bootstrap updates.

prompt: What does `.navbar-expand-lg` mean for a navbar?
optionA: Expanded below lg and collapsed behind a toggler above
optionB: Collapsed behind a toggler below lg, expanded from lg
optionC: Grows taller on large screens to fit all the links
optionD: Always collapsed except on very large monitors only
correctAnswerText: Collapsed behind a toggler below lg, expanded from lg
explanation: Below 992px the links hide in the collapse and the toggler button shows; from lg up they display inline and the toggler hides.

prompt: Why do Bootstrap 5's data attributes start with `data-bs-`?
optionA: To namespace them so they do not clash with other code
optionB: To mark attributes that are bound on the server side
optionC: To tell the browser that it should compile the Sass
optionD: To flag attributes that only work in Safari browsers
correctAnswerText: To namespace them so they do not clash with other code
explanation: v5 prefixed its attributes to avoid collisions with other libraries' data-toggle. It also means v4 markup silently stops working after an upgrade.

prompt: In which situation is Bootstrap the weakest fit?
optionA: A team with little CSS experience and plain needs
optionB: An internal admin dashboard on a short deadline
optionC: A prototype that needs forms and modals quickly
optionD: A distinctive custom design that fights its defaults
correctAnswerText: A distinctive custom design that fights its defaults
explanation: Bootstrap pays off when its look and components are acceptable. A heavily bespoke design spends its effort undoing the framework instead.

prompt: Product cards should show one per row on phones, two per row from md, and three per row from lg. Which classes go on each card's column?
optionA: col-4 col-md-6 col-lg-12
optionB: col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-4
optionC: col-lg-4 col-md-6 col-sm-0
optionD: col-12 col-md-4 col-lg-6
correctAnswerText: col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-4
explanation: Widths are out of 12: 12 is one per row, 6 two, 4 three. List them mobile-first; each breakpoint class takes over from its width upward.

prompt: A login form should be half width and centred from md up. Which classes go on its column?
optionA: col-md-3 offset-md-6
optionB: col-md-6 offset-md-3
optionC: col-md-6 margin-md-3
optionD: col-md-6 center-md-3
correctAnswerText: col-md-6 offset-md-3
explanation: 6 columns wide plus a 3-column offset leaves 3 on each side: 3 + 6 + 3 = 12. (mx-auto on the column also centres it.)

prompt: A sidebar should be hidden on phones and shown as a block from md up. Which classes do it?
optionA: d-block d-md-hidden
optionB: d-none d-md-block
optionC: hidden-sm visible-md
optionD: d-md-none d-block
correctAnswerText: d-none d-md-block
explanation: d-none hides it everywhere, then d-md-block switches display back on from 768px. hidden-*/visible-* are Bootstrap 3 names.

prompt: The server reports that the email is already registered. How do you show that on the email field in Bootstrap 5?
optionA: Add was-validated to the input, with a help-text span
optionB: Add is-invalid to the input, with an invalid-feedback div
optionC: Add invalid to the input, with a feedback-text paragraph
optionD: Add an error class to the form and red to the label
correctAnswerText: Add is-invalid to the input, with an invalid-feedback div
explanation: .is-invalid marks one field invalid regardless of browser checks, and a sibling .invalid-feedback shows the message. was-validated belongs on the form.

prompt: Two buttons in a card footer should sit at the right-hand end of the row. Which classes go on the footer?
optionA: float-end-flex row-end
optionB: d-flex justify-content-end
optionC: d-grid justify-items-right
optionD: d-flex align-items-end
correctAnswerText: d-flex justify-content-end
explanation: justify-content works along the main (horizontal) axis of a row, so -end pushes items right. align-items-end moves them to the bottom instead.

prompt: The space between grid columns should be larger than the default. What is the Bootstrap 5 way?
optionA: Add p-4 to the container
optionB: Add g-4 to the row
optionC: Add m-4 to every col
optionD: Add gx-col to each col
correctAnswerText: Add g-4 to the row
explanation: Gutter classes (g-*, gx-*, gy-*) go on the .row and adjust the padding/negative-margin pair together, so alignment stays intact.

prompt: A modal must open after an AJAX call succeeds. Which call does it in Bootstrap 5?
optionA: $(el).modal('show') with no jQuery loaded
optionB: document.showModal(el) from the browser API
optionC: bootstrap.Modal.getOrCreateInstance(el).show()
optionD: el.classList.add('modal-open') on the dialog
correctAnswerText: bootstrap.Modal.getOrCreateInstance(el).show()
explanation: v5 exposes components as classes on the bootstrap global; getOrCreateInstance avoids creating duplicates. The jQuery plugin form is v4.

prompt: A wide data table must not break the layout on phones. What is the Bootstrap way?
optionA: Set the table's font size to fit using fs-6
optionB: Wrap the table in a div with table-responsive
optionC: Add table-mobile to the table element itself
optionD: Add d-block to each td so cells stack vertically
correctAnswerText: Wrap the table in a div with table-responsive
explanation: .table-responsive gives the wrapper overflow-x: auto, so the table scrolls sideways inside it instead of pushing the page wider.

prompt: In custom.scss you write `$primary: #051d64;`. Where must that line go to take effect?
optionA: In a separate CSS file that is linked after bootstrap.min.css
optionB: After Bootstrap is imported, so it overrides the compiled rules
optionC: Before Bootstrap's variables are imported, as they use !default
optionD: Inside a :root block, since Sass reads the CSS variables
correctAnswerText: Before Bootstrap's variables are imported, as they use !default
explanation: Bootstrap declares $primary with !default, which only assigns if the variable is not already set. Your value must exist before that file is read.

prompt: Buttons should stack full width on phones and sit inline from md up. Which classes go on their wrapper?
optionA: d-grid gap-2 d-md-flex
optionB: d-flex gap-2 d-md-grid
optionC: w-100 d-md-inline-full
optionD: btn-block btn-md-inline
correctAnswerText: d-grid gap-2 d-md-flex
explanation: d-grid makes each button a full-width row; d-md-flex switches to an inline row from md. btn-block was removed in v5 in favour of this pattern.

prompt: In a row, `col-md-8` and `col-md-6` are meant to sit side by side, but the second always drops to a new line. Why?
optionA: col-md-6 needs an offset before it can sit beside
optionB: They total 14, more than 12, so the second wraps
optionC: Two columns always need a nested row between them
optionD: md columns stack whenever their content is long
correctAnswerText: They total 14, more than 12, so the second wraps
explanation: A row holds 12 units; once the sum exceeds that, flex-wrap moves the overflow to a new line. Use 8 + 4 or 6 + 6.

prompt: A `.row` placed directly in `<body>`, with no container, causes a horizontal scrollbar. Why?
optionA: Rows are 110% wide unless the body is also a grid
optionB: Columns default to fixed pixel widths in a body
optionC: The row's negative margins need a container to offset
optionD: The body must have row-fluid for the row to fit
correctAnswerText: The row's negative margins need a container to offset
explanation: Rows pull outward with negative horizontal margins to cancel the columns' padding. A container's padding absorbs that; without it the row overflows the viewport.

prompt: A collapse button copied from an old tutorial uses `data-toggle="collapse" data-target="#more"` and does nothing on a Bootstrap 5 page. Why?
optionA: Collapse only works on elements that also have a card class
optionB: v5 reads data-bs-toggle and data-bs-target, not data-toggle
optionC: Collapse needs jQuery, which must be loaded before Bootstrap
optionD: The target id must include the # sign in its id attribute
correctAnswerText: v5 reads data-bs-toggle and data-bs-target, not data-toggle
explanation: v5 renamed every data API attribute with the bs- prefix. The v4 attributes are simply ignored, so nothing errors — the button is just dead.

prompt:
This form shows red borders on every required field before the user has typed anything. Why?
<form class="needs-validation was-validated" novalidate>
optionA: needs-validation must be removed for the styles to apply
optionB: novalidate tells Bootstrap to style every field as invalid
optionC: Red borders appear because the CSS was loaded twice over
optionD: was-validated is set from the start; add it on submit instead
correctAnswerText: was-validated is set from the start; add it on submit instead
explanation: was-validated turns on :invalid styling immediately, and empty required fields are invalid. The documented pattern adds it in the submit handler.

prompt: A custom rule `.btn-primary { background: green; }` in styles.css has no effect. styles.css is linked before bootstrap.min.css. Why?
optionA: Bootstrap loads later and wins at equal specificity
optionB: Custom colours must be given in hex, not by name
optionC: Button classes ignore any background property
optionD: The rule needs a matching data-bs attribute set
correctAnswerText: Bootstrap loads later and wins at equal specificity
explanation: With equal specificity, the rule that appears later in the cascade wins. Link your stylesheet after Bootstrap, or better, change the variable.

prompt: A modal opens dimmed underneath its own grey backdrop and cannot be clicked. Its markup sits inside a positioned header with a z-index. Fix?
optionA: Remove the fade class so the modal opens instantly
optionB: Move the modal markup to the end of body, outside it
optionC: Raise the backdrop z-index above the modal's own
optionD: Give the modal col-12 so it fills the whole screen
correctAnswerText: Move the modal markup to the end of body, outside it
explanation: The header's z-index creates a stacking context that traps the modal below the body-level backdrop. Modals belong as near-top-level children of body.

prompt: A large photo inside a column overflows it on phones. Which Bootstrap class fixes it?
optionA: img-fluid, so it scales down to the column
optionB: col-auto, so the image shrinks itself to fit
optionC: d-flex, so the image wraps inside the column
optionD: row, so the image gets gutters around it
correctAnswerText: img-fluid, so it scales down to the column
explanation: .img-fluid sets max-width: 100% and height: auto, so the image never exceeds its container and keeps its proportions.

prompt: The navbar looks right on desktop, but on a phone tapping the toggler does nothing. The CSS is loaded. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: Togglers only work in a container-fluid
optionB: The toggler needs type="submit" to fire
optionC: Bootstrap's JavaScript bundle is not loaded
optionD: navbar-expand classes disable the toggler
correctAnswerText: Bootstrap's JavaScript bundle is not loaded
explanation: Collapse is driven by Bootstrap's JS. CSS alone draws the toggler but nothing listens to its clicks.

prompt: Buttons have `data-bs-toggle="tooltip" title="Save"`, and the bundle is loaded, but no tooltips appear. Why?
optionA: Tooltips need their text in a data-bs-text attribute
optionB: Tooltips are opt-in and must be initialised in JS
optionC: Tooltips only appear on button elements, not on links
optionD: Tooltips need Popper loaded after the bundle as well
correctAnswerText: Tooltips are opt-in and must be initialised in JS
explanation: For performance, tooltips and popovers are not auto-initialised; create them with new bootstrap.Tooltip(el) for each element. The bundle already contains Popper.

prompt: custom.scss imports Bootstrap and then sets `$primary: #e91e63;`, but buttons stay blue. Why?
optionA: The variable was set after Bootstrap had compiled its rules
optionB: Sass variables are not able to hold hex colour values
optionC: The import needs a .css extension to read the variables
optionD: In v5, $primary must be spelled $color-primary instead
correctAnswerText: The variable was set after Bootstrap had compiled its rules
explanation: Sass is evaluated top to bottom; the button rules were already generated with the default value. Set overrides before Bootstrap's variables are read.

prompt: A college placement cell needs an internal admin tool in three weeks. Judge Bootstrap versus hand-written CSS.
optionA: Bootstrap: standard components ship fast and look consistent
optionB: Bootstrap: it removes any need to test the tool on phones
optionC: Hand-written CSS: admin tools need a unique brand identity
optionD: Hand-written CSS: Bootstrap cannot render data tables well
correctAnswerText: Bootstrap: standard components ship fast and look consistent
explanation: Internal tools value speed and consistency over distinctiveness, which is exactly what Bootstrap's prebuilt grid, forms and tables provide.

prompt: Lighthouse flags unused CSS and JS from Bootstrap. What is the best response?
optionA: Inline all of bootstrap.css into every page of the site
optionB: Drop Bootstrap and rewrite every component by hand
optionC: Import only the Sass and JS parts that you actually use
optionD: Load the CDN copy twice so the browser caches it faster
correctAnswerText: Import only the Sass and JS parts that you actually use
explanation: Bootstrap's Sass and JS are modular; importing just the needed partials and plugins removes most of the dead weight without a rewrite.

prompt: The same element carries 15 utility classes, copied to 20 places in the app. Judge it.
optionA: Replace them with inline styles, which are more explicit
optionB: Leave it; repeated markup has no maintenance cost at all
optionC: Extract a component or a small CSS class for the pattern
optionD: Add !important to each utility so they stay consistent
correctAnswerText: Extract a component or a small CSS class for the pattern
explanation: Utilities are great for one-offs; a repeated bundle is a design pattern and deserves a name, so a change happens once instead of twenty times.

prompt: The team keeps overriding Bootstrap styles with growing `!important` chains. What is the better approach?
optionA: Copy all of Bootstrap's source into your styles and edit that
optionB: Change Sass or CSS variables instead of piling on !important
optionC: Use !important everywhere so your rules always come out on top
optionD: Edit Bootstrap's dist CSS directly so the change is permanent
correctAnswerText: Change Sass or CSS variables instead of piling on !important
explanation: Variables change the source of the value; !important escalates a specificity war. Editing dist files is lost on the next update.

prompt: Judge the best way to use Bootstrap components such as modals and dropdowns inside a React app.
optionA: Use React-aware components that let React own the DOM
optionB: Avoid Bootstrap's CSS entirely in any React project
optionC: Load Bootstrap's JS and let it change React's DOM freely
optionD: Wrap each React component in a Bootstrap .row div
correctAnswerText: Use React-aware components that let React own the DOM
explanation: Bootstrap's JS toggles classes on DOM nodes React also controls, which can fight re-renders. A React wrapper library (or state-driven classes) keeps one owner. The CSS works fine as is.

prompt: A dashboard needs widgets spanning different numbers of rows and columns. Judge Bootstrap's grid versus CSS Grid.
optionA: Bootstrap's grid only, since CSS Grid lacks browser support
optionB: Absolute positioning, since it gives exact pixel control
optionC: CSS Grid for a true 2D layout; Bootstrap's grid for column rows
optionD: HTML tables for layout, since they align rows and columns
correctAnswerText: CSS Grid for a true 2D layout; Bootstrap's grid for column rows
explanation: Bootstrap's grid is flexbox rows of columns; spanning rows is awkward. CSS Grid places items in two dimensions directly, and they mix happily on one page.

prompt: A site runs Bootstrap 4. Judge upgrading to Bootstrap 5.
optionA: Worth it: no jQuery, but data attributes and classes change
optionB: Pointless: v5 only changes the default colour palette
optionC: Risky: v5 requires a server-side rendering framework
optionD: Free: v5 is a drop-in swap with exactly the same classes
correctAnswerText: Worth it: no jQuery, but data attributes and classes change
explanation: v5 removes the jQuery dependency and modernises utilities, but renames data-* to data-bs-*, drops some classes (btn-block, form-group) and changes others. Plan a migration pass.

prompt: Designers want every Bootstrap component restyled to a new design language. Judge continuing with Bootstrap.
optionA: Continue: Bootstrap forbids restyling, so it stays stable
optionB: Reconsider: overriding everything costs more than it saves
optionC: Reconsider: Bootstrap is unable to change any colours
optionD: Continue: CSS overrides are free and never conflict
correctAnswerText: Reconsider: overriding everything costs more than it saves
explanation: The value of a framework is the styling you accept as is. If nothing is accepted, you carry its weight and fight its specificity for no gain.

prompt: A manager says "we use Bootstrap, so the site is accessible". Judge it.
optionA: Partly: labels, alt text and roles are still your job
optionB: Not at all: Bootstrap strips out ARIA attributes
optionC: Only when the page uses the dark colour mode
optionD: Fully: using Bootstrap guarantees WCAG compliance
correctAnswerText: Partly: labels, alt text and roles are still your job
explanation: Bootstrap's components ship with sensible ARIA and keyboard support, but content choices — labels, alt text, colour contrast of custom colours — remain the author's.

prompt: For a production project with custom theme colours, judge loading Bootstrap from a CDN versus installing it with npm.
optionA: npm always, since browsers block CDN-hosted files
optionB: npm with a bundler, for pinned versions and custom Sass
optionC: CDN always, since bundlers cannot process Sass files
optionD: CDN always, since npm packages are unable to hold CSS
correctAnswerText: npm with a bundler, for pinned versions and custom Sass
explanation: A CDN link is fine for a quick page, but it serves the precompiled default theme. Custom Sass variables need the source, which npm and a bundler provide.

prompt: Which tag stops a phone from laying the page out at desktop width and zooming out?
optionA: <meta name="screen" content="width=device-width">
optionB: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width">
optionC: <link rel="viewport" href="width=device-width">
optionD: <meta name="viewport" content="width=1024px">
correctAnswerText: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width">
explanation: name="viewport" with width=device-width (usually plus initial-scale=1) tells the mobile browser to use the device width as the layout width.

prompt: Which media query targets screens 768px wide and wider?
optionA: @media (max-width: 768px)
optionB: @media (width: 768px)
optionC: @media screen-width > 768
optionD: @media (min-width: 768px)
correctAnswerText: @media (min-width: 768px)
explanation: min-width means "at least this wide", which is the building block of mobile-first CSS. max-width targets this width and narrower.

prompt: What is 1rem equal to?
optionA: Exactly sixteen device pixels always
optionB: The font size of the root <html> element
optionC: One percent of the viewport width
optionD: The font size of the parent element
correctAnswerText: The font size of the root <html> element
explanation: rem is relative to the root font size — 16px by default, but it follows the user's browser setting. em is relative to the parent instead.

prompt: What does `50vw` measure?
optionA: Half of the screen height
optionB: Half of the parent's width
optionC: Half of the viewport's width
optionD: Fifty CSS pixels of width
correctAnswerText: Half of the viewport's width
explanation: One vw is 1% of the viewport width, whatever the parent is. % units are relative to the parent; vh is the viewport height.

prompt: Which property lets flex items move onto a new line when they run out of room?
optionA: flex-flow: nowrap
optionB: align-items: wrap
optionC: flex-wrap: wrap
optionD: flex-direction: row
correctAnswerText: flex-wrap: wrap
explanation: Flex containers default to nowrap, squeezing items onto one line. flex-wrap: wrap lets them flow to the next line instead.

prompt: What does `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr)` create?
optionA: Three rows of equal height
optionB: Three equal-width columns
optionC: Three columns of one pixel
optionD: One column repeated down
correctAnswerText: Three equal-width columns
explanation: fr is a fraction of the free space, and three 1fr tracks share it equally. Rows are set with grid-template-rows.

prompt: Which img attribute offers the browser several files so it can choose one that suits the screen?
optionA: srcset
optionB: alt
optionC: usemap
optionD: loading
correctAnswerText: srcset
explanation: srcset lists candidate files with their widths or densities, and the browser picks one. alt is the text alternative, loading controls lazy loading.

prompt: Which element lets you serve a different crop of an image at different breakpoints?
optionA: <picture>
optionB: <figure>
optionC: <canvas>
optionD: <object>
correctAnswerText: <picture>
explanation: holds entries and a fallback , so the author decides which file matches which query — "art direction".

prompt: Which CSS rule stops images from overflowing a narrow container?
optionA: overflow: auto
optionB: min-width: 100%
optionC: width: 100vw
optionD: max-width: 100%
correctAnswerText: max-width: 100%
explanation: max-width: 100% lets the image shrink to its container but never stretch beyond its natural size; height: auto keeps the ratio.

prompt: Where can you quickly preview a page at common phone widths without a phone?
optionA: The Lighthouse SEO audit category
optionB: The W3C online CSS validator
optionC: The browser DevTools device mode
optionD: The Network panel throttling list
correctAnswerText: The browser DevTools device mode
explanation: Device mode resizes the viewport, emulates touch and device pixel ratio, and switches the user agent — a fast first check before testing on real devices.

prompt: Why do many teams write mobile-first CSS with min-width queries?
optionA: Base styles serve small screens, and larger ones add on
optionB: Desktop browsers cannot read max-width media queries
optionC: Phones ignore every max-width query in CSS files
optionD: min-width queries load faster than max-width ones
correctAnswerText: Base styles serve small screens, and larger ones add on
explanation: The simplest layout (one column) becomes the default, and each min-width query only adds what wider screens need. Overrides stay small and phones parse less layout.

prompt: Why is rem usually a better unit than px for font sizes?
optionA: It stops text from ever wrapping on phones
optionB: It forces the same size on all screen widths
optionC: It renders faster than pixels on every device
optionD: It respects the user's browser font-size setting
correctAnswerText: It respects the user's browser font-size setting
explanation: A user who sets a larger default font gets larger rem text everywhere. px font sizes ignore that preference, which hurts low-vision readers.

prompt: Why can text sized in `em` grow unexpectedly in nested lists?
optionA: em doubles each time a media query starts to match
optionB: em is relative to the parent, so nesting compounds it
optionC: em ignores the parent and uses the <html> font size
optionD: em is relative to the viewport, so it scales with it
correctAnswerText: em is relative to the parent, so nesting compounds it
explanation: A 1.2em list inside a 1.2em list is 1.44 times the base, and so on. rem avoids compounding by always referring to the root.

prompt: What is the core difference between Flexbox and Grid?
optionA: Flexbox lays out one axis; Grid lays out rows and columns
optionB: Flexbox is for images; Grid is for blocks of text content
optionC: Flexbox is newer and has replaced Grid in modern browsers
optionD: Grid is one-dimensional, while Flexbox is two-dimensional
correctAnswerText: Flexbox lays out one axis; Grid lays out rows and columns
explanation: Flexbox distributes items along a single line (wrapping lines are independent). Grid defines both tracks at once, so items align across rows and columns.

prompt: Without a viewport meta tag, why does a responsive page still look tiny on a phone?
optionA: The phone lays it out at about 980px and zooms out
optionB: Mobile browsers block CSS files without the tag
optionC: Media queries are switched off on every phone browser
optionD: Images are not downloaded on mobile data networks
correctAnswerText: The phone lays it out at about 980px and zooms out
explanation: Mobile browsers assume a desktop-width layout for pages that do not opt in, so min-width queries see roughly 980px and the result is scaled down.

prompt: How should breakpoints be chosen?
optionA: Add one every 100 pixels to be completely safe
optionB: Use one phone breakpoint, then stop adding more
optionC: Use exactly the widths of the latest phone models
optionD: Add one where the content starts to look broken
correctAnswerText: Add one where the content starts to look broken
explanation: Resize the page until the layout strains — lines too long, items cramped — and put a breakpoint there. That survives whatever devices come next.

prompt: What does the `sizes` attribute tell the browser when used with a width-based srcset?
optionA: The size in kilobytes of each file it could download
optionB: Which image to show when the network is slow or flaky
optionC: How wide the image will be shown, so it can pick a file
optionD: The pixel dimensions to which the image will be cropped
correctAnswerText: How wide the image will be shown, so it can pick a file
explanation: The browser chooses a file before layout, so sizes describes the display width (e.g. "(min-width: 768px) 50vw, 100vw"); combined with pixel density it selects the best candidate.

prompt: What does the `fr` unit represent in CSS Grid?
optionA: A share of the free space left in the grid
optionB: A fixed fraction of the viewport's width
optionC: A share of the parent element's height
optionD: A unit equal to the root element's font size
correctAnswerText: A share of the free space left in the grid
explanation: After fixed tracks are placed, the remaining space is divided among fr tracks in proportion, so 2fr gets twice what 1fr gets.

prompt: What does `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))` do?
optionA: Creates columns that never shrink to less than 1fr
optionB: Always creates exactly two columns, each 200px wide
optionC: Fits as many columns of 200px or more as the width allows
optionD: Repeats a single 200px column down the whole page
correctAnswerText: Fits as many columns of 200px or more as the width allows
explanation: The browser counts how many 200px tracks fit, makes that many, and lets them stretch to share the extra space — a responsive card grid with no media query.

prompt: Why must tap targets be larger on touch screens than click targets on desktop?
optionA: Mobile browsers block any link that is smaller than 48px
optionB: Small buttons get hidden by the on-screen keyboard always
optionC: A fingertip is imprecise, so small targets get mis-tapped
optionD: Touch screens are unable to render text smaller than 16px
correctAnswerText: A fingertip is imprecise, so small targets get mis-tapped
explanation: A mouse pointer is a pixel; a finger covers far more. Guidelines suggest roughly 44–48px targets with spacing so neighbours are not hit by accident.

prompt: A sidebar should sit beside the main content from 992px up and stack above it on smaller screens. Written mobile-first, what does the CSS look like?
optionA: Two columns always; hide the sidebar with display: none instead
optionB: Stack by default; set two columns in a max-width: 992px query
optionC: Two columns by default; stack them in a min-width: 992px query
optionD: Stack by default; set two columns in a min-width: 992px query
correctAnswerText: Stack by default; set two columns in a min-width: 992px query
explanation: The default single column serves phones, and the min-width query adds the side-by-side layout once there is room for it.

prompt: Cards should wrap into as many columns of at least 250px as fit, with no media queries. Which rule does it?
optionA: grid-template-columns: minmax(auto-fit, 250px) repeat 1fr
optionB: grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr))
optionC: grid-template-columns: repeat(250px, auto-fit, 1fr) wrap
optionD: grid-template-columns: repeat(4, minmax(250px, 1fr)) wrap
correctAnswerText: grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr))
explanation: auto-fit decides the column count from the width; minmax sets the floor and lets columns stretch. A fixed repeat(4, ...) cannot reduce the count on phones.

prompt: What does `font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3rem)` do for a heading?
optionA: Stays at 4vw unless the user zooms in on the page
optionB: Uses 1.5rem on phones and 3rem on every other device
optionC: Picks one of the three sizes based on the type of device
optionD: Scales with the width, never below 1.5rem or above 3rem
correctAnswerText: Scales with the width, never below 1.5rem or above 3rem
explanation: clamp(min, preferred, max) uses the fluid 4vw value but bounds it, so the heading neither shrinks to nothing nor grows absurd on wide screens.

prompt: A phone with a 400px-wide viewport and a device pixel ratio of 2 loads this. Which file is the browser most likely to pick?
optionA: l.jpg, since browsers always choose the largest file
optionB: s.jpg, since the viewport is narrower than 480 pixels
optionC: All three, then it shows whichever one finishes first
optionD: m.jpg, since 400 CSS px at 2x needs about 800 pixels
correctAnswerText: m.jpg, since 400 CSS px at 2x needs about 800 pixels
explanation: The slot is 400 CSS px, which is 800 device pixels at 2x; the smallest candidate covering that is m.jpg (960w). Browsers may also weigh network conditions.

prompt: A flex navbar's links run off the right edge on phones. Which single declaration on the nav makes them flow onto a second line?
optionA: justify-content: wrap
optionB: flex-shrink: 0
optionC: flex-wrap: wrap
optionD: flex-direction: row
correctAnswerText: flex-wrap: wrap
explanation: Wrapping lets the items that do not fit move to a new line. flex-shrink: 0 would make overflow worse, and justify-content has no wrap value.

prompt: An embedded video iframe must fill its column's width and keep a 16:9 shape at every size. Which CSS does it?
optionA: width: 16px; height: 9px;
optionB: width: auto; max-height: 100%;
optionC: width: 100%; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
optionD: width: 50%; height: 56.25vw;
correctAnswerText: width: 100%; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
explanation: aspect-ratio derives the height from the width, so the box keeps its shape as the column resizes. The old padding-top: 56.25% hack did the same.

prompt: A large decorative banner should not be downloaded at all on phones. Which approach achieves that?
optionA: Set display: none on the img; it then never downloads
optionB: Give the img a width of 0 so phones skip the file
optionC: Put the img inside a noscript tag for phone users
optionD: Use <picture> with a media source, not display: none
correctAnswerText: Use <picture> with a media source, not display: none
explanation: An hidden with CSS is usually still fetched. with a and a tiny or empty fallback lets the browser skip the big file.

prompt: A ten-column results table must stay usable on a 360px phone. Which approach is most sensible?
optionA: Remove the table and show only the first column
optionB: Let it scroll sideways in an overflow-x: auto wrapper
optionC: Shrink the font to 6px so all of the columns fit
optionD: Set the table to width: 100vw and hide the overflow
correctAnswerText: Let it scroll sideways in an overflow-x: auto wrapper
explanation: A scroll wrapper keeps every column readable without breaking the page width. Tiny fonts are unreadable and hiding data loses information.

prompt: What does `width: 100%; max-width: 1200px; margin: 0 auto;` do to a page wrapper?
optionA: Fills small screens, caps at 1200px, centres on large ones
optionB: Always full width, with 1200px of margin on each side
optionC: Always 1200px wide and centred, scrolling on small phones
optionD: Shrinks to 1200px only when the page is zoomed in a lot
correctAnswerText: Fills small screens, caps at 1200px, centres on large ones
explanation: Below 1200px the wrapper is the viewport's width; above it, max-width stops growth and auto margins split the leftover space evenly.

prompt: The layout looks right in DevTools device mode. What should still be checked on real phones?
optionA: Only the widest desktop size, since it breaks most
optionB: Only Safari, since all other browsers share one engine
optionC: Nothing more; device mode reproduces phones exactly
optionD: Touch behaviour, real fonts and slow mobile networks
correctAnswerText: Touch behaviour, real fonts and slow mobile networks
explanation: Emulation does not reproduce real touch, on-screen keyboards, browser toolbars, installed fonts or network and CPU limits. A couple of real devices catch what it misses.

prompt:
This hero causes a horizontal scrollbar on phones. Why?
.hero { width: 100vw; padding: 0 20px; }
optionA: The scrollbar appears because 100vw is slightly short
optionB: The 40px of padding is added on top of the 100vw width
optionC: vw units are ignored on phones, so the hero is 980px
optionD: Padding on the hero pushes the viewport meta tag out
correctAnswerText: The 40px of padding is added on top of the 100vw width
explanation: With the default content-box sizing, padding is added outside the width, so the box is 100vw + 40px. box-sizing: border-box or width: 100% fixes it.

optionA: Colours cannot be changed in a media query
optionB: min-width queries never apply above 768 pixels
optionC: Media queries need the screen keyword to work
optionD: The later base rule wins at the same specificity
correctAnswerText: The later base rule wins at the same specificity
explanation: A media query adds no specificity. Both rules match on wide screens, and the one later in the file wins — put the query after the base rules.

prompt: A page with correct media queries shows its tiny desktop layout on every phone. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: The CSS is cached from desktop
optionB: The queries use rem, not pixels
optionC: The viewport meta tag is missing
optionD: Phone browsers lack Flexbox
correctAnswerText: The viewport meta tag is missing
explanation: Without the viewport tag the phone reports a ~980px layout width, so the phone-sized queries never match and the page is zoomed out.

optionA: Both queries match at exactly 768px
optionB: Neither query matches at exactly 768px
optionC: Pixel queries round 768 to the nearest 100
optionD: Only the first query is valid syntax
correctAnswerText: Both queries match at exactly 768px
explanation: Both bounds are inclusive, so at 768px both blocks apply and fight. Use max-width: 767.98px (as Bootstrap does) or range syntax such as (width < 768px).

prompt: A flex child containing a long URL refuses to shrink and overflows its row. What fixes it?
optionA: The URL needs a max-height set before it will shrink
optionB: Flex items never shrink; switch the parent to Grid
optionC: flex-wrap: nowrap must be set on the child element
optionD: Flex items default to min-width: auto; set min-width: 0
correctAnswerText: Flex items default to min-width: auto; set min-width: 0
explanation: A flex item will not shrink below its content's minimum size unless min-width is overridden. min-width: 0 (plus overflow-wrap: anywhere for the URL) lets it shrink.

prompt: Product photos styled `width: 100%; height: 300px;` look squashed on phones. What fixes it while keeping the fixed height?
optionA: Add srcset so the browser keeps the original ratio
optionB: Remove width: 100%, which always distorts phone images
optionC: Add object-fit: cover so the image crops, not stretches
optionD: Add display: flex to the img to keep its proportions
correctAnswerText: Add object-fit: cover so the image crops, not stretches
explanation: A fixed height with a fluid width changes the box's ratio, and the image stretches to fill it. object-fit: cover keeps the ratio and crops the excess.

prompt: Headings set to `font-size: 5vw` look fine on laptops but enormous on a 2560px monitor. What is the best fix?
optionA: Add a second rem size, as headings ignore vw units
optionB: Switch to vh, since vw measures height on monitors
optionC: Wrap it in clamp() with a sensible maximum size
optionD: Set a larger viewport meta width for big monitors
correctAnswerText: Wrap it in clamp() with a sensible maximum size
explanation: Pure vw scales without limit: 5vw is 128px at 2560px. clamp(1.5rem, 5vw, 3.5rem) keeps the fluid behaviour inside sensible bounds.

prompt: A full-screen panel with `height: 100vh` hides its bottom button behind the phone browser's toolbar. Why?
optionA: The height must be set in rem for the toolbar to resize
optionB: On mobile, 100vh ignores the toolbar; dvh units adjust to it
optionC: vh units are not supported on any mobile browser at all
optionD: The button needs position: absolute before it can show
correctAnswerText: On mobile, 100vh ignores the toolbar; dvh units adjust to it
explanation: Mobile browsers size vh to the largest viewport, with toolbars hidden. The newer dvh (dynamic) and svh (small) units track the visible area (supported since about 2022).

prompt: A navigation dropdown opens on `:hover` and works on desktop, but phone users cannot reach its links. Why?
optionA: Phones need a larger font before :hover will fire
optionB: Touch has no true hover; open the menu on tap as well
optionC: The menu needs a z-index above the viewport meta
optionD: :hover only works on phones with a viewport tag
correctAnswerText: Touch has no true hover; open the menu on tap as well
explanation: Touch devices emulate hover inconsistently. Toggle the menu on click/tap (and keyboard focus), and use @media (hover: hover) for hover-only extras.

prompt: With `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` and only two cards on a 1400px screen, the cards stay narrow and leave empty space. Why?
optionA: auto-fill caps every grid at two columns on desktop
optionB: auto-fill keeps empty tracks; auto-fit collapses them
optionC: Grid items cannot be wider than 200px by default
optionD: minmax ignores 1fr when there are only two items
correctAnswerText: auto-fill keeps empty tracks; auto-fit collapses them
explanation: auto-fill creates as many tracks as fit, even empty ones, so the two cards share the space with five empty tracks. auto-fit collapses empty tracks and lets the cards stretch.

prompt: A large existing desktop-first site needs to work on phones next month. Judge the approach.
optionA: Desktop-first CSS can never be made responsive, so start over
optionB: Retrofit with max-width queries now; write new parts mobile-first
optionC: Serve a separate m. site instead of using any media queries
optionD: Rewrite all of the CSS mobile-first before any phone fix ships
correctAnswerText: Retrofit with max-width queries now; write new parts mobile-first
explanation: max-width queries are a legitimate way to adapt existing CSS quickly. Mobile-first is a better default for new work, not a reason to block a fix on a rewrite.

prompt: Judge one responsive site versus a separate m. mobile site.
optionA: A separate m. site: search engines prefer duplicate URLs
optionB: A native app only: browsers cannot adapt page layouts
optionC: One responsive site: one codebase, one URL, one content set
optionD: One fixed-width site: phone users can always zoom in
correctAnswerText: One responsive site: one codebase, one URL, one content set
explanation: Separate mobile sites double maintenance, drift in content and need redirects and canonical tags. Responsive design serves the same HTML to every device.

prompt: Judge content-based breakpoints versus breakpoints copied from popular device widths.
optionA: Device-based, since content never changes after launch
optionB: Device-based, since screens come in just three sizes
optionC: Content-based, since device widths change every year
optionD: Content-based, since queries cannot read the device
correctAnswerText: Content-based, since device widths change every year
explanation: There are hundreds of widths in use. Breakpoints placed where the design strains keep working on devices that do not exist yet.

prompt: Judge a unit policy for a new stylesheet.
optionA: rem for type and spacing; px is fine for thin borders
optionB: vw for everything, so every size scales with screen
optionC: rem for everything, down to 1px borders and shadows
optionD: px for everything, since rem breaks in older browsers
correctAnswerText: rem for type and spacing; px is fine for thin borders
explanation: Text and spacing should follow the user's font setting; a 1px hairline should stay 1px. Pure vw makes text unreadable on phones and huge on monitors.

prompt: To make the phone layout fit, a teammate proposes hiding half the page's sections below 768px. Judge it.
optionA: Hide the navigation on phones, since users rarely need it there
optionB: Hide all images on phones to make every page load faster
optionC: Prioritise and reflow instead; phone users need the content too
optionD: Hide everything below the fold, since phone users rarely scroll
correctAnswerText: Prioritise and reflow instead; phone users need the content too
explanation: Many users only ever see the phone version. Reorder, collapse into accordions and simplify — but content hidden on mobile is content they cannot reach.

prompt: Judge the effort of adding srcset and sizes to a page full of large product photos.
optionA: Worth it only for icons, the heaviest files there
optionB: Not worth it: phones always have unlimited data
optionC: Worth it: phones then download far fewer bytes
optionD: Not worth it: browsers resize images on the server
correctAnswerText: Worth it: phones then download far fewer bytes
explanation: Serving a 1920px photo to a 400px slot wastes most of the bytes and delays rendering. Images are usually the heaviest part of a page.

prompt: For a new site's layouts, judge native Flexbox and Grid against adding a CSS framework just for its grid.
optionA: Floats are best, since Flexbox and Grid are experimental
optionB: Native Flexbox and Grid now cover most layouts on their own
optionC: A framework is required, since browsers lack layout tools
optionD: Tables are best, since they resize with the screen width
correctAnswerText: Native Flexbox and Grid now cover most layouts on their own
explanation: Flexbox and Grid are supported everywhere that matters and handle almost every layout. A framework may still be worth it for components, but not for the grid alone.

prompt: A product card is reused in a wide main column and a narrow sidebar. Judge media queries versus container queries for its layout.
optionA: Media queries, as a card always spans the full viewport
optionB: Container queries, as they replace the viewport meta tag
optionC: Container queries, as the card responds to its own space
optionD: Media queries, as containers can never have a width
correctAnswerText: Container queries, as the card responds to its own space
explanation: A media query sees the viewport, not the slot the card sits in. @container (widely supported since 2023) lets the card adapt to the space it is actually given.

prompt: Judge a testing plan for a responsive student portal with little time and no device lab.
optionA: DevTools only, since it matches every real phone exactly
optionB: One flagship phone, since all others render the same
optionC: A few real phones plus DevTools sizes across breakpoints
optionD: Desktop only, then trust the media queries for phones
correctAnswerText: A few real phones plus DevTools sizes across breakpoints
explanation: DevTools sweeps widths fast; one inexpensive Android and one iPhone catch touch, font and performance issues emulation misses. Budget phones matter for this audience.

prompt: Someone argues a fixed 1200px layout is fine because "phone users can just pinch-zoom". Judge it.
optionA: Unsound: zooming and side-scrolling make reading painful
optionB: Sound: responsive CSS makes page loads much slower
optionC: Sound: every phone displays desktop layouts perfectly
optionD: Unsound: phones cannot zoom unless a viewport tag exists
correctAnswerText: Unsound: zooming and side-scrolling make reading painful
explanation: Zoomed-out text is unreadable and zoomed-in text needs constant sideways scrolling. Most traffic is mobile, and search engines rank mobile-friendliness.

prompt: For JSX to treat <UserCard /> as a component rather than an HTML tag, its name must start with what?
optionA: An uppercase letter
optionB: A lowercase letter
optionC: An underscore
optionD: The prefix "use"
correctAnswerText: An uppercase letter
explanation: JSX treats lowercase tags as built-in DOM elements and capitalised ones as components, so <userCard /> would be rendered as an unknown HTML tag.

prompt: Which JSX attribute sets a CSS class on a <div>?
optionA: class
optionB: cssClass
optionC: styleClass
optionD: className
correctAnswerText: className
explanation: JSX compiles to JavaScript, where class is a reserved word, so React uses the DOM property name className instead.

prompt: In React, what are props?
optionA: Values a component stores and changes itself
optionB: Settings read from the Vite build configuration
optionC: Inputs a parent passes to a child component
optionD: Global variables shared by every component
correctAnswerText: Inputs a parent passes to a child component
explanation: Props flow down from parent to child as the component's inputs. Values a component owns and changes are state, not props.

prompt: Which special prop gives each element of a rendered list a stable identity?
optionA: id
optionB: index
optionC: key
optionD: ref
correctAnswerText: key
explanation: React uses key to match list items between renders. An id attribute is only passed to the DOM; React itself does not use it for matching.

prompt: What does {count} written inside JSX markup do?
optionA: Renders the literal word "count" on screen
optionB: Creates a two-way binding to an input field
optionC: Declares a new state variable named count
optionD: Inserts the value of the JavaScript expression
correctAnswerText: Inserts the value of the JavaScript expression
explanation: Curly braces switch from markup back to JavaScript; whatever the expression evaluates to is rendered in that spot.

prompt: What does a function component return to describe its UI?
optionA: A DOM node made with document.createElement
optionB: JSX, which compiles to React element objects
optionC: An HTML string that React parses at runtime
optionD: The name of a template file React then loads
correctAnswerText: JSX, which compiles to React element objects
explanation: JSX compiles to calls that create plain element objects; React compares those descriptions and updates the real DOM itself.

prompt: What wraps several sibling elements without adding an extra node to the DOM?
optionA: A <div> element wrapper
optionB: A <span> element wrapper
optionC: A Fragment, written <>…</>
optionD: A <template> element tag
correctAnswerText: A Fragment, written <>…</>
explanation: A Fragment groups children for JSX's single-root rule but renders nothing itself, so it does not disturb CSS layouts such as flex or table rows.

prompt: Which prop attaches a click handler to a <button> in React?
optionA: onClick
optionB: onclick
optionC: onPress
optionD: click
correctAnswerText: onClick
explanation: React event props are camelCase (onClick, onChange, onSubmit) and take a function, unlike the lowercase string attributes of plain HTML.

prompt: Which prop holds whatever is nested between a component's opening and closing tags?
optionA: slot
optionB: children
optionC: content
optionD: inner
correctAnswerText: children
explanation: Anything placed between <Card> and </Card> arrives in Card as props.children, which is how wrapper components accept arbitrary content.

prompt: What is a "controlled" input in React?
optionA: One that the browser autofills for you
optionB: One that stays disabled until validated
optionC: One whose value comes from React state
optionD: One whose value lives only in the DOM
correctAnswerText: One whose value comes from React state
explanation: A controlled input gets value from state and reports changes through onChange, so React state is the single source of truth for what it shows.

prompt: Why should a state update create a new array or object instead of changing the existing one?
optionA: React compares references to decide whether to re-render
optionB: State objects are frozen, so any mutation throws an error
optionC: Mutation is forbidden by JavaScript strict mode in modules
optionD: A new object takes less memory than one that was mutated
correctAnswerText: React compares references to decide whether to re-render
explanation: React checks Object.is(old, new). A mutated array is still the same reference, so React can skip the render and the screen goes stale.

prompt: What does React do after a component calls its state setter with a new value?
optionA: Re-renders that component and, by default, its children
optionB: Waits until the parent component re-renders on its own
optionC: Updates only the single DOM node bound to that variable
optionD: Reloads the whole application from the root component
correctAnswerText: Re-renders that component and, by default, its children
explanation: Setting state schedules a render of that component; its children render too unless memoised. React then patches only the DOM that changed.

prompt: Why must a child component never modify the props object it receives?
optionA: Props live in the browser cache and cannot be written to
optionB: Props are recreated as strings, so changes are discarded
optionC: The parent owns that data; changing it breaks one-way flow
optionD: Modifying props makes React unmount the child component
correctAnswerText: The parent owns that data; changing it breaks one-way flow
explanation: Data flows down. If a child wants a change it asks the owner through a callback prop, and the owner updates its state and re-renders.

prompt: Why is the array index a poor key for a list that users can reorder or filter?
optionA: Index values are numbers, and React only accepts string keys
optionB: Keys then follow positions, so row state sticks to the wrong item
optionC: React rejects the same index being reused across two renders
