optionD: Index keys switch off re-rendering for every row in that list
correctAnswerText: Keys then follow positions, so row state sticks to the wrong item
explanation: React matches rows by key. When items move, index 0 now means a different item, so its input text or checkbox state is attached to the wrong row.

prompt: What does "lifting state up" mean in React?
optionA: Moving shared state to the closest common parent
optionB: Storing the state in the URL instead of memory
optionC: Copying the state into each child that needs it
optionD: Moving every piece of state into a Redux store
correctAnswerText: Moving shared state to the closest common parent
explanation: When two components need the same data, the nearest parent owns it and passes the value and an updater down, so there is one copy, not two.

prompt: How does onClick={save()} differ from onClick={save}?
optionA: The first binds save to the parent component instead
optionB: The first calls save during render instead of on click
optionC: The first fires once on the first click and never again
optionD: The first passes the click event to save a second time
correctAnswerText: The first calls save during render instead of on click
explanation: save() runs immediately while JSX is being built and its return value becomes the handler. Pass the function itself, or wrap it in an arrow.

prompt: Why can {count && <Badge />} put a stray "0" on the page?
optionA: Badge falls back to rendering 0 when it receives no props at all
optionB: When count is 0 the expression yields 0, and React renders numbers
optionC: React renders the boolean false as the text "false" on the screen
optionD: The && operator always returns its right-hand side in JSX blocks
correctAnswerText: When count is 0 the expression yields 0, and React renders numbers
explanation: && returns its left operand when that is falsy. React skips false, null and undefined but does render the number 0. Use count > 0 && … instead.

prompt: What does accepting children let a component such as Card or Modal do?
optionA: Let the nested content change the wrapper's own props
optionB: Share state between siblings without a common parent
optionC: Skip re-rendering whenever its parent component renders
optionD: Wrap any content without knowing in advance what it is
correctAnswerText: Wrap any content without knowing in advance what it is
explanation: Composition keeps the wrapper generic: it provides the frame and the caller decides the content, instead of a growing list of special-case props.

prompt: Why can a plain let variable inside a component not replace useState?
optionA: It resets on every render, and changing it triggers no render
optionB: Plain variables are not permitted inside function components
optionC: It is shared by every instance of that component on the page
optionD: React freezes every local variable after the first render
correctAnswerText: It resets on every render, and changing it triggers no render
explanation: Each render calls the function afresh, so the variable starts over; and assigning to it does not tell React anything changed.

prompt: Which statement correctly separates state from props?
optionA: State is shared by the whole app; props stay inside one component
optionB: A component owns and updates its state; props come from its parent
optionC: Props are for class components; state is for function components
optionD: Props can be changed by the child; state is fixed by the parent
correctAnswerText: A component owns and updates its state; props come from its parent
explanation: The same value is often both: state in the parent that owns it, and a read-only prop in every child it is passed to.

prompt: Given const [items, setItems] = useState([]), which line adds newItem so the list re-renders?
optionA: items.push(newItem); setItems(items)
optionB: setItems(items.push(newItem))
optionC: setItems([...items, newItem])
optionD: items[items.length] = newItem
correctAnswerText: setItems([...items, newItem])
explanation: The spread builds a new array, so React sees a new reference. push mutates the old array and returns a number, which is worse still.

prompt: Complete the controlled input: <input value={name} onChange={ ? } />
optionA: e => setName(name)
optionB: e => { name = e.target.value }
optionC: e => setName(e.value)
optionD: e => setName(e.target.value)
correctAnswerText: e => setName(e.target.value)
explanation: The event's target is the input, and its value is what the user typed. Without the setter call the input would ignore keystrokes.

prompt: Each user has id and name. Which renders the list with no key warning?
optionA:
users.map(u =>
  • {u.name}
    • )
optionB:
users.map(u =>
  • {u.name}
    • ).key(u.id)
optionC:
users.forEach(u =>
  • {u.name}
    • )
optionD:
users.map(u =>
  • {u.name}
    • )
correctAnswerText:
users.map(u =>
  • {u.name}
    • )
explanation: map returns the array of elements React renders, and key belongs on the element map returns. forEach returns undefined, so nothing renders.

prompt: SearchBox and ResultList are siblings and both need the query text. Where should query live?
optionA: In their common parent, passed down to both as props
optionB: In both of them, kept in step by a syncing effect
optionC: In a module-level variable that both of them import
optionD: In SearchBox, with ResultList reading it from there
correctAnswerText: In their common parent, passed down to both as props
explanation: A sibling cannot read another sibling's state. The parent holds query, gives ResultList the value and SearchBox the value plus setter.

prompt: State user is { name, email }. Which line changes only the email and keeps the name?
optionA: user.email = newEmail; setUser(user)
optionB: setUser({ email: newEmail })
optionC: setUser({ ...user, email: newEmail })
optionD: setUser(user, { email: newEmail })
correctAnswerText: setUser({ ...user, email: newEmail })
explanation: useState replaces, it does not merge. Spreading copies the old fields into a new object and then overrides email.

prompt: Inside JSX, show <Spinner /> while loading is true and <CourseList /> otherwise.
optionA: {loading : <Spinner /> ? <CourseList />}
optionB: {loading ? <Spinner /> : <CourseList />}
optionC: {loading && <Spinner />, <CourseList />}
optionD: {if (loading) <Spinner /> else <CourseList />}
correctAnswerText: {loading ? <Spinner /> : <CourseList />}
explanation: Only expressions are allowed inside braces. An if statement is not an expression, so use a ternary or compute the element above the return.

optionA:

correctAnswerText:

explanation: Nested JSX arrives as the children prop. Function components have no this, and content or inner are just undefined props here.

prompt: A row's Delete button must call onDelete with that row's item.id. Which prop is right?
optionA: onClick={onDelete(item.id)}
optionB: onClick="onDelete(item.id)"
optionC: onClick={() => onDelete(item.id)}
optionD: onClick={onDelete}(item.id)
correctAnswerText: onClick={() => onDelete(item.id)}
explanation: The arrow creates a function that runs on click and supplies the argument. Calling onDelete(item.id) directly would delete during render.

prompt: Which line removes the item with a given id from items state the React way?
optionA: delete items[index]; setItems(items)
optionB: setItems(items.splice(index, 1))
optionC: items.splice(index, 1); setItems(items)
optionD: setItems(items.filter(i => i.id !== id))
correctAnswerText: setItems(items.filter(i => i.id !== id))
explanation: filter returns a new array without the item. splice mutates in place and returns the removed elements, not the remaining list.

prompt: A CitySelect child must report the chosen city to its parent. How is that done?
optionA: The child returns the city from its render function
optionB: The child mutates the props object it was handed
optionC: The child sets the parent's state variable by its name
optionD: The parent passes a callback prop that the child calls
correctAnswerText: The parent passes a callback prop that the child calls
explanation: Data goes down as props and events come up as callbacks, e.g. <CitySelect onChange={setCity} />; the parent then owns the chosen city.

optionA: 3, because the variable is captured by the arrow
optionB: 0, because nothing tells React to render again
optionC: 1, because the increment applies only once
optionD: Nothing; assigning to count throws an error
correctAnswerText: 0, because nothing tells React to render again
explanation: count does change in memory, but no render is triggered, and the next render would start again at 0. This needs useState.

optionA: push is asynchronous and completes after the render
optionB: todos is a const array, so push silently does nothing
optionC: setTodos accepts only an updater function, not a value
optionD: Same array reference, so React treats it as unchanged
correctAnswerText: Same array reference, so React treats it as unchanged
explanation: React compares the new state with the old using Object.is. Same array, so it bails out. Use setTodos([...todos, t]).

prompt: Rows are rendered with key={index}, each holding its own note input. After deleting the first row, typed notes appear beside the wrong rows. What is the cause?
optionA: Deleting a row forces React to remount the whole list
optionB: The delete handler re-sorted the array before saving it
optionC: React reuses each row's state by position, not by item
optionD: Inputs inside a list must always be uncontrolled ones
correctAnswerText: React reuses each row's state by position, not by item
explanation: After the delete, key 0 belongs to what was the second item, but React keeps the first row's component and its note. Key by the item id.

prompt: With an empty items array, what appears for {items.length && <List items={items} />}?
optionA: The word false
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: An empty <List>
optionD: The digit 0
correctAnswerText: The digit 0
explanation: items.length is 0, && short-circuits and returns 0, and React renders numbers. Write items.length > 0 && … to get nothing.

prompt: <button onClick={setOpen(true)}>Open</button> crashes with "Too many re-renders". Why?
optionA: setOpen runs while rendering, which schedules another render
optionB: The button needs type="button" before onClick will work
optionC: A boolean cannot be passed to a state setter in React 18
optionD: setOpen must be wrapped in useCallback to be used in JSX
correctAnswerText: setOpen runs while rendering, which schedules another render

prompt: A 400-line StudentsPage fetches data, holds a filter form and renders a table. How should it be split?

prompt: A Button takes isPrimary, isDanger and isSecondary booleans. What is the better prop design?

prompt: Tabs render {tab === "a" && <FormA />}. Users complain half-typed input in FormA vanishes when they switch tabs. Best response?

prompt: Should a CartItem child receive the raw setItems setter or an onRemove(id) callback?

prompt: When is key={index} an acceptable choice?

optionD: For a static list that is never reordered, filtered or edited
correctAnswerText: For a static list that is never reordered, filtered or edited

prompt: An EditProfile form seeds its fields from a user prop. Choosing a different user must reset the form. Cleanest approach?

prompt: What does a call to useState(0) return?

prompt: In a production build, when does useEffect(fn, []) run fn?

prompt: What is the function returned from a useEffect callback used for?

correctAnswerText: Cleanup before the effect re-runs and on unmount

prompt: Which hook holds a mutable value that survives renders but does not cause one when changed?

optionB: useRef

prompt: Which hook reads the value supplied by the nearest matching Context Provider above?

optionC: useReducer

prompt: A custom hook's name must begin with which prefix?
optionA: use
optionB: get
optionC: hook
optionD: with
correctAnswerText: use
explanation: The use prefix tells React and the lint rules that the function calls hooks, so the rules of hooks are checked inside it and at its call sites.

prompt: Where are hooks allowed to be called?

prompt: What does useMemo keep between renders?
optionA: A function definition, until a dependency changes
optionB: A reference to a DOM node rendered by the component
optionC: The result of a calculation, until a dependency changes

correctAnswerText: The result of a calculation, until a dependency changes

prompt: What does useCallback(fn, deps) return?

correctAnswerText: The same function object while deps are unchanged

prompt: In development under React 18 StrictMode, what happens to a component's effects on mount?

prompt: Why does calling setCount(count + 1) three times in one click handler add only one?

prompt: What does the updater form setCount(c => c + 1) guarantee?

correctAnswerText: Each update receives the latest pending value

prompt: What does React 18's automatic batching change?

prompt: What does the dependency array of a useEffect tell React?
optionA: Which state variables the effect is permitted to update

correctAnswerText: Which values, when changed, should make the effect re-run

prompt: What is a "stale closure" in a component that uses hooks?

prompt: Why must hooks never be called inside an if statement?

prompt: How does storing a value in useRef differ from storing it in useState?

prompt: What happens when a Context Provider's value changes?

prompt: Why does StrictMode deliberately run effects twice in development?

prompt: Which useWindowWidth() custom hook gives callers the width and keeps it current on resize?

prompt: Typing "java" quickly sometimes shows results for "ja". The effect fetches on [query] with no cleanup. What is happening?

prompt:

prompt: Chart is wrapped in React.memo, yet it re-renders on every parent render. The parent renders <Chart data={data} onHover={() => setHover(true)} />. Why?

prompt: App renders <AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>. Every consumer re-renders whenever App renders, even if user is unchanged. Why?

prompt: A reviewer asks you to wrap every handler in the app in useCallback "for performance". Fair request?
optionA: Yes; React requires useCallback for any handler with state
optionB: Yes; every unwrapped function slows down each render badly

prompt: Is const total = useMemo(() => price * qty, [price, qty]) a good idea?

correctAnswerText: No; the memo bookkeeping costs more than the multiplication

prompt: A component keeps visibleTodos in state and sets it in useEffect whenever todos or filter change. Better design?
optionA: Compute visibleTodos during render from todos and filter
optionB: Keep the effect but add visibleTodos to its dependencies
optionC: Use a second effect to keep the two states in step

correctAnswerText: Compute visibleTodos during render from todos and filter

prompt: A teammate removes <StrictMode> from main.jsx because a chat effect opens two connections in development. Your view?
optionA: Fine; production will open two connections either way
optionB: Keep StrictMode, but guard the effect with a global flag
optionC: Fine; StrictMode is only for class component warnings
optionD: Keep StrictMode; add cleanup that closes the connection
correctAnswerText: Keep StrictMode; add cleanup that closes the connection
explanation: Two connections means the effect leaks without cleanup, which will also bite on real remounts. A global flag hides the symptom and breaks remounting.

prompt: The exhaustive-deps lint rule wants count in an interval effect's deps, which would restart the timer each tick. Best response?
optionA: Use setCount(c => c + 1) so the effect no longer reads count
optionB: Disable the lint rule on that line and leave the array empty
optionC: Add count and accept a fresh timer being created every tick
optionD: Store count in a global variable that the lint rule ignores
correctAnswerText: Use setCount(c => c + 1) so the effect no longer reads count
explanation: Remove the dependency by removing the read, not by lying to the linter. The updater form needs no access to count at all.

prompt: One AppContext holds a theme that rarely changes and a mouse position that changes constantly. What would you do?
optionA: Split them into separate contexts by how often they change
optionB: Wrap every consumer in React.memo to stop the re-renders
optionC: Keep one context; React skips consumers that ignore a field
optionD: Move both into refs so no consumer re-renders at all
correctAnswerText: Split them into separate contexts by how often they change
explanation: A context consumer re-renders on any change to the value. Separate contexts keep theme readers from re-rendering on every mouse move; memo does not block context.

prompt: Six components each repeat the same fetch, loading and error effect code. What is the best improvement?
optionA: Extract a custom hook such as useFetch(url) that all six use
optionB: Copy the code into a utility that is not a hook at all
optionC: Move all six fetches into App and pass the data down by props
optionD: Merge the six components into one large shared component
correctAnswerText: Extract a custom hook such as useFetch(url) that all six use
explanation: A custom hook shares the stateful logic while each caller keeps its own state. A plain function cannot hold state or run effects.

prompt: To "avoid re-renders", a student stores a character counter shown under a textarea in a ref. Good trade?
optionA: No; a ref cannot store any value except a DOM node
optionB: Yes; refs are always faster than state for numbers
optionC: Yes; the ref will show up on the next render anyway
optionD: No; the counter is displayed, so it must be state
correctAnswerText: No; the counter is displayed, so it must be state
explanation: Skipping the render is exactly what makes the counter wrong on screen. Refs are for values the UI does not display.

prompt: A checkout step has status, error, retries and payment data that change together on each event. useState for each, or useReducer?
optionA: useState for each, as useReducer needs Redux to be installed
optionB: useState for each, since useReducer cannot hold an object
optionC: useReducer, so each event updates related fields in one place
optionD: useReducer, because it never re-renders the component
correctAnswerText: useReducer, so each event updates related fields in one place
explanation: When one event changes several fields, a reducer keeps those transitions together and testable instead of scattering setters across handlers.

prompt: A Buy button sets bought=true, and an effect on [bought] posts the order. A refresh that restores bought from storage sends a second order. Which design is right?
optionA: Keep the effect and add the order id to its dependencies
optionB: Storage values cannot be used to initialise React state
optionC: Logic caused by a click belongs in the handler, not an effect
optionD: The POST request should have been wrapped in useMemo
correctAnswerText: Logic caused by a click belongs in the handler, not an effect
explanation: An effect runs because something rendered, not because the user acted. Posting in the click handler sends the order exactly once.

prompt: Which router component gives a React app clean URLs such as /courses/42?
optionA: MemoryRouter
optionB: StaticRouter
optionC: HashRouter
optionD: BrowserRouter
correctAnswerText: BrowserRouter
explanation: BrowserRouter uses the History API for real paths. HashRouter puts the route after a # and MemoryRouter keeps it out of the address bar entirely.

prompt: In React Router v6, which component wraps a group of <Route> elements?
optionA: Router
optionB: Routes
optionC: RouteGroup
optionD: Switch
correctAnswerText: Routes
explanation: v6 replaced v5's Switch with Routes, which picks the best match by ranking rather than by the order routes are written.

prompt: In v6, which Route prop says what to render for the matched path?
optionA: element
optionB: view
optionC: component
optionD: render
correctAnswerText: element
explanation: v6 takes a JSX element: <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />. component and render were v5 props.

prompt: Which component moves to another route without reloading the page?
optionA: Outlet
optionB: <a href>
optionC: Link
optionD: Route
correctAnswerText: Link
explanation: Link renders an anchor but intercepts the click and updates the URL through the router, so the app keeps running and its state survives.

prompt: Which hook reads the :id segment of a route declared as /courses/:id?
optionA: useOutlet
optionB: useParams
optionC: useSearchParams
optionD: useNavigate
correctAnswerText: useParams
explanation: useParams returns an object of the dynamic segments, so const { id } = useParams() gives "42" for /courses/42.

prompt: Which v6 hook sends the user to another route from code, for example after a form saves?
optionA: useParams
optionB: useRoute
optionC: useNavigate
optionD: useHistory
correctAnswerText: useNavigate
explanation: const navigate = useNavigate(); navigate("/courses"). useHistory was the v5 equivalent and does not exist in v6.

prompt: Which component marks where a parent layout route renders its matched child route?
optionA: Outlet
optionB: Slot
optionC: Routes
optionD: Navigate
correctAnswerText: Outlet
explanation: A layout route's element renders <Outlet />, and React Router puts the matching child route's element there.

prompt: Which path value makes a Route match any URL that no other route matched?
optionC: default
explanation: path="*" is a splat that matches anything; because v6 ranks routes, more specific paths still win over it.

prompt: What does NavLink add to what Link already does?
optionA: It opens its target route in a brand-new tab
optionB: It preloads the target page's data in advance
optionC: It blocks navigation until a form is saved
optionD: It knows whether it matches the current URL
correctAnswerText: It knows whether it matches the current URL
explanation: NavLink exposes isActive to its className and style props and adds an active class by default, which is what navigation menus need.

prompt: Which hook reads and updates the ?page=2 part of the current URL?
optionA: useLocationState
optionB: useSearchParams
optionC: useQuery
optionD: useParams
correctAnswerText: useSearchParams
explanation: useSearchParams returns a URLSearchParams object and a setter, much like useState but stored in the query string.

prompt: Why do SPAs use <Link to="/courses"> instead of <a href="/courses"> for internal pages?
optionA: Link fetches the next page's HTML from the server more quickly
optionB: Link is rendered as a button, which screen readers prefer
optionC: Link changes the URL through history without reloading the app
optionD: Anchors cannot point at paths served by the Vite dev server
correctAnswerText: Link changes the URL through history without reloading the app
explanation: A plain anchor makes the browser request a new document, which restarts React and discards in-memory state. Link swaps components in place.

prompt: After deploying the built app, refreshing /courses/42 gives the server's 404 page. Why?
optionA: The build step removed every route except the home route
optionB: No file exists at that path; the server must return index.html
optionC: The browser caches a 404 for paths it has not seen before
optionD: BrowserRouter cannot handle numbers in a URL in production
correctAnswerText: No file exists at that path; the server must return index.html
explanation: On refresh the browser asks the server for /courses/42. The Vite dev server falls back to index.html; a static host must be told to do the same.

prompt: Under a /dashboard layout route, what does <Route index element={<Overview />} /> do?
optionA: Shows Overview only when no child route matches
optionB: Shows Overview in the Outlet at exactly /dashboard
optionC: Shows Overview on every page under /dashboard
optionD: Lists the links of all child routes as an index
correctAnswerText: Shows Overview in the Outlet at exactly /dashboard
explanation: An index route is the default child: it fills the parent's Outlet when the URL is the parent path itself and nothing deeper.

prompt: For /courses/42, why is useParams().id === 42 false?
optionA: URL segments are text, so id holds the string "42"
optionB: React Router adds a leading slash to every param
optionC: useParams returns undefined until the effect has run
optionD: Route params are wrapped in an object like { value }
correctAnswerText: URL segments are text, so id holds the string "42"
explanation: Everything parsed out of a URL is a string. Compare with "42" or convert with Number(id) before doing arithmetic.

prompt: What is gained by keeping a list's filter and page number in the query string instead of useState?
optionA: It keeps the values hidden from the user's address bar
optionB: The browser validates the values before React sees them
optionC: The view survives a reload and can be shared as a link
optionD: Query-string values make the list render more quickly
correctAnswerText: The view survives a reload and can be shared as a link
explanation: Component state disappears on refresh and cannot be sent to a friend. The URL is state that the browser keeps and shares for you.

prompt: What does a client-side protected route actually achieve?
optionA: Encrypts the page so only signed-in users can read it
optionB: Stops anyone from downloading that page's JavaScript code
optionC: Sends signed-out users to login; the API must still check
optionD: Makes the server refuse requests from signed-out users
correctAnswerText: Sends signed-out users to login; the API must still check
explanation: The bundle is public and the guard runs in the user's browser. It improves the experience; real protection is the server rejecting unauthorised calls.

prompt: What does navigate(-1) do?
optionA: Goes back one entry, like the Back button
optionB: Reloads the current route from the server
optionC: Goes to the parent path, such as /courses
optionD: Goes to the route at index -1 in the config
correctAnswerText: Goes back one entry, like the Back button
explanation: A number moves through browser history. For the parent path you would navigate("..") instead, which does not depend on where the user came from.

prompt: Why should a page that fetches a list render loading, error and empty states separately?
optionA: Each is a different situation the user needs telling about
optionB: React Router requires all three before it renders the page
optionC: Separate states let the browser cache each response on its own
optionD: One combined state would make the fetch run more than once
correctAnswerText: Each is a different situation the user needs telling about
explanation: "Still loading", "it failed, try again" and "there is nothing yet" need different messages. A blank list for all three misleads users.

prompt: What does the replace option do in navigate("/home", { replace: true })?
optionA: Swaps the current history entry, so Back skips it
optionB: Replaces the page's components without re-rendering
optionC: Swaps the route config for the one at /home
optionD: Clears all of the history the user has built up
correctAnswerText: Swaps the current history entry, so Back skips it
explanation: A normal navigation pushes a new entry. replace overwrites the current one, which is right for redirects such as leaving a login page.

prompt: Inside the element for route /courses/:id, where does <Link to="edit"> lead when viewing /courses/42?
optionA: /courses/42edit
optionB: /courses/edit
optionC: /edit
optionD: /courses/42/edit
correctAnswerText: /courses/42/edit
explanation: A path without a leading slash is relative to the route that rendered the link, so "edit" is appended to /courses/42.

prompt: Which v6 configuration serves a course list at /courses and one course at /courses/7?
optionA: <Routes><Route path="/courses/*" element={<CourseList />} /><Route path=":id" element={<Course />} /></Routes>
optionB: <Routes><Route path="/courses" element={<CourseList />} /><Route path="/courses/:id" element={<Course />} /></Routes>
optionC: <Routes><Route path="/courses" element={<CourseList />} /><Route path="/courses/id" element={<Course />} /></Routes>
optionD: <Switch><Route path="/courses" component={CourseList} /><Route path="/courses/:id" component={Course} /></Switch>
correctAnswerText: <Routes><Route path="/courses" element={<CourseList />} /><Route path="/courses/:id" element={<Course />} /></Routes>
explanation: The colon makes id a dynamic segment; without it only the literal path /courses/id matches. Switch and component= are v5 API.

prompt: The Course page must load the course named in the URL. Which code fits?
optionA: const { id } = useParams(); useEffect(() => { load(id); }, []);
optionB: const id = useNavigate().id; useEffect(() => { load(id); }, []);
optionC: const { id } = useParams(); useEffect(() => { load(id); }, [id]);
optionD: const { id } = useSearchParams(); useEffect(() => { load(id); }, [id]);
correctAnswerText: const { id } = useParams(); useEffect(() => { load(id); }, [id]);
explanation: The id comes from the path via useParams, and listing it in the deps makes the page reload when the URL moves to another course.

prompt: After a successful login, go to /dashboard so that Back does not return to the login form. Which call?
optionA: navigate("/dashboard")
optionB: window.location.href = "/dashboard"
optionC: navigate(-1, { to: "/dashboard" })
optionD: navigate("/dashboard", { replace: true })
correctAnswerText: navigate("/dashboard", { replace: true })
explanation: replace overwrites the login entry in history. Setting window.location reloads the whole app and loses in-memory auth state.

prompt: Which RequireAuth body shows its children to a signed-in user and sends others to /login?
optionA: return user ? children : <Link to="/login">Log in</Link>;
optionB: return user ? <Navigate to="/login" replace /> : children;
optionC: return user ? children : <Navigate to="/login" replace />;
optionD: if (!user) { navigate("/login"); } return children;
correctAnswerText: return user ? children : <Navigate to="/login" replace />;
explanation: <Navigate> redirects as it renders. Calling navigate() during render is a side effect, and a Link only waits for a click.

prompt: Every student page should share one header and sidebar. How is that set up in v6?
optionA: A parent route with element={<Layout />} whose Layout renders <Outlet />
optionB: A Layout import inside each page, wrapped around that page's own content
optionC: A Layout passed as the component prop to every individual student Route
optionD: A Layout placed inside <Routes> as a sibling of all the student routes
correctAnswerText: A parent route with element={<Layout />} whose Layout renders <Outlet />
explanation: Nest the pages as children of a layout route. The layout stays mounted while the Outlet swaps the page, so it is not re-created on each navigation.

prompt: const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams(); page is Number(params.get("page") || 1). Which Next handler moves to the following page?
optionA: setParams({ page: String(page + 1) })
optionB: params.set("page", page + 1)
optionC: setParams(page + 1)
optionD: params.page = page + 1
correctAnswerText: setParams({ page: String(page + 1) })
explanation: The setter updates the URL and re-renders. Mutating params with set() changes the object but not the URL, so nothing re-renders.

prompt: Which route shows a NotFound page for any URL the app does not define?
optionA: <Route path="/" element={<NotFound />} />
optionB: <Route index element={<NotFound />} />
optionC: <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
optionD: <Route path="/404" element={<NotFound />} />
correctAnswerText: <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
explanation: The splat matches whatever nothing else did. A /404 route only matches the literal path /404, which no unknown URL is.

prompt: Give the Bootstrap class "active" to the Courses menu item only while its page is open.
optionA: <NavLink to="/courses" className={isActive ? "nav-link active" : "nav-link"}>
optionB: <NavLink to="/courses" active="nav-link active" inactive="nav-link">
optionC: <Link to="/courses" className={({ isActive }) => isActive ? "nav-link active" : "nav-link"}>
optionD: <NavLink to="/courses" className={({ isActive }) => isActive ? "nav-link active" : "nav-link"}>
correctAnswerText: <NavLink to="/courses" className={({ isActive }) => isActive ? "nav-link active" : "nav-link"}>
explanation: NavLink calls a className function with { isActive }. Link has no notion of active, and a bare isActive variable does not exist in scope.

prompt: The Vite dist folder is served by Nginx. Which location rule lets deep links like /courses/42 load on refresh?
optionA: try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
optionB: rewrite ^/courses/(.*)$ /$1;
optionC: return 301 /index.html;
optionD: error_page 404 /404.html;
correctAnswerText: try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
explanation: Serve the real file if it exists (JS, CSS, images) and otherwise index.html, so the router can read the path. A 301 would change the URL to /index.html.

prompt: A page has loading, error and courses state. In what order should the component check them before rendering the list?
optionA: the list first, then error, and loading only if neither
optionB: loading, then error, then an empty list, then the list
optionC: error only, since a loading check is not required
optionD: empty first, then loading, then error, then the list
correctAnswerText: loading, then error, then an empty list, then the list
explanation: While loading the list is legitimately empty, so check loading first; an error is not "no courses"; only then is an empty array a true empty state.

prompt: Code copied from a tutorial, <Switch><Route path="/" component={Home} /></Switch>, fails with react-router-dom 6 installed. Why?
optionA: component only accepts class components, not functions
optionB: Switch and component are v5 APIs; v6 uses Routes and element
optionC: The home route must be written as path="" in version 6
optionD: Home has to be imported from react-router-dom before use
correctAnswerText: Switch and component are v5 APIs; v6 uses Routes and element
explanation: v6 removed Switch, component and render. The v6 form is <Routes><Route path="/" element={<Home />} /></Routes>.

prompt: Clicking "Next course" moves the URL from /courses/1 to /courses/2, but the old course stays on screen. The fetch effect has [] deps. Why?
optionA: useParams only reads the URL once, when the app first loads
optionB: The link needs reloadDocument so that the new course loads
optionC: React Router caches each page and serves the earlier render
optionD: The same component stays mounted, and the effect never re-runs
correctAnswerText: The same component stays mounted, and the effect never re-runs
explanation: Both URLs match one route, so React keeps the component and only its params change. Put id in the effect's deps.

prompt: At /dashboard/profile the layout's header and sidebar appear but the profile page never does. The routes are nested correctly. What is missing?
optionA: A second <Routes> inside the profile page
optionB: An <Outlet /> inside the layout component
optionC: A leading slash on the child route's path
optionD: An exact prop on the parent layout route
correctAnswerText: An <Outlet /> inside the layout component
explanation: The child matched, but the layout has nowhere to put it. Outlet is the placeholder that renders the matched child.

prompt: After signing in, pressing Back shows the login page, which immediately bounces the user forward again. What causes it?
optionA: The browser restores login from its cache before React runs
optionB: The post-login redirect pushed a new entry instead of replacing
optionC: Back clears the auth token, so the login page is shown again
optionD: The login page is missing a path="*" fallback route of its own
correctAnswerText: The post-login redirect pushed a new entry instead of replacing
explanation: Login is still in history. Redirect with replace: true (or <Navigate replace />) so the login entry is overwritten.

prompt: A signed-in user refreshes /dashboard and is sent to /login, although the session is valid. The guard checks user, which is filled by a /me request. What is wrong?
optionA: Navigate needs the replace prop to keep the user on the page
optionB: Refreshing the page always deletes the session on the server
optionC: A protected route cannot be the first page the browser loads
optionD: The guard decides before /me returns, while user is still null
correctAnswerText: The guard decides before /me returns, while user is still null
explanation: Track an "auth checked" flag and render a spinner until /me finishes; only then redirect if there is no user.

prompt: The cart empties every time a user clicks Courses in the navbar. The cart lives in React state. The navbar uses <a href="/courses">. Why does the cart empty?
optionA: The anchor reloads the page, restarting React from scratch
optionB: Navigating to /courses resets state in every component
optionC: Anchors clear localStorage when they leave the current page
optionD: The cart is unmounted because it is outside of <Routes>
correctAnswerText: The anchor reloads the page, restarting React from scratch
explanation: A full document load re-runs main.jsx, so all in-memory state starts again. Link navigates within the running app.

prompt: On /courses?page=2, const next = params.get("page") + 1 gives what, and why?
optionA: 3, since get converts digits into a number for you
optionB: null, since get only reads path segments like :id
optionC: NaN, since a string cannot be added to a number
optionD: "21", since get returns a string and + concatenates
correctAnswerText: "21", since get returns a string and + concatenates
explanation: URLSearchParams.get returns a string or null. Convert first: Number(params.get("page") || 1) + 1.

prompt: "No courses yet" flashes for half a second before the courses appear. State starts as [] and there is no loading flag. Why?
optionA: Before the fetch ends, [] looks exactly like a real empty list
optionB: The router shows the empty state while the route is matching
optionC: React renders the empty-state markup before any other markup
optionD: The fetch runs twice, and the first response is always empty
correctAnswerText: Before the fetch ends, [] looks exactly like a real empty list
explanation: The page cannot tell "not loaded" from "loaded and empty". Add a loading state (or start with null) and render the empty message only after loading.

prompt: With the server fallback set up, /courses loads but refreshing /courses/42 gives a blank page; the console shows /courses/assets/index.js 404. vite.config has base: "./". Cause?
optionA: The server fallback must point to /courses/index.html
optionB: The route /courses/:id must be listed in vite.config
optionC: Vite does not support routes more than one level deep
optionD: Relative asset paths resolve under /courses/; use base "/"
correctAnswerText: Relative asset paths resolve under /courses/; use base "/"
explanation: With base "./", index.html loads ./assets/…, which the browser resolves against /courses/. An absolute base "/" loads /assets/… from any depth.

prompt: A component calls navigate("/login") directly in its body when user is null, and React warns about it. What is the fix?
optionA: Wrap the navigate call in useMemo with [user] deps
optionB: Call navigate twice so the second call takes effect
optionC: Use window.history.pushState in the body instead
optionD: Return <Navigate to="/login" /> from render instead
correctAnswerText: Return <Navigate to="/login" /> from render instead
explanation: navigate is a side effect and must run in a handler or effect. For "redirect while rendering", the <Navigate> component is the declarative tool.

prompt: Mentors want to send students a link straight to the "Assignments" tab of a course page. Where should the active tab live?
optionA: In a Redux store, so every page can read the active tab
optionB: In the URL, e.g. ?tab=assignments, so the link opens it
optionC: In localStorage, so each browser recalls the last tab
optionD: In useState, since tabs are purely presentational state
correctAnswerText: In the URL, e.g. ?tab=assignments, so the link opens it
explanation: Only the URL travels with a link. State, localStorage and a store all belong to the sender's browser, not the student's.

prompt: A team says the /admin route is safe because RequireAdmin redirects non-admins. Is that enough?
optionA: Yes; React Router hides admin code from other users
optionB: Yes, provided the role check uses replace in Navigate
optionC: No; the admin API must reject non-admin requests itself
optionD: No; the route must also be removed from the sitemap
correctAnswerText: No; the admin API must reject non-admin requests itself
explanation: Anyone can call the API with curl or edit the client in DevTools. Authorisation has to happen on the server for every request.

prompt: A college demo server serves static files but its rewrite rules cannot be configured. What is a reasonable routing choice?
optionA: No router, putting every page in one long scrolling screen
optionB: BrowserRouter with a link to the home page on every 404
optionC: BrowserRouter, since modern browsers resolve deep links alone
optionD: HashRouter, accepting /#/courses URLs to avoid server config
correctAnswerText: HashRouter, accepting /#/courses URLs to avoid server config
explanation: The part after # never reaches the server, so every refresh loads index.html. The cost is less clean URLs; where rewrites exist, prefer BrowserRouter.

prompt: Should a learning app fetch every page's data once in App at startup, or let each route fetch its own?
optionA: App fetches everything once, so no page ever waits
optionB: Each route fetches what it needs, when it is visited
optionC: App fetches everything, refreshing it every minute
optionD: No page fetches; data is bundled into the build
correctAnswerText: Each route fetches what it needs, when it is visited
explanation: Up-front loading slows the first screen and goes stale. Per-route loading keeps each page responsible for its data and its loading state.

prompt: Twelve pages each render <Header /> and <Sidebar /> themselves. Is a nested layout route worth the change?
optionA: No; repeating two tags per page costs nothing at all
optionB: Yes; one layout keeps the chrome mounted and in one place
optionC: No; nested routes make deep links fail after deploying
optionD: Yes, but only once the app grows past fifty pages
correctAnswerText: Yes; one layout keeps the chrome mounted and in one place
explanation: With a layout route the header and sidebar keep their state between pages and changes happen once. Repetition invites pages that drift apart.

prompt: A list passes the whole course object to the detail page with navigate("/course", { state: course }). Better design?
optionA: Store the course in localStorage before navigating
optionB: Keep it; router state is the fastest way to share data
optionC: Put the id in the path (/courses/:id) and fetch by it
optionD: Encode the entire course object as JSON in the query
correctAnswerText: Put the id in the path (/courses/:id) and fetch by it
explanation: Router state is lost on a shared link or a fresh tab, so the page cannot load on its own. An id in the URL makes the page addressable.

prompt: For an unknown URL, silently redirect to the home page or show a NotFound page with a link home?
optionA: Redirect, since users should never see an error page
optionB: Show a blank page, so no wrong content is displayed
optionC: Show NotFound, so the user learns the link was wrong
optionD: Redirect, since NotFound pages hurt app performance
correctAnswerText: Show NotFound, so the user learns the link was wrong
explanation: A silent redirect hides broken links and confuses people who expected a specific page. Say what happened and offer a way on.

prompt: The courses request on one page fails. Which handling is best?
optionA: Reload the whole app until the request eventually succeeds
optionB: Show a message and Retry inside the page, keeping the layout
optionC: Show an empty list, since there are no courses to display
optionD: Redirect to the 404 page, since the data could not be found
correctAnswerText: Show a message and Retry inside the page, keeping the layout
explanation: An error is neither "not found" nor "empty". Keeping navigation usable and offering a retry lets the user recover without losing their place.

prompt: A large admin section is used by a few staff, yet every student downloads its code. Is React.lazy on the admin routes worth it?
optionA: Yes, but only if every route in the app is lazy too
optionB: No; Vite already sends each route's code as it is needed
optionC: No; lazy loading only works with class components
optionD: Yes; split rarely used heavy routes out of the first load
correctAnswerText: Yes; split rarely used heavy routes out of the first load
explanation: Vite splits on dynamic import(). lazy(() => import("./Admin")) with Suspense keeps admin code out of the student bundle.

prompt: A search box writes ?q= to the URL on every keystroke. Users complain Back steps through each letter. What would you change?
optionA: Push one history entry per keystroke but hide them all
optionB: Update the query with replace, so typing adds no history
optionC: Move q into useState and drop it from the URL entirely
optionD: Disable the Back button on the search page while typing
correctAnswerText: Update the query with replace, so typing adds no history
explanation: setSearchParams({ q }, { replace: true }) keeps the URL shareable without flooding history; dropping it from the URL loses the shareable search.

prompt: Which Redux Toolkit function generates a reducer and its action creators from one definition?
optionA: makeReducer
optionB: createStore
optionC: createState
optionD: createSlice
correctAnswerText: createSlice
explanation: createSlice takes a name, initialState and reducers and returns slice.reducer plus slice.actions, one action creator per case.

prompt: Which Redux Toolkit function creates the store, with DevTools and thunk support built in?
optionA: configureStore
optionB: buildStore
optionC: createStore
optionD: initStore
correctAnswerText: configureStore
explanation: configureStore wraps the classic createStore and adds the thunk middleware, DevTools and development checks by default.

prompt: Which react-redux hook reads a value out of the Redux store inside a component?
optionA: useDispatch
optionB: useSelector
optionC: useReducer
optionD: useRedux
correctAnswerText: useSelector
explanation: useSelector(state => state.cart.items) subscribes the component to that piece of the store and returns it.

prompt: Which react-redux hook gives a component the function it uses to send actions?
optionA: useStore
optionB: useSelector
optionC: useAction
optionD: useDispatch
correctAnswerText: useDispatch
explanation: const dispatch = useDispatch(); dispatch(addItem(p)). Actions are the only way components ask the store to change.

prompt: In Redux, what is an action?
optionA: A promise that resolves to the next store state
optionB: A function that writes straight into the store
optionC: A plain object whose type describes what happened
optionD: A component that re-renders when the store changes
correctAnswerText: A plain object whose type describes what happened
explanation: For example { type: "cart/addItem", payload: product }. Reducers read it; nothing changes until a reducer handles it.

prompt: What is a Redux reducer?
optionA: A pure function from state and action to the next state
optionB: A hook that trims the store down to fewer fields
optionC: A middleware that merges several actions into one
optionD: A function that fetches data and stores the result
correctAnswerText: A pure function from state and action to the next state
explanation: Reducers compute the next state without side effects: no fetching, no random values, no changing anything outside themselves.

prompt: Which Redux Toolkit helper wraps an async request and dispatches pending, fulfilled and rejected actions?
optionA: createListener
optionB: createAsyncThunk
optionC: createSelector
optionD: createAction
correctAnswerText: createAsyncThunk
explanation: createAsyncThunk("courses/fetch", async () => …) dispatches the lifecycle actions for you, which slices handle in extraReducers.

prompt: What must wrap the React tree so that useSelector can reach the store?
optionA: <StoreContext> from @reduxjs/toolkit
optionB: <Provider store={store}> from react-redux
optionC: <BrowserRouter store={store}> at the root
optionD: <StrictMode store={store}> from react
correctAnswerText: <Provider store={store}> from react-redux
explanation: react-redux's Provider puts the store into context; without it the hooks throw because there is no store to find.

prompt: Which library lets createSlice reducers write state.count++ yet still produce immutable updates?
optionA: Axios
optionB: Reselect
optionC: Immer
optionD: Lodash
correctAnswerText: Immer
explanation: Immer hands the reducer a draft, records the changes made to it, and produces a new immutable state from them.

prompt: In Redux, what is a selector?
optionA: A middleware that chooses which reducer should run
optionB: An action that picks one item out of a list in state
optionC: A function that takes the state and returns part of it
optionD: A dropdown component wired up to the store's values
correctAnswerText: A function that takes the state and returns part of it
explanation: const selectCartCount = state => state.cart.items.length. Selectors keep components ignorant of the store's exact shape.

prompt: Why must a reducer have no side effects, such as calling an API?
optionA: Redux runs every reducer twice, so any API call would duplicate
optionB: Reducers run on a web worker that cannot open network sockets
optionC: Same input must give the same output, so state stays predictable
optionD: Side effects in a reducer are skipped by the production build
correctAnswerText: Same input must give the same output, so state stays predictable
explanation: Pure reducers can be tested, replayed in DevTools and reasoned about. Side effects belong in thunks or other middleware.

prompt: Why is state.items.push(item) acceptable inside a createSlice reducer?
optionA: The store re-reads every slice after each action anyway
optionB: Immer applies it to a draft and builds a new state from it
optionC: Redux Toolkit allows mutation now that React 18 is in use
optionD: push on a Redux array returns a fresh copy automatically
correctAnswerText: Immer applies it to a draft and builds a new state from it
explanation: The reducer receives a proxy. Immer turns the recorded changes into a new object tree, so the old state is untouched.

prompt: How does server state differ from client state?
optionA: Server state is a cached copy that can go stale; client state is not
optionB: Server state never changes after loading, unlike client state does
optionC: Server state is stored in cookies, and client state in Redux slices
optionD: Server state is only read by class components, client by functions
correctAnswerText: Server state is a cached copy that can go stale; client state is not
explanation: The courses list belongs to the backend and others can change it; a modal's open flag belongs to this browser alone. They need different tools.

prompt: Why is Context a poor carrier for a value that changes many times a second?
optionA: Context values are copied to disk on each change made
optionB: Context can only hold strings, so values are re-parsed
optionC: Every consumer re-renders on each change to the value
optionD: React throttles Context to one update every second
correctAnswerText: Every consumer re-renders on each change to the value
explanation: Context has no way to subscribe to part of its value. Redux's useSelector re-renders a component only when its selected slice changes.

prompt: What does dispatching a createAsyncThunk thunk cause to be dispatched?
optionA: one action per line of the async function
optionB: fulfilled only, once the promise resolves
optionC: pending only; the slice must fetch itself
optionD: pending first, then fulfilled or rejected
correctAnswerText: pending first, then fulfilled or rejected
explanation: The slice can set status to "loading" on pending, store the data on fulfilled and keep the error on rejected.

prompt: What is the order of events when a button in a Redux app changes shared state?
optionA: the store polls components for changes and merges what it finds
optionB: the component writes the store, then dispatches a notification
optionC: reducers run on click, then the component dispatches the result
optionD: dispatch an action, reducers compute state, subscribers re-render
correctAnswerText: dispatch an action, reducers compute state, subscribers re-render
explanation: Redux is a one-way loop: UI dispatches, reducers produce the next state, and components whose selected data changed re-render.

prompt: When the store changes, how does useSelector decide whether to re-render its component?
optionA: It re-renders on every action that reaches the store
optionB: It re-renders only if the action type names that slice
optionC: It re-runs the selector and compares the result with ===
optionD: It deep-compares the whole store with its old version
correctAnswerText: It re-runs the selector and compares the result with ===
explanation: A selector returning the same reference means no render; returning a new array or object each time means a render every time.

prompt: When is plain useState in one component the right home for a piece of state?
optionA: When the app is too small to install Redux at all
optionB: When the value must survive a full page refresh
optionC: When the value is a number rather than an object
optionD: When only that component, or its children, use it
correctAnswerText: When only that component, or its children, use it
explanation: State belongs as close as possible to where it is used. Lift it only when siblings need it; go global only when distant parts do.

prompt: What is a slice's extraReducers field for?
optionA: Defining extra action creators for other slices to use
optionB: Handling actions the slice did not define, like thunk results
optionC: Holding reducers that run again after every other one
optionD: Adding reducers that only run in a development build
correctAnswerText: Handling actions the slice did not define, like thunk results
explanation: reducers define the slice's own actions. extraReducers responds to actions created elsewhere, such as fetchCourses.fulfilled.

prompt: Why compute a cart total in a selector rather than keep a total field in the slice?
optionA: Selectors run on the server, so totals are more secure
optionB: A total field would be erased by Immer on every update
optionC: A stored total must be kept in step by hand and can drift
optionD: Slices are not allowed to contain any numeric fields
correctAnswerText: A stored total must be kept in step by hand and can drift
explanation: The items already determine the total. Store the minimum and derive the rest, so no reducer can forget to update it.

prompt: In a cart slice with initialState { items: [] }, which addItem reducer is correct?
optionA: addItem(state, action) { state.items.push(action.payload); }
optionB: addItem(state) { state.items.push(state.payload); }
optionC: addItem(state, action) { return state.items.push(action.payload); }
optionD: addItem(state, action) { state = { items: [action.payload] }; }
correctAnswerText: addItem(state, action) { state.items.push(action.payload); }
explanation: Mutate the draft and return nothing. Returning push's result returns a number; reassigning state only changes a local variable.

prompt: cartSlice exports addItem from slice.actions. How does an Add button add the product?
optionA: addItem(product)
optionB: dispatch(addItem, product)
optionC: store.cart.addItem(product)
optionD: dispatch(addItem(product))
correctAnswerText: dispatch(addItem(product))
explanation: addItem(product) only builds the action object; dispatch sends it to the store. Calling it without dispatch changes nothing.

prompt: The store is configured with reducer: { cart: cartReducer }. Which line gives the navbar the number of cart items?
optionA: useSelector(state => state.items.length)
optionB: useDispatch(state => state.cart.items.length)
optionC: useSelector(cartReducer.items.length)
optionD: useSelector(state => state.cart.items.length)
correctAnswerText: useSelector(state => state.cart.items.length)
explanation: The reducer map's keys become top-level state keys, so the cart lives at state.cart. A number is a primitive, so re-renders are cheap.

prompt: Set status to "loading" when fetchCourses starts. Which extraReducers entry does it?
optionA: builder.addCase("loading", state => { state.status = fetchCourses.pending; })
optionB: builder.addCase(fetchCourses.fulfilled, state => { state.status = "loading"; })
optionC: builder.addCase(fetchCourses.pending, state => { state.status = "loading"; })
optionD: builder.addCase(fetchCourses, state => { state.status = "loading"; })
correctAnswerText: builder.addCase(fetchCourses.pending, state => { state.status = "loading"; })
explanation: Each lifecycle action is a property of the thunk: .pending, .fulfilled, .rejected. fulfilled fires at the end, not the start.

prompt: Build a store holding the cart and auth slices under state.cart and state.auth.
optionA: configureStore({ reducer: { cart: cartReducer, auth: authReducer } })
optionB: configureStore({ reducer: [cartReducer, authReducer] })
optionC: configureStore({ reducers: { cart: cartReducer, auth: authReducer } })
optionD: configureStore({ reducer: combine(cartReducer, authReducer) })
correctAnswerText: configureStore({ reducer: { cart: cartReducer, auth: authReducer } })
explanation: An object under reducer is combined automatically, and its keys name the state branches. An array gives no names to select by.

prompt: A light/dark theme is read by components all over the app and changes only when the user flips a switch. Where should it live?
optionA: A Redux slice with its own async thunk
optionB: Local state in every component that uses it
optionC: A React Context provided near the app root
optionD: A module variable each component imports
correctAnswerText: A React Context provided near the app root
explanation: Widely read and rarely changed is exactly what Context suits. A module variable would not re-render anything when it changes.

prompt: A "confirm delete" dialog is opened and closed by one CourseRow and nothing else cares. Where does isOpen belong?
optionA: A Context at the app root
optionB: The URL's query string
optionC: useState inside CourseRow
optionD: A global ui slice in Redux
correctAnswerText: useState inside CourseRow
explanation: One component uses it, so it lives there. Putting it in a store makes every row share one flag and adds code for nothing.

prompt: Which thunk loads courses with axios so that fulfilled carries the course array?
optionA: createAsyncThunk("courses/fetch", () => { axios.get("/api/courses"); })
optionB: createAsyncThunk("courses/fetch", async () => (await axios.get("/api/courses")).data)
optionC: createAsyncThunk(async () => (await axios.get("/api/courses")).data)
optionD: createSlice("courses/fetch", async () => (await axios.get("/api/courses")).data)
correctAnswerText: createAsyncThunk("courses/fetch", async () => (await axios.get("/api/courses")).data)
explanation: The type prefix comes first, and whatever the payload creator returns becomes action.payload. Not returning the promise gives undefined.

prompt: On logout the cart slice must go back to its initialState. Which reducer does that?
optionA: clearCart: () => initialState
optionB: clearCart: (state) => { state = initialState; }
optionC: clearCart: (state) => { delete state.items; }
optionD: clearCart: (state) => { state.items.length; }
correctAnswerText: clearCart: () => initialState
explanation: Returning a value replaces the state outright. Assigning to the state parameter only rebinds a local name, so nothing changes.

prompt: On one page, CourseList and CoursePreview both need selectedCourseId. Nothing else in the app uses it. Where should it live?
optionA: In localStorage, read by both of the components
optionB: In their shared parent page, passed down as props
optionC: In a new Redux slice for the selected course id
optionD: In CourseList, with CoursePreview importing it
correctAnswerText: In their shared parent page, passed down as props
explanation: Lifting to the nearest common parent solves sibling sharing with no new machinery. A store is for state many distant parts need.

optionA: action.payload is undefined inside createSlice reducers
optionB: push cannot be called on an array that lives in a slice
optionC: Reducers in createSlice must be declared as arrow functions
optionD: It edits the draft and returns a value, which Immer rejects
correctAnswerText: It edits the draft and returns a value, which Immer rejects
explanation: Immer allows either mutating the draft or returning new state, not both. Here the return value is push's new length. Drop the return.

optionA: It returns the same mutated object, so React sees no change
optionB: A switch statement cannot be used inside a reducer function
optionC: useReducer requires every case to call dispatch once more
optionD: useReducer ignores any action that carries an item field
correctAnswerText: It returns the same mutated object, so React sees no change
explanation: There is no Immer here. Return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] } so the reference changes.

prompt: A list re-renders on every action in the app, even unrelated ones. Its selector is state => state.courses.list.filter(c => c.active). Why?
optionA: filter returns a new array every time, so === always fails
optionB: useSelector re-renders whenever any part of the store updates
optionC: filter mutates the list, which forces Redux to notify all
optionD: The selector ought to read state.courses rather than .list
correctAnswerText: filter returns a new array every time, so === always fails
explanation: useSelector compares results by reference. Memoise with createSelector so the same input returns the same array.

optionA: createAsyncThunk ignores errors that occur inside a try block
optionB: Catching and returning makes the thunk resolve, so it is fulfilled
optionC: Returning null from a thunk always skips the pending action too
optionD: The rejected case only runs for 404 responses, not network errors
correctAnswerText: Catching and returning makes the thunk resolve, so it is fulfilled
explanation: A thunk is rejected only if its promise rejects. Rethrow, or return rejectWithValue(message) so the slice gets the error.

prompt: An exam timer stores secondsLeft in an AppContext that also carries user and settings. The whole exam page stutters every second. Why?
optionA: The timer's interval is slower inside a Provider
optionB: user and settings are refetched on each value change
optionC: Every AppContext consumer re-renders on each tick
optionD: Context timers run on the main thread, unlike state
correctAnswerText: Every AppContext consumer re-renders on each tick
explanation: Any change to the context value re-renders all its readers. Keep the ticking value local to the timer, or in its own context.

prompt: In development, the console warns "A non-serializable value was detected in an action" after dispatch(setDeadline(new Date())). What should change?
optionA: Store a string or timestamp instead of the Date object
optionB: Turn off DevTools, which is what raises the warning
optionC: Wrap the Date in an array so Redux will accept it
optionD: Move the dispatch call into a useEffect with no deps
correctAnswerText: Store a string or timestamp instead of the Date object
explanation: Redux Toolkit checks that state and actions are plain data so DevTools and persistence work. Use date.toISOString() or getTime().

prompt: Courses are fetched into a slice once at login. A mentor adds a course, but students see it only after logging out and in. What is the underlying problem?
optionA: The thunk ran before the mentor's course was published
optionB: Immer froze the courses array, so nothing could be added
optionC: Server data is cached in Redux with no refetch or expiry
optionD: Redux cannot store arrays longer than its initial value
correctAnswerText: Server data is cached in Redux with no refetch or expiry
explanation: Server state goes stale. It needs refetching on focus, on navigation or after edits — which server-state tools such as RTK Query do for you.

prompt: onClick={() => dispatch(clearCart)} does nothing and no clearCart action appears in DevTools. Why?
optionA: Actions without a payload are dropped by the store
optionB: dispatch is not available inside an arrow function
optionC: clearCart can only be dispatched from inside a thunk
optionD: It dispatches the creator itself instead of calling it
correctAnswerText: It dispatches the creator itself instead of calling it
explanation: The thunk middleware treats a dispatched function as a thunk and calls it; it builds an action object that is never dispatched. Use dispatch(clearCart()).

prompt: The cart slice keeps items and total. addItem updates both; removeItem only removes the item. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
optionA: Immer recomputes total itself, so nothing goes wrong
optionB: removeItem throws, since total must change in every case
optionC: total drifts after a removal; derive it with a selector
optionD: addItem double-counts; total should be updated in a thunk
correctAnswerText: total drifts after a removal; derive it with a selector
explanation: A stored derived value is only right if every reducer remembers it. Computing it from items cannot fall out of step.

prompt: const cart = useSelector(s => s.cart); cart.items.push(p); throws "Cannot add property 1, object is not extensible". Why?
optionA: useSelector returns a string copy of the requested state
optionB: The items array is full and must be resized before push
optionC: push only works inside useEffect, not in event handlers
optionD: Store state is frozen; changes must go through a dispatch
correctAnswerText: Store state is frozen; changes must go through a dispatch
explanation: Redux Toolkit (via Immer) freezes the state it produces, so outside mutation fails loudly. Dispatch addItem(p) instead.

prompt: A five-page portfolio app has a contact form and lists fetched from an API, and no state shared across pages. Add Redux Toolkit?
optionA: Yes; every React app should start with a global store
optionB: No; Redux Toolkit cannot be used with a Vite project
optionC: No; local state and per-page fetching are simpler here
optionD: Yes; without Redux the fetched lists cannot be shown
correctAnswerText: No; local state and per-page fetching are simpler here
explanation: A store pays for itself when many distant components share changing state. With none, it is ceremony with no benefit.

prompt: Most of an app's "state" is API data with loading flags, refetching and cache invalidation written by hand in thunks. What is the better direction?
optionA: A server-state tool such as RTK Query that handles caching
optionB: Context in place of Redux for all of the fetched API data
optionC: localStorage as the main cache, read on every page load
optionD: More thunks, one per screen, to keep each request separate
correctAnswerText: A server-state tool such as RTK Query that handles caching
explanation: Caching, deduplication, refetching and invalidation are the hard parts of server state. Tools built for it remove that hand-written code.

prompt: A student puts every keystroke of a single enquiry form into Redux "so all state is in one place". Good idea?
optionA: No; Redux cannot hold strings typed by the user
optionB: Yes; a single store is always easier to debug than none
optionC: Yes; React forms cannot work without a global store
optionD: No; keep it local and dispatch only the submitted result
correctAnswerText: No; keep it local and dispatch only the submitted result
explanation: Draft input matters to one form only. Global keystrokes add actions, re-render subscribers and couple the form to the store.

prompt: An app with no other global state needs the signed-in user in the navbar, profile and a few guards. Context or Redux?
optionA: Neither; fetch the user again in each component
optionB: Redux; Context cannot hold an object like a user
optionC: Redux; user data must always live inside a store
optionD: Context; it is read widely but changes very rarely
correctAnswerText: Context; it is read widely but changes very rarely
explanation: Rarely changing, widely read data is Context's sweet spot. Adding Redux for one value is cost without benefit.

prompt: The same lesson object appears inside several courses in the store, and editing it means finding every copy. What structure is better?
optionA: Keep a single array of courses and drop the lesson objects
optionB: Store each course as a JSON string and parse when needed
optionC: Normalise: lessons by id, with courses holding lesson ids
optionD: Keep nesting, and update each copy with a loop in a thunk
correctAnswerText: Normalise: lessons by id, with courses holding lesson ids
explanation: One copy per entity, referenced by id, makes an update a single write. createEntityAdapter in Redux Toolkit provides this shape.

prompt: All app state sits in one appSlice with forty reducers. How should it be organised?
optionA: Leave it; one slice makes every action easy to find
optionB: Into one slice per reducer, forty files in total
optionC: Into separate stores, one store for every feature
optionD: Into feature slices, such as cart, auth and courses
correctAnswerText: Into feature slices, such as cart, auth and courses
explanation: Slices by feature keep related state and reducers together and let each feature own its piece; one store is still the norm.

prompt: Should a slice store filteredCourses alongside courses and filter, or compute it?
optionA: Store it, since filtering on every render is too expensive
optionB: Compute it inside each component with a fresh filter call
optionC: Store it, and recompute it in each reducer that changes data
optionD: Compute it with a memoised selector from courses and filter
correctAnswerText: Compute it with a memoised selector from courses and filter
explanation: createSelector recomputes only when its inputs change, so it is both cheap and always correct. A stored copy can go stale.

prompt: A slice tracks fetched courses with only isLoading: boolean. Why is a status field ("idle" | "loading" | "succeeded" | "failed") plus error better?
optionA: isLoading is reset by Immer each time an action arrives
optionB: Booleans cannot be stored in a Redux Toolkit slice at all
optionC: A status string makes the fetch itself complete sooner
optionD: It tells "not started" and "failed" apart, which UI needs
correctAnswerText: It tells "not started" and "failed" apart, which UI needs
explanation: With only a boolean, "never fetched", "finished" and "failed" all look like false. Distinct states let the page decide what to show.

prompt: A teammate wants to save the entire Redux store to localStorage after every action. Your judgement?
optionA: Persist only what must survive reload, such as the cart
optionB: Fine, but only if the store is written as JSON strings
optionC: Never persist any state; reload must always start empty
optionD: Fine; persisting everything means nothing is ever lost
correctAnswerText: Persist only what must survive reload, such as the cart
explanation: Persisted server data goes stale, tokens there are readable by any script, and writes on every action cost time. Choose what to keep.

prompt: A team updates deeply nested state in a hand-written reducer with four levels of spreads, and bugs keep appearing. Best judgement?
optionA: Use createSlice (Immer) or flatten the state; deep spreads breed bugs
optionB: Deep-clone the whole state with JSON on every single action
optionC: Switch to mutating state directly, since React will notice
optionD: Keep the spreads; Immer is far slower than spreads, so avoid it here
correctAnswerText: Use createSlice (Immer) or flatten the state; deep spreads breed bugs
explanation: Each nested level must be copied by hand, and one missed level is a silent mutation. Immer drafts or a flatter shape remove that risk.

prompt: In a typical chat-style model API, what does your code send to get a reply?
optionA: A single SQL query and the database name
optionB: A file path the model will read from disk
optionC: A list of role-tagged messages plus settings
optionD: A compiled program for the model to run
correctAnswerText: A list of role-tagged messages plus settings
explanation: Chat APIs take an ordered list of messages, each tagged with a role, plus settings such as temperature and a token cap.

prompt: Which message role usually carries the application's standing instructions to the model?
optionA: The user message
optionB: The tool result message
optionC: The system message
optionD: The assistant message
correctAnswerText: The system message
explanation: The system message holds the app's rules and persona; user messages carry what the person typed, assistant messages the model's earlier replies.

prompt: What does the temperature setting of a model call mainly control?
optionA: How long the model may take to reply
optionB: How many tokens the reply may contain
optionC: How random the choice of next token is
optionD: How much each call costs to make
correctAnswerText: How random the choice of next token is
explanation: Temperature reshapes the probabilities the model samples from: low is steadier and repeatable, high is more varied. Length is a separate cap.

prompt: What is a token, in the sense a language model uses the word?
optionA: A secret string proving who you are
optionB: A single complete sentence of input
optionC: Exactly one character of the input
optionD: A chunk of text, often part of a word
correctAnswerText: A chunk of text, often part of a word
explanation: Models read and write tokens — pieces of text that are often sub-words. Limits, cost and speed are all counted in them.

prompt: What is a model's context window?
optionA: The part of the screen where replies show
optionB: The time a session stays open on the server
optionC: The number of users it can serve at once
optionD: The most tokens it can handle in one call
correctAnswerText: The most tokens it can handle in one call
explanation: The context window is the token budget for one call: instructions, history, retrieved text and, in most APIs, the reply all share it.

prompt: What does streaming a model response mean?
optionA: Running several models at the same moment
optionB: Saving every reply to a log for later review
optionC: Sending the prompt split across many calls
optionD: Receiving the reply in pieces as it is made
correctAnswerText: Receiving the reply in pieces as it is made
explanation: With streaming the provider sends tokens as they are generated, so the client can render text before the whole reply is finished.

prompt: Where should the API key for a model provider live in a web application?
optionA: On the server, read from config or a vault
optionB: In the browser code so calls go out directly
optionC: In local storage after the user logs in
optionD: In the HTML page as a hidden form field
correctAnswerText: On the server, read from config or a vault
explanation: Anything shipped to a browser can be read by its user. The key stays server-side and the browser calls your own backend.

prompt: What is a hallucination in a language model's output?
optionA: A reply written in the wrong human language
optionB: Fluent text stated as fact that is not true
optionC: An error code returned by the provider API
optionD: A reply that is cut off at the token limit
correctAnswerText: Fluent text stated as fact that is not true
explanation: A hallucination is confident, well-formed text that is false or unsupported. It reads exactly like a correct answer, which is the danger.

prompt: In an LLM-backed app, what does the term prompt injection describe?
optionA: Input that tries to override the app's instructions
optionB: Adding examples to a prompt to guide the format
optionC: Inserting variables into a prompt template
optionD: Sending the same prompt twice for reliability
correctAnswerText: Input that tries to override the app's instructions
explanation: Prompt injection is text — typed by a user or hidden in data — written to make the model ignore its instructions and do something else.

prompt: What is an evaluation set for an LLM feature?
optionA: Fixed inputs with expected outcomes to score it
optionB: The log of every live request users have sent
optionC: The list of models a provider currently offers
optionD: The settings file holding temperature and caps
correctAnswerText: Fixed inputs with expected outcomes to score it
explanation: An eval set is a stable collection of inputs with known good outcomes, so a prompt or model change can be scored rather than eyeballed.

prompt: Why do apps that extract fields from invoices usually set temperature low?
optionA: A low temperature lets the prompt be much longer
optionB: A low temperature guarantees no hallucinations
optionC: A low temperature makes the model read faster
optionD: They want the same input to give a steady answer
correctAnswerText: They want the same input to give a steady answer
explanation: Extraction wants repeatable output, which low temperature gives. It does not make the model faster or truthful — wrong fields can still come back steadily.

prompt: Why does a long chat history make each new call slower and more costly?
optionA: The provider charges more for returning customers
optionB: The model must retrain itself on the earlier turns
optionC: The whole history is sent and counted as input again
optionD: Older messages are stored in a slower database
correctAnswerText: The whole history is sent and counted as input again
explanation: The model is stateless between calls; the app resends prior turns each time, so input tokens grow with the conversation.

prompt: Why validate a model's JSON output even when the prompt asks for JSON?
optionA: The provider requires a schema check on every call
optionB: JSON from a model always uses a different encoding
optionC: The model can still return malformed or wrong fields
optionD: Validation makes the model reply in fewer tokens
correctAnswerText: The model can still return malformed or wrong fields
explanation: A prompt is a request, not a guarantee. Replies can be truncated, wrapped in prose, or carry fields with the wrong type or value.

prompt: Why must a model API key never be shipped inside a React bundle?
optionA: The bundle becomes too large for a browser to load
optionB: React refuses to make calls to outside domains
optionC: Anyone can read it from the bundle and spend on it
optionD: The key expires as soon as it reaches a browser
correctAnswerText: Anyone can read it from the bundle and spend on it
explanation: Build-time env vars are inlined into the JavaScript users download. Whoever opens dev tools can copy the key and run up your bill.

prompt: Why does a model sometimes give a confident but wrong answer?
optionA: Its temperature setting was exactly zero
optionB: Its context window was left mostly empty
optionC: It copies the answer from another user's chat
optionD: It predicts likely text rather than checked facts
